# Kirana documentation

Every page, in reading order. Generated from the same source as https://kirana.style/docs.

---
# Introduction
Source: https://kirana.style/docs
# Introduction

Kirana compiles the styles you write next to your components into a plain CSS file.
There is no style engine in the browser, no class-name soup to decode, and no
guessing about which rule wins: the compiler decides at build time, and tells you
when it cannot.

## Start here

The docs have five parts: learn the model, set up your framework, move an
existing project, look something up, or see where the project stands.

- **Documentation**: The model, writing styles, tokens and configuration. [Quick start](/docs/start/quick-start), [How it works](/docs/start/how-it-works), [Mental model](/docs/start/mental-model)
- **Frameworks**: An install guide for every framework and bundler, each built on every change. [Vue](/docs/frameworks/vue), [Next.js](/docs/frameworks/nextjs), [TanStack Start](/docs/frameworks/tanstack-start)
- **Guides**: Moving from Tailwind or StyleX, and building larger systems. [From Tailwind](/docs/migration/from-tailwind), [From StyleX](/docs/migration/from-stylex), [A design system](/docs/building/design-system)
- **Reference**: The API, the command line, and every diagnostic with its code. [API](/docs/reference/api), [CLI](/docs/tooling/cli), [Diagnostics](/docs/tooling/diagnostics)
- **Project**: Where Kirana stands, what comes next, and how to help. [Status](/docs/project/status), [Roadmap](/docs/project/roadmap), [Contributing](/docs/project/contributing)

## A first look

A card, as you would write it, and what the compiler in this repository made of
it when this site was built. Nothing under CSS or Classes is written by hand:

<!-- ::example name="compile-card" -->

Each declaration became one class, and the `sx` prop became `className`. Nothing
of Kirana is left at runtime.

## Works with your framework

React, Next.js, React Router, TanStack Start, Gatsby, Remix, Waku, Vike, Docusaurus, Preact, Solid, SolidStart, Vue, Nuxt, VitePress, Svelte, SvelteKit, Astro, Qwik, Angular, Ember and Meteor; server templates in Laravel, Symfony, Rails, Phoenix and AdonisJS; or no
framework at all, on Vite, Rolldown, webpack, Rspack, Rsbuild, Parcel, Bun and esbuild, or Angular's CLI. Each has a complete
install guide, and each is built and checked in a browser on every change:
**[pick yours](/docs/frameworks/overview)**.

## What it gives you

- **Typed styles.** Ordinary objects, checked by TypeScript, with camelCase CSS
  property names and real values, not a string vocabulary you have to learn.
- **Conditions inside values.** `{ base: x, ":hover": y }` reads in the order it
  applies, instead of scattering `hover:` prefixes across a class list.
- **Predictable precedence.** A stated ladder decides which value wins, and the
  `ambiguous-precedence` diagnostic tells you when two values could both apply.
- **Tokens and themes.** Design tokens compile to constants or custom properties,
  and every colour can be a `light-dark()` pair, so dark mode needs no variant.
- **Real diagnostics.** 50 checks with codes, severities and help text, from
  unknown properties to a component that forgets to pass `sx` on.

## What it is not

Kirana is not a utility-class framework, and it does not generate CSS in the
browser. It does not try to style markup you do not render: the compiler works on
the source it can see.

> [!NOTE] Before 1.0
> Kirana is on npm and follows semantic versioning: before 1.0, a minor version
> may change the API, and its release notes say how to move. Every page tells you
> what works today.
---
# Why Kirana
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/start/why-kirana
# Why Kirana

"CSS-in-JS" means two different things, and most of the dislike is for the
first one. This page separates them, says what Kirana is, what it answers that
StyleX left open, and where it costs you something.

## The CSS-in-JS people left

The first generation (styled-components, Emotion and their relatives) kept
styles in JavaScript and turned them into CSS **in the browser, while
rendering**. Every component that rendered serialised its styles, hashed them
and inserted a `<style>` rule. That had costs that no amount of tuning removed:

- **Work on every render.** Styles were computed at runtime, so pages started
  slower and got slower as the number of components grew.
- **A library in every bundle.** The runtime that did that work shipped to every
  user.
- **Server rendering got harder.** Styles had to be collected during the render
  and serialised into the HTML.
- **The browser recalculated styles more often.** React's own documentation
  lists two problems with runtime `<style>` injection: it "forces the browser to
  recalculate the styles a lot more often", and it "can be very slow if it
  happens at the wrong time in the React lifecycle". It recommends
  [static extraction to CSS files, plus inline styles for dynamic values](https://react.dev/reference/react/useInsertionEffect),
  and says the first of those two problems "is not solvable" for runtime
  injection.

GitHub's Primer is the public example. Starting with Primer React v37 it moved
its components from styled-components to CSS Modules, finished that by December
2024, and reports **55 % less time to server-render a page and 25 % less time for
the components on a page to initialise**
([GitHub Engineering, 2026](https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/improving-site-performance-by-shipping-more-css/)).
Its stated reasons were exactly the list above: styles initialised on the client,
server rendering slowed by style collection, and style updates that "grew out of
control as component count grew".

That is a verdict on **runtime** CSS-in-JS. It is not a verdict on writing styles
next to components.

## What a compiler changes

A compiled system reads the same style objects **at build time** and writes a
plain stylesheet. Nothing about styling happens in the browser except applying
class names. Kirana is this kind, and it is exactly what the React team
recommends: static CSS files for static styles, and a custom property in
`style` for a value only known at runtime.

| The complaint                       | Runtime CSS-in-JS         | Kirana                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Styles are computed while rendering | Yes                       | No. Styles become CSS during the build                                                                                                                                             |
| A styling runtime in the bundle     | Yes, the whole library    | A module with only static styles imports nothing; merging and bridging need a helper under 1.1 kB gzipped                                                           |
| Server rendering collects styles    | Yes                       | No. The stylesheet is a file, linked like any other                                                                                                                                |
| `<style>` tags inserted at runtime  | Yes                       | Never. The runtime [never generates CSS](/docs/styling/dynamic)                                                                                                                    |
| CSS grows with markup               | Often, one rule per usage | [Atomic](/docs/building/output): one rule per distinct declaration, shared by every element that uses it                                                                           |
| Class names you cannot read         | Hashed                    | Hashed too, but `kirana-style trace file:line property` prints every entry for a style and the one that wins, and [hovering it in the editor](/docs/tooling/editor) shows the same |
| Order bugs between style sheets     | Insertion order decided   | One [precedence ladder](/docs/styling/precedence), in [layers](/docs/config/layers)                                                                                                |

What you keep from CSS-in-JS is the part people liked: styles are values, next to
the component, typed, passed as props, and deleted with the component.

## You can see the CSS again

Runtime cost was one reason teams left CSS-in-JS. The other was reading. A
Tailwind class list _is_ the CSS, written on the element: `grid gap-4 p-4
md:p-6` tells you what the `<article>` gets without leaving the line. A style
object moves that into a constant somewhere else, and reading a component turns
into jumping to `styles.card` and back.

Kirana's [language server](/docs/tooling/editor) gives the class list back,
without putting it in your markup:

- **At the end of every element's line**, what it ends up with, in a class list's
  words and coloured by kind: `▦ grid · gap 1rem · p 1rem · md: p 1.5rem`. Values
  under a guard lead with it (`featured: shadow lg`).
- **On hover**, a card: the box model drawn as DevTools draws it, every
  declaration with `rem` in pixels and the token it reads, and the compiled rule.
  On one property, every entry in precedence order and the step that decided.
- **In VS Code**, a Style Inspector that follows the cursor and turns `:hover` or
  `md` on to show what applies then, and Style Fold, which reads a long object as
  its summary until you edit it, like Tailwind Fold, for objects.

It works in `.tsx`, `.vue`, `.svelte` and `.astro` files and Angular templates, in VS Code, Zed,
Neovim and Helix. It answers from the compiler session the build uses, so the
editor and the stylesheet never disagree.

So the trade is no longer readability for types. You keep what made object
styles worth it (a typo is a compile error, a token is a typed import, a style is
a value you pass and delete with its component), and the output is still atomic:
one rule per distinct declaration, shared by every element that uses it. On the
same three applications built three ways, Kirana 0.3.4's cold
builds are 5 % faster than Tailwind and 1.7× faster than StyleX (SWC), and its
CSS and JavaScript, gzipped, are 2 % smaller than StyleX (SWC) and
2 % smaller than Tailwind. Every measure, with its confidence interval, is on the
[benchmarks page](/docs/project/benchmarks).

## What StyleX got right, and what Kirana adds

StyleX, which Meta open-sourced at the end of 2023, showed that compiled, atomic
CSS-in-JS works at scale. Kirana keeps its premise: atomic output, constants
that cost nothing until used, styles as values passed through one prop, and
`light-dark()` colours.

The same shadcn/ui app, ported from Tailwind to StyleX (0.19) for comparison,
shows these problems, each measured and written down with evidence. Kirana
answers them:

| In the StyleX port                                                                                                                              | In Kirana                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| No descendant selectors: every `[&_svg]` became a custom property handed down and read by the child                                             | [`select.child` / `select.descendant`](/docs/styling/contextual), in a layer below the target's own styles, so the child's own size still wins                                                       |
| A marker on the wrong element compiled and never matched, 36 times                                                                              | [Relations](/docs/styling/relations) are declared; a read without an anchor, or an anchor that cannot match, is a compile error                                                                      |
| A shorthand lost to a longhand regardless of order (`padding: 0` did not beat `paddingTop`)                                                     | Styles [merge per longhand](/docs/styling/merging)                                                                                                                                                   |
| `default: null` removed a value where the author meant "nothing here"                                                                           | Omitting keeps; `base: null` removes, and only when you write it                                                                                                                                     |
| `@media` outranked `:hover` and attributes, the reverse of Tailwind                                                                             | One ladder, stated and [traceable](/docs/tooling/debugging): state beats breakpoint, as in Tailwind                                                                                                  |
| Custom-property assignments were emitted unlayered and beat conditions beside them                                                              | Nothing is emitted outside a layer                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Tokens had to live in `*.stylex.ts` files and be imported by name                                                                               | Tokens are ordinary exports, imported any way TypeScript allows                                                                                                                                      |
| `sx` passed to a component that ignores it, or spread past a wrapper, was silent                                                                | `sx-on-external-component` and `unused-sx`, including one module away                                                                                                                                |
| Six silent bug classes needed a hand-written checking script; the lint plugin lagged the compiler and was turned off after ~150 false positives | [50 diagnostics](/docs/tooling/diagnostics) come from the compiler itself; the [lint plugin](/docs/tooling/lint) reads the compiler's own validation instead of re-implementing it |
| The official compiler is Babel; the Rust one is a community port behind it                                                                      | The engine is Kirana's own, in Rust on [oxc](https://oxc.rs), with a WASI build that writes the same bytes where no native one runs                                                                  |
| No utility vocabulary: a Tailwind team rebuilt the scales by hand                                                                               | [`@kirana-style/preset-scales`](/docs/tokens/preset-scales) is Tailwind v4's scales, and [utility strings](/docs/styling/utilities) compile to the same atoms as the object form                     |
| A port from Tailwind was done by hand                                                                                                           | [`kirana-style migrate tailwind`](/docs/migration/from-tailwind), measured below                                                                                                                     |

Framework reach is the other half: `sx` works in React, Preact, Solid, Qwik, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Angular and Ember (Angular
templates take it as a directive, Ember's as a helper), and Kirana has adapters
for Vite, Rolldown, webpack, Rspack, Rsbuild, Parcel, Bun and esbuild, with Next.js on Turbopack or webpack. See
[frameworks](/docs/frameworks/overview).

StyleX has things Kirana does not: it is published, used in production at Meta
and elsewhere, and has a community. [Migrating from StyleX](/docs/migration/from-stylex)
is honest about that.

## Why not Tailwind and `cn()`?

Tailwind is excellent, and Kirana borrows its vocabulary on purpose. What Kirana
replaces is the merging. A component library built on Tailwind lets callers
override styles by appending classes, and resolves conflicts at runtime with
tailwind-merge (`cn()`), which parses class strings in the browser and keeps the
last class of each conflict group. Measured with tailwind-merge 3.6.0:

| Call                                  | Result                  | What happened                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `twMerge("px-2 py-1", "p-3")`         | `p-3`                   | Correct: the later padding replaces both axes                                                           |
| `twMerge("text-sm", "text-[0.8rem]")` | `text-[0.8rem]`         | `text-sm` is deleted whole, so its paired **line height** goes too, and the element now inherits one    |
| `twMerge("shadow-sm", "shadow-glow")` | `shadow-sm shadow-glow` | A custom value it was not told about is not a conflict; CSS source order decides which shadow shows     |
| `twMerge("text-sm", "text-brand")`    | `text-sm text-brand`    | It cannot know whether `text-brand` is a size or a colour without configuration (`extendTailwindMerge`) |

None of these is a bug in tailwind-merge; it works from class names, because
class names are all it has. Kirana merges **declarations**, at build time, per
longhand: `fontSize` and `lineHeight` are separate entries, a custom token is a
typed value, and there is nothing to configure or parse at runtime. And a typo
(`text-smm`) is a compile error, not a class that silently does nothing.

## "It doubles the code"

It is the most common first reaction, and it is true in one sense: a style object
takes more **lines** than a class string. It does not contain more **meaning**.

```tsx
// Tailwind: one line, read left to right
<button className="inline-flex items-center gap-2 rounded-md px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium hover:bg-accent disabled:opacity-50" />

// Kirana: the same declarations, one per line
const button = css({
  display: "inline-flex",
  alignItems: "center",
  gap: space[2],
  borderRadius: radius.md,
  paddingInline: space[4],
  paddingBlock: space[2],
  fontSize: fontSize.sm,
  lineHeight: lineHeight.sm,
  fontWeight: fontWeight.medium,
  backgroundColor: { ":hover": theme.accent },
  opacity: { ":disabled": 0.5 },
})
```

Tailwind is **horizontal**; Kirana is **vertical**. The vertical form earns its
lines:

- **Diffs and reviews show one change per line.** Changing the padding changes
  one line, not a 120-character string where the reviewer hunts for `px-4`.
- **Conditions group by property.** Everything that can happen to the background
  colour is in one place; in a class string, its `bg-` utilities and their
  `hover:`, `dark:` and `data-[state=open]:` forms can sit anywhere in the line.
- **Nothing is implicit.** `text-sm` sets two properties; the object says so.
  The single most common drift in our port was a font size without its line
  height.
- **Every key and value is typed.** Autocompletion, go-to-definition on tokens,
  rename, and errors before the build.
- **Styles have names.** `styles.header` says what it is for; the markup stays
  readable because the styling is not inline in it.
- **Comments fit.** A line can say why a value is what it is.

And you do not have to choose one form for a whole project. With the scales
preset, `sx="px-4 py-2 text-sm"` is valid Kirana and compiles to the same atoms as
the object. Use strings where a short line reads best and objects where a
component has states. The compiler also does not care how long your source is:
the output is atomic either way, and a declaration used in a hundred components
is still one rule.

## Where Kirana costs you something

- **It is before 1.0.** A minor version may still change the API, and its
  release notes say how to move; see [what works today](/docs/project/status).
- **It is a compiler.** Styles must be statically known in shape: a computed key
  or a spread object is an error, and a value the compiler cannot enumerate goes
  through a custom property.
- **It is stricter than CSS.** Contextual rules rank below the target's own
  styles, and two conditions that tie are reported instead of left to source
  order. That is what makes the result predictable, and it is why a migration
  from Tailwind needs a few hand fixes (the [migration guide](/docs/migration/from-tailwind)
  lists every one we met).
- **The richest editor is VS Code.** Every LSP editor gets the card, the hints
  and the fixes; the Style Inspector, Style Fold and coloured hints are VS
  Code's. The VS Code extension is on the Marketplace and Open VSX; Zed's
  installs as a dev extension until it is in Zed's registry.
---
# Quick start
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/start/quick-start
# Quick start

Pick your framework. The steps below are read from its guide, so they always match it.

```bash
```

Or let the command line set it up. In your project's root:

```console
$ npx kirana-style@latest init
$ npx kirana-style doctor
```

`kirana-style init` recognises the framework, the bundler and the package manager, and shows every change
it would make as a diff; nothing is written until you say yes. `kirana-style doctor` then checks the
engine, the installed versions and the wiring. [Installation](/docs/start/installation) has the
same first run for pnpm, Yarn and Bun.

## Where to go next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Mental model](/docs/start/mental-model): the five ideas that make the rest predictable.
- [Every framework guide](/docs/frameworks/overview), with what `sx` compiles to in each.

# Installation
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/start/installation
# Installation

## Let `kirana-style init` do it

In your project's root, through your package manager's runner. It fetches the
command for this one run, the way `npx shadcn@latest` does, and writes nothing
until you say yes:

```bash
# npm
npx kirana-style@latest init
# pnpm
pnpm dlx kirana-style@latest init
# yarn
yarn dlx kirana-style@latest init
# bun
bunx --bun kirana-style@latest init
# deno
deno run -A npm:kirana-style@latest init
```

> [!NOTE] Right after a release
> Yarn and Deno hold back a version for its first 24 hours on npm, a guard against
> supply-chain attacks, and install the one before it meanwhile. To take a new
> release on its first day, pass Deno `--minimum-dependency-age=0`, or set Yarn's
> `npmMinimalAgeGate` lower.

It reads `package.json` and your lockfile, recognises the framework, bundler and
package manager, and shows every change it would make as a diff: the configuration
file, the adapter in your bundler's configuration, the stylesheet and the `sx`
types. Nothing is written until you say yes, and the install command is
printed for you to run (or pass `--install`). Then:

```bash
# npm
npx kirana-style doctor
# pnpm
pnpm exec kirana-style doctor
# yarn
yarn kirana-style doctor
# bun
bunx kirana-style doctor
# deno
deno run -A npm:kirana-style doctor
```

checks the engine, the installed versions, the configuration and the wiring, and
says what is missing. Both are described in [the CLI](/docs/tooling/cli#kirana-style-init).

`init` adds `kirana-style` to your dev dependencies, so every later command runs
the version your project pins: `npx kirana-style check`, `npx kirana-style build`
and the rest. [A shorter name](/docs/tooling/cli#a-shorter-name) is one script away.

## Pick your framework

Each guide takes you from an empty project to a styled component, and names the
example that CI builds and checks in a browser on every change.

Frameworks:

- [React](/docs/frameworks/react): The library for web and native user interfaces, on Vite.
- [Next.js](/docs/frameworks/nextjs): The React framework, with server components, on Turbopack.
- [React Router](/docs/frameworks/react-router): A standards-focused router and framework you can deploy anywhere.
- [TanStack Start](/docs/frameworks/tanstack-start): Full-stack React powered by TanStack Router. This site runs on it.
- [Gatsby](/docs/frameworks/gatsby): Static sites with React and GraphQL, built by webpack.
- [Remix](/docs/frameworks/remix): Remix 3: web standards, server-rendered components and client entries.
- [Waku](/docs/frameworks/waku): The minimal React framework, built on React Server Components.
- [Vike](/docs/frameworks/vike): The framework you assemble: your renderer, your server, on Vite.
- [Docusaurus](/docs/frameworks/docusaurus): Documentation websites with React, built by webpack.
- [Preact](/docs/frameworks/preact): A fast 3 kB alternative to React with the same API.
- [Solid](/docs/frameworks/solid): Simple, performant reactivity for user interfaces.
- [SolidStart](/docs/frameworks/solid-start): Solid's full-stack framework: routes, server rendering and server functions.
- [Vue](/docs/frameworks/vue): The progressive framework, with :sx in single-file components.
- [Nuxt](/docs/frameworks/nuxt): The intuitive Vue framework for universal applications.
- [VitePress](/docs/frameworks/vitepress): The Vite and Vue static site generator for documentation.
- [Svelte](/docs/frameworks/svelte): Cybernetically enhanced web apps, with sx on elements.
- [SvelteKit](/docs/frameworks/sveltekit): The fastest way to build apps of all sizes with Svelte.
- [Astro](/docs/frameworks/astro): The web framework for content-driven sites, sx in .astro files.
- [Qwik](/docs/frameworks/qwik): Instantly interactive apps, rendered on the server and resumed.
- [Angular](/docs/frameworks/angular): The platform for web apps, with an [sx] directive in templates.
- [Ember.js](/docs/frameworks/ember): A framework for ambitious web apps, on Embroider and Vite.
- [Meteor](/docs/frameworks/meteor): The full-stack JavaScript platform for web and mobile apps.
- [No framework](/docs/frameworks/vanilla): Plain TypeScript and web components: handles are class strings.

Server frameworks:

- [Laravel](/docs/frameworks/laravel): The PHP framework for web artisans: @kirana in Blade.
- [Symfony](/docs/frameworks/symfony): The PHP framework for websites and apps: kirana() in Twig.
- [Ruby on Rails](/docs/frameworks/rails): The full-stack Ruby framework: a kirana helper in ERB views.
- [Phoenix](/docs/frameworks/phoenix): Rich, interactive Elixir apps: kirana/1 in HEEx templates.
- [AdonisJS](/docs/frameworks/adonisjs): The fully featured Node.js framework: kirana() in Edge.

Bundlers:

- [Vite](/docs/integrations/vite): The build tool most frameworks run on, with hot style updates.
- [Rolldown](/docs/integrations/rolldown): The Rust bundler under Vite, on its own.
- [webpack](/docs/integrations/webpack): A pre loader for sx and a plugin that writes the stylesheet.
- [Rspack and Rsbuild](/docs/integrations/rspack): The fast Rust-based web bundler, and its build tool.
- [Parcel](/docs/integrations/parcel): The zero-configuration build tool for the web.
- [Bun](/docs/integrations/bun): Bun's bundler and its dev server, from one plugin.
- [esbuild](/docs/integrations/esbuild): An extremely fast bundler, in watch and serve modes too.
- [PostCSS](/docs/integrations/postcss): The project's stylesheet wherever @kirana; stands.
- [Jest](/docs/integrations/jest): A transformer, so tests see the class names you ship.
- [Storybook](/docs/integrations/storybook): Stories built with your project's Vite config, styled as the app is.

The overview of all of them, with what `sx` compiles to in each, is
[supported frameworks](/docs/frameworks/overview).

## Install by hand

The runtime package, the command line and your bundler's adapter (Vite here; your
[guide](#pick-your-framework) names yours):

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D kirana-style @kirana-style/vite
```

## Machines without a native build

The engine is native code for eight platforms. Anywhere else (a WebContainer, an
unusual CPU), install its WebAssembly build as well; Kirana uses it when no native
engine loads, and it writes exactly the same CSS, about twice as slowly:

```bash
npm install -D @kirana-style/compiler-wasm32-wasi --force
```

`KIRANA_FORCE_WASI=1` uses it even where the native engine works.

## What every setup has

The guides differ in names, not in shape. Whatever the framework, a project needs
the same four things.

### 1. The bundler plugin

Kirana compiles modules, so it runs in the bundler, ahead of the framework's own
plugin. Here it is for React on Vite 8; the [guides](#pick-your-framework) show it
for every other framework and bundler.

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"

export default defineConfig({
  // Kirana goes before the framework plugins, so they only ever see compiled
  // JavaScript.
  plugins: [kirana(), react()],
})
```

### 2. The configuration file

`kirana.config.ts` sits in the project root. It is optional, since every key has a
default, but this is where layers, targets and diagnostic levels live.

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"

export default defineConfig({
  // Your own layers, placed below every Kirana rule.
  layers: { before: ["reset", "base"] },
})
```

Every key is listed in the [configuration reference](/docs/reference/config).

### 3. The stylesheet entry

Kirana writes one stylesheet. Import it once, in your entry, before your own
global CSS, and the adapter fills it in:

```tsx file="src/main.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

A framework that renders the whole document as a component, such as
[TanStack Start](/docs/frameworks/tanstack-start), links it from that component
instead:

```tsx file="root.tsx"
import kiranaCss from "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css?url"

// Before your own global stylesheet: its `@layer reset, base, kirana`
// statement fixes the layer order.
<link rel="stylesheet" href={kiranaCss} />
```

Your framework's guide shows which of the two it uses.

In development the adapter serves the live stylesheet and updates it over HMR. In
a production build it replaces the placeholder rule and renames the file to a
content hash.

### 4. The `sx` prop's types

`sx` is not an import: the compiler recognises it on any element in a module it
compiles. TypeScript needs one reference to know about it:

```ts file="src/types.d.ts"
/// <reference types="@kirana-style/core/react" />
```

Put it in a `.d.ts` file that your `tsconfig.json` includes, and every host
element accepts `sx`.

The other frameworks have their own entry, such as `@kirana-style/core/vue`, and
each guide names the one to use. Angular needs none: the `[sx]` directive carries
its type.

## Browsers

The CSS Kirana writes runs in Chrome 123, Safari 17.5, Firefox 120 and later, the first
versions with `light-dark()`: every colour token is one `light-dark()` value, so
light and dark mode need no second stylesheet and no class to toggle. Every
current browser qualifies. To reach older ones, set
[`targets`](/docs/reference/config#targets) below that floor and the compiler
lowers what it can.

## Check it worked

```bash
# no diagnostics, exit code 0
npx kirana-style check src
```

If a module that uses `css()` was never compiled, calling it throws at runtime
with a message that says exactly that: the failure is loud, never a silently
unstyled page.

> [!TIP] Troubleshooting
> **Styles missing in development?** The stylesheet entry must be imported, and
> `kirana()` must come before the framework plugin.
> **`unresolved-import` warnings?** The compiler follows imports to find token
> and style definitions; check the specifier and your `tsconfig.json` paths.
> **A component ignores `sx`?** Components from installed packages do not read it.
> Spread the compiled props instead; see
> [styling other people's components](/docs/styling/external-components).

## Unreleased changes

The published packages are the release. To try a change that is on `main` but not
released yet, use the packages from a checkout.

### From tarballs

A checkout packs every package the way it would be published, as compiled
JavaScript with declarations and the engine as its own per-platform package:

```bash
vp run engine          # the engine for this machine
bun run kirana:pack    # tarballs in packages/kirana/dist-packages
```

Point your project at those tarballs, including the ones it does not name itself,
through your package manager's overrides. With npm or Bun:

```json file="package.json"
{
  "dependencies": {
    "@kirana-style/core": "file:/path/to/dist-packages/kirana-style-core-0.3.4.tgz"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "kirana-style": "file:/path/to/dist-packages/kirana-style-0.3.4.tgz",
    "@kirana-style/vite": "file:/path/to/dist-packages/kirana-style-vite-0.3.4.tgz"
  },
  "overrides": {
    "@kirana-style/compiler": "file:/path/to/dist-packages/kirana-style-compiler-0.3.4.tgz",
    "@kirana-style/rolldown": "file:/path/to/dist-packages/kirana-style-rolldown-0.3.4.tgz",
    "@kirana-style/compiler-linux-x64-gnu": "file:/path/to/dist-packages/kirana-style-compiler-linux-x64-gnu-0.3.4.tgz"
  }
}
```

pnpm reads the same map from `overrides` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, and Yarn from
`resolutions`. This is what CI does on every change: it installs the tarballs with
npm, pnpm, Yarn (both linkers) and Bun on Linux, macOS, Windows and Alpine, builds
an example, and checks its styles in a browser. No package runs an install script,
so there is nothing to allow-list.

> [!NOTE] Yarn needs every platform
> Yarn looks up all eight platform packages to write its lockfile, even the seven
> it will not install. A tarball set packed on one machine has only that
> machine's, so use npm, pnpm or Bun there.

### From a checkout of the repository

Kirana lives in a Bun workspace alongside the apps that use it. In that setup an
app depends on the packages by workspace protocol:

```json file="apps/your-app/package.json"
{
  "dependencies": {
    "@kirana-style/core": "workspace:*"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@kirana-style/vite": "workspace:*"
  }
}
```

To use Kirana from a project outside the repository, link the packages from a
checkout:

```bash
cd kirana/packages/kirana/npm/core && bun link
cd ../vite && bun link
cd /your/project && bun link @kirana-style/core @kirana-style/vite
```

The native engine comes from the checkout's build (`vp run build` there, or
`vp run engine`).
---
# Your first component
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/start/first-component
# Your first component

A button, with a hover state and a second variant. Everything below is one file,
and the tabs show what the compiler made of it: the CSS and the class names on
this page came out of the compiler, not out of prose.

<!-- ::example name="button-variants" -->

## What to notice

**The condition lives inside the value.** `backgroundColor` is written once, with
its resting value and its hover value together:

```tsx
backgroundColor: {
  base: "light-dark(oklch(0.21 0 0), oklch(0.92 0 0))",
  ":hover": "light-dark(oklch(0.31 0 0), oklch(0.85 0 0))",
}
```

You never look in two places to find out what colour a button is.

**Colours are `light-dark()` pairs.** There is no dark variant, no `dark:` prefix
and no second stylesheet. The browser picks the half that matches the page's
`color-scheme`, which the app sets once on `<html>`.

**The second variant is a second handle.** `sx={[styles.base, styles.quiet]}`
merges them in order, and the merge happens **per entry**: the quiet style's base
colour replaces the first one's base colour, and its hover colour replaces the
hover colour. Everything it does not mention (the padding, the radius, the font)
is still there. [Merging](/docs/styling/merging) has the rule, and how to drop an
entry you did not name.

**One class per declaration.** Open the Classes tab: thirteen classes, each a
single declaration. [How it works](/docs/start/how-it-works#the-pipeline) explains
why that keeps the stylesheet small.

## Next

- [How it works](/docs/start/how-it-works): what happens between the file and
  the stylesheet.
- [Mental model](/docs/start/mental-model): the five ideas the rest builds on.
---
# Mental model
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/start/mental-model
# Mental model

Five ideas. Everything else in these docs is a consequence of one of them.

<!-- ::figure-mental-model -->

## 1 · You write properties, not classes

A style is an object of CSS properties with real values. There is no vocabulary
to memorise, no scale to look up before you can write a length, and no class-name
grammar to decode when you read it back.

```tsx
const card = css({
  borderRadius: "0.75rem",
  padding: "1.5rem",
  boxShadow: "0 1px 2px oklch(0 0 0 / 0.08)",
})
```

Design tokens are ordinary imported values, so a token is just a constant your
editor can show you; see [tokens](/docs/tokens/overview).

## 2 · Merging replaces entries, not properties

This is the one that catches people, and it is worth ten minutes now rather than
an afternoon later.

A property can hold several **entries**: one per condition. When you merge two
styles, the later one replaces **the entries it names** and leaves the rest alone.

```tsx
const base = css({
  color: { base: "black", ":hover": "blue" },
})

// Replaces the base entry. The `:hover` entry is still there.
const override = css({ color: "grey" })

<a sx={[base, override]} /> // grey, and blue on hover
```

[Merging](/docs/styling/merging) shows how to remove the entries you did not name.

## 3 · A ladder decides what wins, not specificity

Every rule Kirana writes is one class, so every rule has the same specificity. A
stated ladder decides instead, and two of its steps cover most days:

- **More conditions win.** A `:hover` value beats a base value.
- **Then the narrower declaration.** `paddingTop` beats `padding`, in either order.

When the ladder cannot separate two values, the compiler reports
`ambiguous-precedence` instead of picking. [Precedence](/docs/styling/precedence)
is the whole ladder.

## 4 · Style what you render

The compiler styles elements it can see in your source. An element rendered inside
a component from an installed package is not yours, so `sx` on that component does
nothing unless the component reads it, and the compiler will tell you so
(`sx-on-external-component`).

Three ways out, in order of preference:

1. Pass compiled props, `{...props(styles.thing)}`, which works with any component
   that spreads props onto an element.
2. Style it from an ancestor you do render, with
   [`select`](/docs/styling/contextual).
3. Read its state from a parent with a [relation](/docs/styling/relations).

## 5 · Your editor shows what the element gets

A class list puts the CSS on the element; a style object puts it behind a name. So
the language server writes it back where you read: every element's line ends with
what it gets, in a class list's words.

```tsx editor file="src/plan.tsx"
export function Plan({ featured }: { featured: boolean }) {
  return (
    <article sx={[card, featured && raised]}>
      {" "}
      //: ▦ grid · gap 1rem · p 1rem · featured: shadow lg
      <h2 sx={title}>Pro</h2> //: text 1.25rem · 600 · ink
    </article>
  )
}
```

Read it the way you read `grid gap-4 p-4`. Hover it for the box model, every
declaration with `rem` in pixels and the token it reads, and the compiled rule;
hover one property to see which entry wins and why. The answers come from the same
compiler session as the build, so the editor never disagrees with the stylesheet:
if it shows `p 1rem`, the element gets `padding: 1rem`. See
[editor support](/docs/tooling/editor).

## Coming from somewhere else

- **From Tailwind:** the vocabulary is the same (`@kirana-style/preset-scales` carries
  Tailwind's scales), but conditions nest inside values instead of prefixing class
  names, and the merge story is different from `cn()`. The class list you read is
  still there, at the end of the line in your editor (idea 5).
  [Migration guide](/docs/migration/from-tailwind).
- **From StyleX:** the API will look familiar. The difference that bites is idea
  2: StyleX's `default: null` means "no base value", Kirana's `base: null`
  _removes_ an earlier one. [Migration guide](/docs/migration/from-stylex).
---
# How it works
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/start/how-it-works
# How it works

Kirana is a compiler. It reads your modules at build time, works out every style
they can produce, writes one stylesheet, and rewrites the modules to reference
classes instead of style objects.

## The pipeline

<!-- ::figure-pipeline -->

**1 · Prefilter.** Most files in an application have nothing to do with styling.
Before parsing anything, the adapter skips any module whose text contains neither
`@kirana-style/`, an `sx` attribute, nor a call of a relation's read such as
`.within(`, so the compiler's work scales with the number of styled modules, not
with the size of the dependency graph.

**2 · Evaluate.** The modules that survive are parsed, and the parts that feed a
style are evaluated by a restricted evaluator: constants, imported token values,
template literals, simple functions. It follows imports across files, so a token
defined in one module and used in another is a build-time value. Anything it
cannot evaluate statically is reported rather than guessed at.

**3 · Normalise.** Declarations are expanded to longhands and normalised, so
`padding: "1rem"` and `paddingTop: "1rem"` compare as the same kind of thing, and
`margin` written twice in two modules merges per side rather than per shorthand.

**4 · Atomise.** Each declaration becomes one atom (one CSS rule with one
declaration), named by hashing the property, the value and the conditions. Two
modules that write `display: flex` get the same class. The stylesheet grows with
distinct declarations, not with components.

**5 · Order.** Atoms are placed in layers, and inside the layer their order comes
from the [precedence ladder](/docs/styling/precedence). Specificity is not used to
express intent: every rule is a single class.

**6 · Rewrite.** `css({ … })` becomes a class string, and `sx` becomes
`className`. A value known only at runtime becomes either a choice between class
strings or a custom-property bridge.

## What reaches the browser

- **One stylesheet**, containing the atoms your application actually uses.
- **Class strings** in your JavaScript.
- **No style engine.** Nothing parses styles, computes classes, or injects CSS at
  runtime.

The only runtime code is a private helper under 1.1 kB, and it is included only when
a module needs it: when styles are merged at runtime, or a value is bridged
through a custom property. It merges class strings; it never generates CSS.

## In development

The adapter keeps a compiler session alive. When you save a file it recompiles
that module, updates the stylesheet and pushes it over Vite's hot channel, so the
page restyles without reloading. Diagnostics appear in the terminal as warnings
and errors, with the file, line and a suggested fix.

## In a build

The same session produces the final stylesheet, minified through Lightning CSS and
lowered for the browser targets you configured. The output is deterministic: the
same sources produce byte-identical CSS, independent of thread scheduling or file
order.

## What it deliberately does not do

- It does not generate CSS in the browser.
- It does not read class names to decide what wins; it has a stated ladder.
- It does not style markup it cannot see. If a component from a package renders
  the element, you style it from the outside, with a
  [contextual selector](/docs/styling/contextual) or by passing compiled props.

Next: [the mental model](/docs/start/mental-model), five ideas that follow from
this design, and make everything else predictable.
---
# Writing styles
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/styles
# Writing styles

`css()` takes style objects and returns a handle. A handle is an opaque value:
you pass it to `sx`, merge it with others, or export it. It is not an object you
can read at runtime: by then it is a class string.

```tsx
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const panel = css({
  display: "grid",
  gap: "0.75rem",
  padding: "1rem",
})
```

## Property names

Properties are camelCase: `backgroundColor`, `paddingInlineStart`, `gridTemplateColumns`.
Anything CSS knows about is allowed; anything else is an error
(`unknown-property`), so a typo fails the build instead of disappearing.

Custom properties are written as they are in CSS, in quotes:

```tsx
css({
  "--card-gap": "1rem",
  gap: "var(--card-gap)",
})
```

## Values

Values are strings and numbers, exactly as CSS reads them. Kirana does **not**
add units for you:

```tsx
css({ width: "5rem" }) // fine
css({ width: 5 }) // error: unitless-length
css({ flexGrow: 1 }) // fine - flex-grow takes a number
css({ zIndex: 10 }) // fine
```

The rule is the CSS rule: a property that takes a `<length>` needs a unit. A
property whose value is a plain number takes a plain number. Guessing `px` is how
a styling system ends up with values it cannot explain, so the compiler asks you
instead.

Invalid values are errors too (`invalid-value`), checked against the property's
grammar as MDN writes it:

```tsx
css({ display: "center" }) // error: invalid-value - a keyword display does not take
css({ padding: "-4px" }) // error: invalid-value - padding is never negative
css({ padding: color.accent }) // error: invalid-value - a colour token on a length
css({ margin: "1px;" }) // error: invalid-value - a stray semicolon
```

A word or a function the data does not know is left alone, because it may be
newer CSS than the data, or a name of your own (`animationName: "spin"`). So is
whatever is inside a function's parentheses, and a value made of `var()`.

## Several objects, one handle

`css()` takes any number of arguments (objects, or handles you already made) and
merges them left to right:

```tsx
const base = css({ padding: "0.5rem" })
const wide = css(base, { paddingInline: "1.5rem" })
```

Merging follows the [merge rules](/docs/styling/merging): later entries replace
matching entries and leave the rest alone.

## Shorthands

Shorthands are expanded to longhands, so two styles that touch the same box merge
per side rather than wholesale:

```tsx
const a = css({ padding: "1rem" })
const b = css({ paddingTop: "2rem" })

<div sx={[a, b]} /> // 2rem on top, 1rem on the other three sides
```

A shorthand whose value cannot be split exactly (`border: "var(--line)"`, where
the value is one custom property) stays whole, and the compiler warns
(`unsplittable-shorthand`) because removing one of its longhands later cannot be
done precisely.

Mixing logical and physical longhands of the same box (`paddingLeft` and
`paddingInlineStart`) is allowed, but they are _different_ declarations, and when
the result could mislead the compiler says so (`mixed-logical-physical`).

`translate` and `transform` have no logical form. To centre an element, pair them
with a physical inset (`left: "50%"`, `translate: "-50% 0"`): a logical inset
changes side in right-to-left text while the translate keeps pulling the same way,
and the compiler warns about that pair too.

## Where styles live

A handle is usually a module-level constant, because it compiles to a constant:

```tsx
const styles = {
  root: css({ … }),
  title: css({ … }),
}
```

Writing `css({ … })` inside a component body is fine too, since it still
compiles, but there is no reason to unless the style depends on a value only
known at render time, which is its own topic:
[dynamic values](/docs/styling/dynamic).

## Next

- [The `sx` prop](/docs/styling/sx): putting a handle on an element.
- [Conditions](/docs/styling/conditions): hover, breakpoints, attributes.
---
# The sx prop
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/sx
# The `sx` prop

`sx` is not an import. The compiler recognises it on any element in a module it
compiles, and turns it into `className`:

```tsx
<div sx={styles.root} />
// becomes
<div className="k5O_23ai kJ_1O3s" />
```

It takes a handle, or an array of handles, and skips `null`, `undefined` and
`false`:

```tsx
<div sx={[styles.root, isOpen && styles.open, sx]} />
```

Order is merge order, so a component's own styles come first and the caller's
`sx` last.

## On your own components

For a component you wrote, `sx` is an ordinary prop. Accept it, type it as `Sx`,
and apply it:

```tsx
import { css, type Sx } from "@kirana-style/core"

const styles = { root: css({ borderRadius: "0.5rem" }) }

export function Card({
  sx,
  ...props
}: { sx?: Sx } & React.ComponentProps<"div">) {
  return <div {...props} sx={[styles.root, sx]} />
}
```

Taking `sx` and never applying it is reported (`unused-sx`), because from the
outside the component looks styleable and silently is not.

## On components you did not write

A component from an installed package does not read `sx`. Passing it one does
nothing, and the compiler says so (`sx-on-external-component`), including the
case where your own component forwards its rest props into one. Pass compiled
props instead:

```tsx
import { props as styleProps } from "@kirana-style/core"

<Dialog.Popup {...styleProps(styles.popup, sx)} />
```

[Styling other people's components](/docs/styling/external-components) covers the
cases.

## `className` and `style` still work

If an element has both `sx` and a `className`, they are merged, not replaced:
the class from `sx` is appended to whatever the element already had, including a
`className` arriving through a spread:

```tsx
<div {...props} className="legacy" sx={styles.root} />
```

The same is true of `style`. When a style needs a value known only at render time,
the compiler bridges it through a custom property and puts that in `style`, after
anything you passed.

## Typing

`sx` reaches React's element types through a reference, once per project:

```ts
/// <reference types="@kirana-style/core/react" />
```

The `Sx` type is what a component should accept: a handle, `null`, `undefined`,
`false`, or an array of those, nested.

## What it is not

`sx` does not take a bare style object:

```tsx
<div sx={{ color: "red" }} /> // error - wrap it in css({ … })
```

A string is not a class list either. With a preset that declares a utility
grammar, `sx="p-4"` is a [utility string](/docs/styling/utilities) that compiles
to the same atoms as its object; without one it is the `utility-surface-disabled`
error.
---
# Conditions
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/conditions
# Conditions

A condition goes **inside** the value it changes, not around the object that
holds it:

```tsx
css({
  color: {
    base: "black",
    ":hover": "blue",
    '[aria-current="page"]': "crimson",
  },
})
```

<!-- ::figure-conditions -->

`base` is the unconditional value. Every other key is a condition. The property is
written once, so the whole story of `color` is in one place, and so is the reason
the compiler can tell you when two of those values could both apply.

## What a key may be

| Key                     | Example                                                                       |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A pseudo-class          | `":hover"`, `":focus-visible"`, `":disabled"`, `":nth-child(2)"`              |
| An attribute selector   | `'[data-state="open"]'`, `"[aria-expanded]"`                                  |
| A compound of both      | `'[aria-haspopup]:active'`                                                    |
| An at-rule, as a string | `"@media (min-width: 40rem)"`, `"@supports (height: 100dvh)"`                 |
| A condition value       | `[breakpoint.md]`, `[container("(width >= 20rem)")]`, `[media("print")]`      |
| A relation read         | `[group.within('[data-disabled]')]`; see [relations](/docs/styling/relations) |
| A component state       | `[Switch.Root.checked]`; see [component states](/docs/styling/states)         |

Condition values come from `media()`, `container()` and `supports()`, and from
presets:

```tsx
import { css, media, supports } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { breakpoint } from "@kirana-style/preset-scales"

css({
  gap: { base: "0.5rem", [breakpoint.md]: "1rem" },
  height: { base: "100vh", [supports("(height: 100dvh)")]: "100dvh" },
  display: { [media("print")]: "none" },
})
```

## Nesting

Conditions nest, and nesting is how you say "both":

```tsx
css({
  backgroundColor: {
    base: "white",
    ":hover": {
      base: "whitesmoke",
      [breakpoint.md]: "gainsboro", // hovered *and* at least md
    },
  },
})
```

Two conditions beat one, so the nested value wins wherever both hold. This is also
the answer when the compiler reports `ambiguous-precedence`: nest the one that
should win inside the other.

## Pseudo-elements are different

`::before` and `::after` are not conditions: they are other elements. They are
top-level keys, holding a style object of their own:

```tsx
css({
  position: "relative",
  "::after": {
    content: '""',
    position: "absolute",
    insetInline: 0,
    blockSize: "1px",
    backgroundColor: { base: "gainsboro", ":hover": "black" },
  },
})
```

Only pseudo-elements and [`select.*`](/docs/styling/contextual) targets are
top-level keys. Everything else nests inside a value.

## Responsive design

Breakpoints are conditions like any other, which has two consequences worth
knowing:

- **A state beats a breakpoint.** `:hover` wins over `md` at every width, because
  attributes and pseudo-classes rank above at-rules. That is what people
  usually mean, and what the Tailwind components this compiler was built against
  relied on.
- **Ranges read as ranges.** For a value that applies only between two widths,
  write the range: `"@media (min-width: 40rem) and (max-width: 47.999rem)"`.

```tsx
css({
  gridTemplateColumns: {
    base: "1fr",
    [breakpoint.sm]: "repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr))",
    [breakpoint.lg]: "repeat(4, minmax(0, 1fr))",
  },
})
```

## Container queries

Containers work the same way, and need a container to query:

```tsx
css({
  containerType: "inline-size",
  containerName: "card",
})

css({
  flexDirection: {
    base: "column",
    [container("(width >= 24rem)", "card")]: "row",
  },
})
```

## What the compiler checks

- An unrecognised condition is an error (`unknown-condition`), including the
  common mistake of writing a condition as a top-level key.
- Two values that could both apply, with nothing to separate them, get
  `ambiguous-precedence`. Fix it by nesting, or by declaring that the two
  conditions never hold together; see
  [`conditions.exclusive`](/docs/reference/config).

Next: [precedence](/docs/styling/precedence), the ladder that decides which
condition wins.
---
# Utility strings
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/utilities
# Utility strings

With a preset that declares a utility grammar, `sx` also takes a string:

```tsx
<button sx="inline-flex items-center gap-1.5 px-3 hover:bg-blue-600/90 md:px-4" />
```

That string is not a class list. The compiler reads each utility, turns the
whole string into the style object you would have written by hand, and compiles
that object exactly as it compiles `css()`:

```tsx
css({
  display: "inline-flex",
  alignItems: "center",
  gap: space[1.5],
  paddingInline: { default: space[3], "@media (width >= 48rem)": space[4] },
  backgroundColor: {
    ":hover": "color-mix(in oklab, <blue-600> 90%, transparent)",
  },
})
```

There is one style path, so a utility and its object produce **the same atoms**,
share tokens, merge the same way, and get every diagnostic the object form gets.
The object form stays the reference; strings are a shorter way to write it.

## Turning it on

Utility strings are off until a preset declares a grammar.
`@kirana-style/preset-scales` ships Tailwind v4's names over its own scales:

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"
import scales from "@kirana-style/preset-scales/preset"

export default defineConfig({ presets: [scales()] })
```

Import the preset from `/preset`, not from the package root: a configuration file
runs uncompiled, and the root exports tokens, which only exist inside the
compiler.

Without a grammar, a string `sx` is the `utility-surface-disabled` error and the
attribute is left as written.

## Where strings go

Anywhere `sx` takes a style: on elements and on your components, alone, in an
array, or in a condition:

```tsx
<div sx="flex gap-2" />
<Card sx={["p-4", selected && "bg-muted", styles.card]} />
<li sx={open ? "font-semibold" : "text-muted-foreground"} />
```

Later utilities override earlier ones property by property, as later entries in
an array do. A template literal works only without substitutions:
``sx={`p-${n}`}`` is the `utility-not-static` error; write
`css({ padding: n })`, which Kirana bridges at runtime.

`className` strings are never read. Only `sx` is Kirana's.

## What a utility can say

| Form           | Example                            | Compiles to                                      |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Scale key      | `p-4`, `bg-blue-600`, `rounded-lg` | the preset's token                               |
| Keyword        | `items-center`, `flex`, `hidden`   | a fixed value                                    |
| Brackets       | `p-[3px]`, `bg-[rgb(1, 2, 3)]`     | the value as written                             |
| Negative       | `-mt-2`, `-inset-x-1`              | `calc(<value> * -1)`                             |
| Number         | `w-50`, `z-1`, `duration-450`      | 50 × `0.25rem`, `1`, `450ms`                     |
| Variable       | `w-(--sidebar-width)`              | `var(--sidebar-width)`                           |
| Colour + alpha | `bg-blue-600/50`                   | `color-mix(in oklab, <colour> 50%, transparent)` |
| Fraction       | `w-1/2`                            | `calc(1/2 * 100%)`                               |

Spaces inside brackets are fine (`bg-[rgb(1, 2, 3)]` is one utility), and
Tailwind's `_` for a space works too.

Tailwind's `--spacing(n)` inside brackets counts steps of the space scale, so
`gap-[--spacing(var(--gap))]` is the scale's first step times `var(--gap)`.

Variants go before the utility and stack, in Tailwind's own forms. There is no
`dark:`: every colour token is already a `light-dark()` pair.

| Kind              | Variants                                                                  |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| States            | `hover:`, `focus-visible:`, `disabled:`                                   |
| Media             | `md:`, `motion-reduce:`, `print:`                                         |
| Direction         | `rtl:`                                                                    |
| Attributes        | `data-open:`, `data-[state=open]:`, `data-side=left:`, `aria-invalid:`    |
| Structure         | `has-[svg]:`, `not-first:`, `nth-3:`, `[&:nth-child(2)]:`                 |
| Feature queries   | `supports-[display:grid]:`                                                |
| Container queries | `@md:`, `@md/card:`, `@[250px]:`; name a container with `@container/card` |
| Pseudo-elements   | `before:`, `after:`, `placeholder:`, `file:`, `selection:`                |

A pseudo-element variant becomes a block of its own, and `before:` and `after:`
get `content: ""`, as Tailwind gives them.

## Composed utilities

Some utilities share one CSS property, and combine instead of the later one
winning. As in Tailwind, each sets its own layer (a registered, non-inheriting
custom property from the preset's `compose` tokens), and the shared property reads
them all:

| Utilities                                                    | Share             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------- |
| `ring-2`, `shadow-sm`                                        | `box-shadow`      |
| `translate-x-4`, `translate-y-2`                             | `translate`       |
| `scale-*`                                                    | `scale`           |
| The filters, such as `grayscale`, `brightness-50`, `blur-sm` | `filter`          |
| The backdrop filters, such as `backdrop-blur-xs`             | `backdrop-filter` |

Transitions and outlines work the same way, so the order of the utilities does
not matter:

- `transition` reads the timing that `duration-*` and `ease-*` set;
- `outline-2` reads the style that `outline-hidden` set.

Uniform box utilities such as `p-4`, `m-4` and `inset-0` set both logical axes
(block and inline) rather than the shorthand.

The value is the same on every side, and a later `p-0` then replaces an earlier
`py-4` entry for entry, as `cn()` did.

## Animations

Tailwind's `animate-*` utilities (spin, ping, pulse and bounce) are here, and so is
the vocabulary of `tw-animate-css`, which shadcn/ui uses:

```tsx
<div sx="data-open:animate-in data-open:fade-in-0 data-open:zoom-in-95 duration-100" />
```

| Utilities                                                                 | What they do                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `animate-in`, `animate-out`                                               | Play the `enter` and `exit` keyframes                                      |
| `fade-in-0`, `zoom-in-95`, `spin-in-45`, `blur-in`, `slide-in-from-top-2` | Set what the animation starts from; their `-out` forms set what it ends at |
| `duration-*`, `ease-*`                                                    | Time the animation as well as transitions                                  |
| `delay-*`, `repeat-*`, `direction-*`, `fill-mode-*`                       | Set the animation's own properties                                         |

`slide-in-from-start` and `-end`, which depend on the writing direction, are not
utilities; write them with an `rtl:` condition.

## What it will not do

These are errors that point to the Kirana way, never silently dropped classes:

| You wrote                         | Error                     | Instead                                                    |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `p-huge`, `bg-blu-600`            | `unknown-utility`         | the message lists the nearest names                        |
| `hovr:underline`                  | `unknown-utility-variant` | the message lists the nearest variants                     |
| `!p-4`                            | `utility-unsupported`     | [precedence](/docs/styling/precedence) has no `!important` |
| `group-hover:…`, `peer-checked:…` | `utility-unsupported`     | [relations](/docs/styling/relations)                       |
| `[&_svg]:size-4`                  | `utility-unsupported`     | [select](/docs/styling/contextual)                         |
| `[mask-type:luminance]`           | `unknown-utility`         | write the property in `css()`                              |

There is no scan of your files, no `@apply`, no plugins, and no arbitrary
properties (`[mask-type:luminance]`).

## Your own tokens

A grammar reads its scales from modules, the way an `import` would. Point a
scale at your theme and `bg-primary` reaches your semantic tokens:

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
export default defineConfig({
  presets: [scales()],
  utilities: {
    scales: {
      color: [
        { module: "@kirana-style/preset-scales", export: "color" },
        { module: "./src/theme.ts", export: "theme" },
      ],
    },
  },
})
```

Later presets and your own `utilities` replace earlier ones scale by scale, root
by root and variant by variant. The full shape is in the
[configuration reference](/docs/reference/config#utilities).
---
# At-rules
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/at-rules
# At-rules

An at-rule that a style depends on is written by Kirana, under a hashed name and
only when something uses it. An at-rule that belongs to the whole page stays in
a stylesheet, where CSS already says it well.

| At-rule                             | With Kirana                                                                        |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@media`, `@container`, `@supports` | [Conditions](/docs/styling/conditions): `media()`, `container()`, `supports()`     |
| `@keyframes`                        | [`keyframes()`](/docs/styling/animation)                                           |
| `@position-try`                     | [`positionTry()`](/docs/styling/anchor-positioning)                                |
| `@counter-style`                    | [`counterStyle()`](#counter-styles), below                                         |
| `@property`                         | A [registered token](/docs/tokens/overview#registered-tokens), `{ value, syntax }` |
| `@layer`                            | Kirana's own layers, and [yours around them](/docs/config/layers)                  |
| View-transition parts               | [`viewTransition()`](/docs/styling/view-transitions)                               |
| `@font-face`, `@page`               | [A stylesheet](#in-a-stylesheet)                                                   |
| `@custom-media`                     | [A `media()` constant](#a-named-media-query), since browsers do not read it yet    |

## Counter styles

`counterStyle()` defines how a list or a counter writes its numbers: ticks,
letters, roman numerals, any symbols you choose.

```tsx
import { counterStyle, css } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const check = counterStyle({
  system: "cyclic",
  symbols: '"✓"',
  suffix: '" "',
})

export const steps = css({ listStyleType: check })
export const label = css({
  "::before": { content: `counter(step, ${check}) ". "` },
})
```

The result is the rule's name, `kc…`, for a list's marker or a counter. The rule
ships once, in `kirana.tokens`, and only if a style uses it:

```css
@layer kirana.tokens {
  @counter-style kc4HMO {
    system: cyclic;
    symbols: "✓";
    suffix: " ";
  }
}
```

The keys are the CSS descriptors in camel case:

| Descriptor                   | What it sets                                  |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `system`                     | How the symbols count: `cyclic`, `additive` … |
| `symbols`, `additiveSymbols` | The symbols, each a quoted string             |
| `prefix`, `suffix`           | What comes before and after the marker        |
| `negative`, `range`, `pad`   | Negative numbers, the range drawn, padding    |
| `fallback`, `speakAs`        | Another style outside the range; speech       |

Each value is CSS text, so a symbol keeps its quotes. One counter style can build
on another, and the other ships with it:

```tsx
export const bracketed = counterStyle({
  system: `extends ${check}`,
  prefix: '"("',
  suffix: '") "',
})

export const roman = counterStyle({
  system: "additive",
  additiveSymbols: '10 "X", 5 "V", 1 "I"',
  range: "1 39",
  fallback: check,
})
```

### Why not a stylesheet

A counter style in a global stylesheet has a global name that any other can
collide with. It ships whether a page uses it or not. And a name misspelt in
`listStyleType` gives no error: the list quietly falls back to decimal numbers.
With `counterStyle()` the name is a value your editor completes and the compiler
checks.

### What the compiler checks

A browser drops a broken counter style without a word, so `invalid-counter-style`
reports each way it breaks:

- a key that is not a descriptor (`color`);
- a value that reads a custom property, which descriptors cannot (a variable token);
- a value that is empty, or not CSS, or only known at runtime;
- a system without what it draws with: most need `symbols`, an additive one
  needs `additiveSymbols`, and one that extends another style takes neither.

An inlined token works as a value, since it is plain text by then. A system newer
than the compiler is left to the browser.

## In a stylesheet

`@font-face` and `@page` belong to the page rather than to an element, so they
stay in CSS, imported once from your entry point.

```css
/* src/fonts.css */
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("./fonts/inter.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 100 900;
  font-display: swap;
}

@page {
  margin: 2cm;
}
```

```tsx
// src/main.tsx
import "./fonts.css"
```

Your bundler resolves the font's `url()` and fingerprints the file. That works in
a stylesheet and cannot work from a value inside a module, which is why Kirana
has no `fontFace()`. A style then names the family like any other value, and a
[token](/docs/tokens/overview) can hold it:

```tsx
export const body = css({ fontFamily: "Inter, system-ui, sans-serif" })
```

These rules are not inside a layer, and they need not be: neither styles an
element, so they never compete with Kirana's atoms. Element styles of your own
that must sit beside Kirana's go in [a layer](/docs/config/layers).

## A named media query

`@custom-media` gives a media query a name, but no browser reads it yet. A
condition in a constant does the same today:

```tsx
// src/breakpoints.ts
import { media } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const tablet = media("(width >= 48rem)")
export const reducedMotion = media("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)")
```

```tsx
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { tablet } from "./breakpoints"

export const grid = css({
  gridTemplateColumns: { base: "1fr", [tablet]: "1fr 1fr" },
})
```

The compiler reads the constant across modules, so a query is written once and
every style that names it is checked.
---
# Merging and removal
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/merging
# Merging and removal

Styles combine in three places: `css(a, b)`, `cx(a, b)`, and `sx={[a, b]}`. All
three merge the same way, in order, and the rule is the one from the
[mental model](/docs/start/mental-model):

> A later style replaces the entries it names, and leaves the others alone.

## Entries, not properties

A property holds one entry per condition set. `color` with a base value and a
`:hover` value is two entries.

```tsx
const link = css({
  color: { base: "navy", ":hover": "royalblue" },
  textDecorationLine: "underline",
})

const quiet = css({ color: "grey" })

<a sx={[link, quiet]} />
```

The anchor is grey, still royal blue on hover, and still underlined. `quiet` named
the base entry of `color`, so that is the entry it replaced.

<!-- ::figure-merge -->

This is the single biggest difference from class-string systems, where a later
`text-grey` removes the whole colour idea, hover included.

## Removing

`null` removes. There are three forms, and they differ in reach:

```tsx
// one entry
css({ color: { base: null } })

// every entry of one property
css({ color: null })

// everything except what this style lists
css({ color: { "*": null, base: "grey" } })
```

`{ "*": null, base: "grey" }` is the one to reach for when you want a component's
conditional chrome gone and your own value in its place, such as an input inside a
group that should lose the group's focus ring.

> [!WARNING] `base: null` is not "no value"
> In StyleX, `default: null` means "this variant sets nothing here". In Kirana,
> `base: null` **removes** a base value an earlier style set. If you are porting,
> this is the line to re-read; see
> [migrating from StyleX](/docs/migration/from-stylex).

## `cx()`

`cx()` merges handles and skips `null`, `undefined` and `false`, which makes
conditional composition read naturally:

```tsx
import { cx } from "@kirana-style/core"

const handle = cx(styles.root, isOpen && styles.open, props.sx)
```

`sx={[a, b]}` accepts the same shapes, including nested arrays, so you rarely need
`cx()` on an element: it is for building a handle to pass on.

## Order is the order you wrote

Merging is left to right, and the last writer of an entry wins **that entry**.
What order does _not_ decide is a conflict between two different conditions: that
is the [precedence ladder](/docs/styling/precedence), and it applies after
merging.

```tsx
// Both entries survive the merge; the ladder decides which applies when hovered.
css({ color: "black" }, { color: { ":hover": "blue" } })
```

## Class strings come from a merge

A merge leaves an element one class per entry, and the stylesheet relies on it:
two classes for the same entry never reach one element, so the compiler orders
them however writes the smallest stylesheet. Joining two compiled class strings
by hand skips the merge, and when both name the same entry, which one applies is
not defined.

```tsx
// Both strings may set the base `color`: either can win.
<a className={`${props(link).className} ${props(quiet).className}`} />

// The merge keeps one: `quiet`'s.
<a sx={[link, quiet]} />
```

Pass handles instead, and combine them with `sx`, `cx()` or `props()`.

## Shorthands merge per longhand

```tsx
css({ padding: "1rem" }, { paddingTop: "2rem" })
```

`padding` expands to four longhands, `paddingTop` replaces one of them, and the
other three keep `1rem`. The same is true across modules and across components:
merging is defined on longhands, so nothing depends on which shorthand each author
happened to use.

## A component's own `sx`

A component that takes `sx` should merge it **last**, so its caller can override:

```tsx
export function Card({
  sx,
  ...props
}: { sx?: Sx } & React.ComponentProps<"div">) {
  return <div {...props} sx={[styles.root, sx]} />
}
```

Declaring `sx` and never applying it is reported (`unused-sx`).
---
# Precedence
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/precedence
# Precedence

Every rule Kirana writes is a single class, so every rule has the same
specificity. What wins is decided by a stated ladder, compared in order: the
first difference decides.

| Step | Comparison              | Higher wins                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1    | **Origin**              | An element's own style beats a style it inherited from a [contextual selector](/docs/styling/contextual).                                                                                                    |
| 2    | **Condition count**     | More conditions win. `md + :hover` beats `:hover` beats `base`.                                                                                                                                              |
| 3    | **Condition class**     | `attribute` > `pseudo-class` > `relation` > `at-rule`; a relation's `parent()` read ranks as a pseudo-class.                                                                                                 |
| 4    | **Within a class**      | Pseudo-classes by a fixed table (roughly: structural → `:hover` → `:focus` → `:active` → `:checked` → `:invalid` → `:disabled`). At-rules: `@container` > `@media` > `@supports`; a larger `min-width` wins. |
| 5    | **Declaration breadth** | The narrower declaration wins: `paddingTop` beats `padding`, `borderWidth` beats `border`. At equal breadth, a physical longhand beats a logical one.                                                        |
| 6    | **Tie-break**           | Lexicographic, and never meaningful: reaching this step emits `ambiguous-precedence`.                                                                                                                        |

<!-- ::figure-precedence -->

## The two steps you will feel

**State beats breakpoint** (step 3). A `:hover` or `[data-state="open"]` value
wins over a breakpoint value at every width. That is almost always what an author
means, and it is what the Tailwind components this compiler was built against
relied on.

**Narrow beats broad** (step 5), regardless of who wrote first:

```tsx
// paddingTop wins for the top side, wherever it was written.
<div sx={[css({ paddingTop: "2rem" }), css({ padding: "1rem" })]} />
```

## Ambiguity is reported, not guessed

When two entries for the same property could both match, set different values, and
the ladder cannot separate them, the compiler emits `ambiguous-precedence` rather
than picking one:

```tsx
css({
  color: {
    '[data-state="open"]': "red",
    "[aria-expanded]": "blue", // both can be true at once
  },
})
```

Three ways to resolve it:

1. **Nest the winner** inside the loser. Two conditions beat one, and the
   ambiguity is gone:

   ```tsx
   css({
     color: {
       "[aria-expanded]": {
         base: "blue",
         '[data-state="open"]': "red",
       },
     },
   })
   ```

2. **Say they are exclusive.** When a library guarantees two attributes never
   appear together (`[data-open]` and `[data-closed]`), declare it once in
   [`conditions.exclusive`](/docs/reference/config).

3. **Use the same value**, if that is the truth. Two entries with the same value
   are never ambiguous.

The compiler already knows some pairs are exclusive on their own: two values of
one attribute, a selector and its negation, or two fixed positions counted from
the same end.

## Combinations that cannot match

A key nested in another it can never meet, such as two values of one attribute or
two libraries' states declared apart with
[`conditions.exclusiveAcross`](/docs/reference/config), matches no element. Its
entries are left out of the stylesheet. A style written once for several libraries
can nest one state helper inside another without shipping rules nothing can match,
and without a word from the compiler, since the configuration declared the libraries
apart. Any other such key is a mistake, and the compiler says so with an info,
`unreachable-entry`.

An attribute your component writes itself, whatever library it is built on, is
yours even where a vocabulary names it: a sheet's `data-side`, which Base UI also
names for its popups. List it in
[`conditions.ownAttributes`](/docs/reference/config), and its keys meet every
library's states instead of being left out beside them.

## Layers

Everything Kirana emits is inside layers, in this order:

```css
@layer reset, base, kirana; /* your layers, from configuration */
@layer kirana.tokens, kirana.themes, kirana.contextual, kirana.atoms;
```

Your own global CSS (a reset, base element styles) goes in layers you name in
