[configuration](/docs/config/layers), which sit below every Kirana rule. Nothing
Kirana writes is unlayered, custom-property assignments included.

## Asking why

When a value does not win and you want the reason, ask:

```bash
kirana-style trace src/components/card.tsx:24 padding-top
```

It prints one line per candidate declaration (value, conditions, layer), marks
the winner, and names the step that decided it, for example
`step 5 (set 1 longhand < 4)`.
---
# Styling other people's components
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/external-components
# Styling other people's components

`sx` works on elements your module renders. A component from an installed package
renders its own elements, and unless it happens to read a prop called `sx`, giving
it one does nothing.

The compiler catches this rather than letting you find it in the browser:

```console
$ kirana-style check src
warning[KRN1703] sx-on-external-component: a component from "@base-ui/react"
receives `sx`, which it does not read
  help: spread the compiled props instead: {...props(styles.root, sx)}
```

## `props()`

`props()` compiles the same handles into `{ className, style }`, which every
component that spreads its props onto an element will apply:

```tsx
import { css, props as styleProps } from "@kirana-style/core"

const styles = { popup: css({ borderRadius: "0.5rem" }) }

export function Popup({ sx, ...rest }: { sx?: Sx }) {
  return <Dialog.Popup {...rest} {...styleProps(styles.popup, sx)} />
}
```

<!-- ::figure-external -->

The alias `props as styleProps` is a convention, not an API: `props` is a common
identifier, and the alias keeps the import from shadowing a parameter.

To style a part's states (a switch that is checked, a popup that opened below its
trigger), take the keys from [component states](/docs/styling/states) instead of
typing the attributes.

## The case one module away

The diagnostic also fires when the component that receives `sx` is yours, but it
hands its rest props to an installed component without reading `sx` first:

```tsx
// Menubar.tsx
export function MenubarTrigger({ ...props }) {
  return <Menu.Trigger {...props} /> // `sx` rides along, unread
}

// page.tsx
<MenubarTrigger sx={styles.trigger} /> // reported here
```

Take `sx` out of the rest props and apply it:

```tsx
export function MenubarTrigger({ sx, ...props }: { sx?: Sx }) {
  return <Menu.Trigger {...props} {...styleProps(sx)} />
}
```

## Components that render something else

Some libraries let you supply the element a part renders as. The classes belong to
whichever element ends up in the DOM, so pass the styles to the part, and let it
merge:

```tsx
<SidebarMenuButton render={<a href="/docs" />} sx={styles.button} />
```

If instead you style the inner element and the outer part also sets classes, the
outer part's classes can be dropped: the part is not merging anything, it is
rendering your element.

## When you cannot pass props at all

Two options, in order:

1. **Style it from an ancestor you do render** with
   [`select.descendant`](/docs/styling/contextual). Contextual styles sit in a
   lower layer, so the element's own styles still win.
2. **Global CSS**, scoped by an attribute the library sets. This is the last
   resort: it is markup you do not own, and nothing checks it.
---
# Component states
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/states
# Component states

A headless component library renders the behaviour and leaves the styling to you. It
tells you each part's state through data attributes: a switch's root gets
`data-checked` when it is on, a popup gets `data-side="bottom"` when it opened
below its trigger. In Kirana those are [condition keys](/docs/styling/conditions),
and `@kirana-style/states` lists them, so you pick a state instead of typing its
attribute:

```tsx
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { Select, Switch } from "@kirana-style/states/base-ui"

const styles = {
  track: css({
    backgroundColor: {
      base: "gray",
      [Switch.Root.checked]: { base: "blue", [Switch.Root.disabled]: "silver" },
    },
  }),
  thumb: css({
    translate: { base: "0", [Switch.Thumb.checked]: "1rem" },
  }),
  popup: css({
    marginTop: { [Select.Popup.side.bottom]: "4px" },
    marginBottom: { [Select.Popup.side.top]: "4px" },
  }),
}
```

- **A misspelt state is a type error.** `Switch.Root.chekced` does not exist, and
  your editor completes the states a part has.
- **Hover shows the library's own words.** Each state carries its description,
  `Present when the switch is checked.`, as Base UI writes it.
- **It is a condition like any other.** A state nests inside another, sits beside
  `media()`, reads through a [relation](/docs/styling/relations)
  (`field.within(Switch.Root.disabled)`) and goes in [recipes](/docs/styling/recipes).
  The compiler checks it as it checks every condition: above, `checked` and
  `disabled` can hold together, so the nested value says which wins.
- **Nothing ships.** Each entry is a plain string, `Switch.Root.checked` is
  `"[data-checked]"`; the compiler reads it and it leaves nothing behind.

The style is not tied to one part, so one handle can style several parts that
share a state, or the same state of your own component.

## Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/states
```

Apply the handles to Base UI's parts with [`props()`](/docs/styling/external-components),
since the parts do not read `sx`:

```tsx
import { props as styleProps } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { Switch as Base } from "@base-ui/react/switch"

export function Switch() {
  return (
    <Base.Root {...styleProps(styles.track)}>
      <Base.Thumb {...styleProps(styles.thumb)} />
    </Base.Root>
  )
}
```

## The vocabularies

Each one is generated from what its library publishes about its parts, so the
names are the library's own and a state the library does not document is not
there. CI regenerates them and checks every name against the library's exports.

| Import                               | Library                                 | Generated from                                                   |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@kirana-style/states/base-ui`       | Base UI                                 | each part's `*DataAttributes` declarations                       |
| `@kirana-style/states/ark-ui`        | Ark UI, on React, Vue, Solid and Svelte | `@zag-js/docs`, the reference of the Zag machines Ark UI runs on |
| `@kirana-style/states/react-aria`    | React Aria Components                   | each component's render props, by their `@selector`              |
| `@kirana-style/states/reka-ui`       | Reka UI, for Vue                        | each part's template, as the package ships it                    |
| `@kirana-style/states/bits-ui`       | Bits UI, for Svelte                     | each part's state class, by the types of its `props`             |
| `@kirana-style/states/ng-primitives` | Angular Primitives                      | each primitive's data bindings, and the interactions it turns on |

They differ where the libraries do:

- **Base UI and Ark UI** have parts: `Select.Popup.side.bottom`,
  `Switch.Thumb.state.checked`. Ark UI marks most states with one attribute's
  values (`data-state="checked"`), so `state` holds one key per value.
- **Ark UI's orientation**, which Zag describes only in prose, takes its values
  from Zag's own type, as Base UI's does: `Tabs.Root.orientation.vertical`.
- **React Aria** names a component per part, with no namespace:
  `Button.focusVisible`, `ListBoxItem.selected`. A state a component inherits
  from another's render props is there too.
- **Reka UI, Bits UI and Angular Primitives** document their states only in
  prose, so their vocabularies are read from the code the packages ship, with
  no descriptions. A value the code computes rather than writes, such as Reka
  UI's `side`, is its attribute's presence.
- **Angular Primitives** keys the primitive named for its component
  (`ngpPopover`) as `Root`, and lists the interactions a primitive turns on
  (hover, press, focus) as its states.

| State                     | Example                       | Selector                     |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Present or absent         | `Switch.Root.checked`         | `[data-checked]`             |
| One of a set of values    | `Select.Popup.side.inlineEnd` | `[data-side="inline-end"]`   |
| Free text or a number     | `Accordion.Item.index`        | `[data-index]`, its presence |
| A component without parts | `Toggle.pressed`              | `[data-pressed]`             |

How states are named:

- **Values are in camel case:** `inlineEnd` for `inline-end`.
- **React Aria's states are named for its render props, without `is`:**
  `isFocusVisible` is `focusVisible`.

## States that never hold together

A part is checked or unchecked, open or closed, never both. Two values of one
attribute say so on their own, but Base UI marks those with two attributes
(`data-checked`, `data-unchecked`), and nothing in the selectors proves they
exclude each other. So a property set under both is reported as
`ambiguous-precedence`, a warning that the order between them is left to chance.

Each vocabulary exports the groups its library sets one at a time. Give them to
[`conditions.exclusive`](/docs/reference/config) in your configuration, and the
compiler knows:

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"
import { exclusive } from "@kirana-style/states/base-ui"

export default defineConfig({ conditions: { exclusive } })
```

The groups are what the library documents: a state and its opposite, both on one
part.

| A state         | and its opposite |
| --------------- | ---------------- |
| `checked`       | `unchecked`      |
| `open`          | `closed`         |
| `startingStyle` | `endingStyle`    |
| `valid`         | `invalid`        |

Ark UI and React Aria mark those with one attribute's values or not at all, so
their lists are empty.

### One look for several libraries

A design system that writes each component once for several libraries spreads
every library's key for a state: Base UI's `[data-starting-style]` and React Aria's
`[data-entering]` for a popup's first frame. A component is built on one library,
so those keys never meet on an element, but nothing in the selectors says so, and
each pair is reported. `exclusiveAcross()` gives the compiler one vocabulary per
library; two keys that no single library sets are then exclusive:

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"
import { exclusiveAcross } from "@kirana-style/states"
import * as baseUi from "@kirana-style/states/base-ui"
import * as reactAria from "@kirana-style/states/react-aria"

export default defineConfig({
  conditions: {
    exclusive: [...baseUi.exclusive, ...reactAria.exclusive],
    exclusiveAcross: exclusiveAcross(baseUi, reactAria),
  },
})
```

Keys that both libraries set, such as `[data-disabled]`, still meet as they would
on any element.

## Other libraries, and your own components

A vocabulary is a plain object of selectors, so writing one takes a few lines. Any
library that marks state with data attributes works: Radix and its ports
(`data-state="open"`), Reka UI, Bits UI, or the components you write yourself. Put it in a module of your project:

```ts file="src/states.ts"
export const Dialog = {
  Content: {
    open: '[data-state="open"]',
    closed: '[data-state="closed"]',
  },
} as const
```

```tsx
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { Dialog } from "./states"

const content = css({
  opacity: { base: 1, [Dialog.Content.closed]: 0 },
  scale: { [Dialog.Content.open]: 1, [Dialog.Content.closed]: 0.95 },
})
```

`as const` is what makes a misspelt state an error. The compiler knows two values
of one attribute never hold together, so `open` and `closed` need no nesting.

## Next

- [Conditions](/docs/styling/conditions): every key a condition can be.
- [Relations](/docs/styling/relations): style an element from another element's
  state.
---
# Relations
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/relations
# Relations

Sometimes an element's style depends on _another_ element's state: a label that
dims when its field is disabled, an icon that rotates when its menu is open.

A relation names that connection once, and both ends refer to it:

```tsx
import { css, relation } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const field = relation("field")

const styles = {
  root: css({ display: "grid", gap: "0.25rem" }),
  label: css({
    opacity: {
      base: 1,
      [field.within('[data-disabled="true"]')]: 0.5,
    },
  }),
}

export function Field({ disabled, children }) {
  return (
    <div data-disabled={disabled} sx={[field.anchor, styles.root]}>
      <label sx={styles.label}>{children}</label>
    </div>
  )
}
```

`field.anchor` marks the element whose state is read. `field.within(state)` reads
it from a descendant.

<!-- ::figure-relation -->

## The four reads

| Read             | Means                                | Tailwind equivalent  |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------ | -------------------- |
| `within(state?)` | the anchor is an **ancestor**        | `group-*`            |
| `parent(state?)` | the anchor is the **parent**         | `*:`, from the child |
| `after(state?)`  | the anchor is an **earlier sibling** | `peer-*`             |
| `before(state?)` | the anchor is a **later sibling**    | none                 |

The `state` argument is any selector the anchor may match, such as
`'[data-open]'`, `":hover"` or `'[data-size="lg"]'`. Omit it to mean "the anchor exists", which is
how you style by structure rather than state.

## Why declare it at all

Because the compiler checks it. Two errors you get for free:

- **`relation-without-anchor`**: a style reads a relation, but nothing applies
  its anchor. In a class-string system this is a `group-hover:` that silently
  never fires. An application's build checks the relations whose module it
  compiled, so a shared component may read an ancestor that only some
  applications render; `kirana-style check` checks every relation in the project.
- **`relation-placement`**: the anchor cannot be proven to be in the right
  position: `after()` used where the anchor is not an earlier sibling, for
  example.

A relation that is anchored and never read is reported too (`relation-unused`),
so dead relations do not accumulate. One that its module keeps to itself is
checked in every build. One that is exported is checked where the whole project
is compiled, by `kirana-style check` and in your editor: a bundler build compiles
only the modules it reaches, so a shared component's reader may simply not be
in this application. And because a relation is identified by its
package and name, two modules of one package that both write `relation("card")`
would share one marker without meaning to: `relation-name-collision` names both
files. Export the relation from one module and import it where it is read.

A module that holds only the reads, with no `css()` of its own, compiles them too.

A component set installed one item at a time can have a reader whose anchor's
component is not installed: a select that fills the Field it sits in, in a
project without Field. Declare that relation optional, and the read is left
alone where no anchor exists, where it never matches:

```ts
export const fieldScope = relation("field", { optional: true })
```

Where both are installed, an optional relation is placed and checked like any
other; only the missing anchor is not an error.

### Nested in its own kind

A component can read its own relation to know it sits inside another of its
kind: shadcn/ui's FieldGroup tightens a group directly inside another group. The
group anchors the relation and reads it from the parent:

```tsx
const group = relation("field-group")

const styles = {
  group: css(group.anchor, {
    gap: { base: "1.75rem", [group.parent()]: "1rem" },
  }),
}
```

An element that carries an anchor and reads it can only mean an outer one, so the
placement check accepts it, for both kinds of ancestor read. A parent read reaches
the anchor's children only, where `within` reaches any depth: a port of `*:w-full`
written with `within` would also widen a grandchild inside a wrapper.

The same holds beside it. shadcn/ui's `ItemContent` keeps its width when it
follows another, and its caller is the one that repeats it, so the part anchors
the relation and reads it `after()`:

```tsx
const content = relation("item-content")

const styles = {
  content: css(content.anchor, {
    flex: { base: "1 1 0%", [content.after()]: "none" },
  }),
}
```

The placement check accepts an `after()` or `before()` read on an element that
carries its own anchor: another instance beside it, which only the caller's tree
holds.

## Anchors are placed, not guessed

The anchor must sit on the element whose state you are reading. That sounds
obvious, and it is the most common mistake when porting: the state lives on the
root, the anchor gets attached to an inner wrapper, and the read never matches.

```tsx
// The attribute and the anchor belong on the same element.
<div data-state={open ? "open" : "closed"} sx={[menu.anchor, styles.root]}>
```

## `:has()` is not a relation

Styling a parent by its children is a plain condition, because the selector does
it on its own:

```tsx
css({
  paddingBlockEnd: { ":has([data-slot='footer'])": "0.5rem" },
})
```

Relations exist for the other direction (a descendant or sibling reading state
that lives elsewhere), where CSS needs the two ends to agree on a class.

## Precedence

A relation read is its own condition class, ranked below attributes and
pseudo-classes on the element itself, and above at-rules
([ladder](/docs/styling/precedence), step 3). So an element's own `:hover` beats a
value that depends on an ancestor's `:hover`, which is what an author usually
means.

A parent read is the exception: it ranks as a pseudo-class, as the
`:where([data-slot] > *)` selector it replaces does. A group inside another group
takes the nested gap over a style's wider one without restating it under every
style.
---
# Contextual styles
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/contextual
# Contextual styles

`select` styles elements _below_ an element you render, by name or attribute:

```tsx
import { css, select } from "@kirana-style/core"

const button = css({
  display: "inline-flex",
  gap: "0.5rem",
  // Every svg inside this button, unless the svg says otherwise.
  [select.descendant("svg")]: {
    width: "1rem",
    height: "1rem",
    flexShrink: 0,
  },
})
```

`select.descendant(target)` reaches any depth; `select.child(target)` only direct
children. Both are top-level keys holding a style object, like a pseudo-element.

## They lose to the element's own styles

Contextual rules are written to a layer below element styles, so anything the
target sets for itself wins, whatever conditions it carries.

That is the point. In a class-based system a parent's `[&_svg]:size-4` competes
with the icon's own size class and usually wins, which is why such rules grow
guards like `:not([class*='size-'])`. Here the guard is unnecessary: give the icon
a size and it keeps it.

```tsx
<button sx={button}>
  <Icon sx={css({ width: "1.25rem", height: "1.25rem" })} />{" "}
  {/* 1.25rem wins */}
</button>
```

## What a target may be

One compound selector: an element name, attribute selectors and pseudo-classes,
alone or together:

```tsx
select.descendant("svg")
select.child("li")
select.descendant('[data-slot="indicator"]')
select.child("span:last-child") // the last span child
select.descendant("a:hover") // a link while it is hovered
```

No combinators (`a > b`) and no pseudo-elements: a target is the element itself.

## A state under a target is the parent's

A condition nested inside a target's style object reads the element that carries
the style, as it does under a pseudo-element. The target's own state goes into the
target:

```tsx
const nav = css({
  // Links turn red while the nav is hovered.
  [select.child("a")]: { color: { ":hover": "red" } },
  // A link turns red while it is hovered itself.
  [select.child("a:hover")]: { color: "red" },
})
```

Tailwind's `*:hover:text-red-500` means the second. The first compiles, and the
compiler adds an info (`select-state-on-parent`) suggesting the target form. When
the parent's state is what you mean, read it through a
[relation](/docs/styling/relations) and the info goes away.

Class selectors are not targets: Kirana's class names are hashes, and a
handwritten class is markup the compiler cannot verify. An unsupported target is
an error (`unsupported-contextual-target`).

## When to reach for it

- Styling an icon, a bullet, or any element a library renders inside yours.
- Giving a wrapper's children a shared rhythm you do not want to repeat on each
  one.

When you own the element, style it directly instead: it is easier to read, and it
lands in the higher layer where it belongs.

## Alternatives

| Situation                                                 | Use                                            |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| The element is rendered by a component that spreads props | [`props()`](/docs/styling/external-components) |
| The element's style depends on an ancestor's _state_      | [relations](/docs/styling/relations)           |
| The element is below you and you just need a default      | `select`                                       |
---
# Recipes
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/recipes
# Recipes

A recipe is a component's variants in one place: a base style, named groups of
options, and the combinations that need a value of their own.

```tsx
import { recipe } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const button = recipe({
  base: {
    display: "inline-flex",
    alignItems: "center",
    borderRadius: "0.5rem",
    fontWeight: 500,
  },
  variants: {
    tone: {
      solid: { backgroundColor: "black", color: "white" },
      quiet: { backgroundColor: "transparent", color: "black" },
    },
    size: {
      sm: { paddingInline: "0.5rem", fontSize: "0.75rem" },
      md: { paddingInline: "0.875rem", fontSize: "0.875rem" },
    },
  },
  compoundVariants: [
    { tone: "quiet", size: "sm", css: { paddingInline: "0.375rem" } },
  ],
  defaultVariants: { tone: "solid", size: "md" },
})

<button sx={button({ tone: "quiet" })} />
```

## Static calls compile to a constant

When the options are known at build time, the call disappears: the element gets a
class string, and no recipe table ships. When an option is a runtime value, the
recipe resolves through the small private runtime instead, and the compiler tells
you it did (`dynamic-variant`, informational).

```tsx
button({ tone: "quiet" }) // compiles to a constant
button({ tone: props.tone }) // resolved at runtime, reported as dynamic-variant
```

Both work. The diagnostic exists so you can see which components carry a runtime
cost.

## Slots

A component with several parts gives them one recipe. Each variant lists the
slots it changes, and calling the recipe returns a handle per slot:

```tsx
export const field = recipe({
  slots: ["root", "label", "input"],
  base: {
    root: { display: "grid", gap: "0.25rem" },
    label: { fontSize: "0.875rem" },
    input: { borderRadius: "0.375rem" },
  },
  variants: {
    invalid: {
      true: {
        label: { color: "crimson" },
        input: { borderColor: "crimson" },
      },
    },
  },
})

const parts = field({ invalid })
<div sx={parts.root}>
  <label sx={parts.label} />
  <input sx={parts.input} />
</div>
```

Boolean variants are written as the string keys `"true"` and `"false"`, and
called with real booleans.

## Checks

- An option that names a group or value the recipe does not define is an error
  (`unknown-variant`).
- A style that names a slot the recipe does not declare is an error
  (`unknown-slot`).

Both catch the rename that used to leave a component silently unstyled.

## Recipes or plain handles?

Use a recipe when a component has variants a caller chooses by name. Use plain
handles when it does not: an object of `css()` handles is simpler to read, and
merging already gives you composition:

```tsx
const styles = {
  root: css({ … }),
  open: css({ … }),
}
<div sx={[styles.root, isOpen && styles.open]} />
```
---
# Animation
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/animation
# Animation

## Keyframes

`keyframes()` returns a name you can use as `animationName` from any module:

```tsx
import { css, keyframes } from "@kirana-style/core"

const pulse = keyframes({
  "0%, 100%": { opacity: 1 },
  "50%": { opacity: 0.5 },
})

const dot = css({
  animationName: pulse,
  animationDuration: "2s",
  animationIterationCount: "infinite",
  animationTimingFunction: "ease-in-out",
})
```

The name is hashed like a class, so two modules that define the same frames share
one `@keyframes` rule, and a set of frames nothing references emits nothing. That
holds for a library too: a production build with the Vite or Rolldown plugin writes
a library's animations only if the finished bundle still uses them, so importing a
scale from a module that also declares keyframes ships none of them.

## Transitions

Transitions are ordinary declarations, and the thing worth saying is about the
property you name:

```tsx
const panel = css({
  translate: { base: "0 -4px", "[data-open]": "0 0" },
  opacity: { base: 0, "[data-open]": 1 },
  transitionProperty: "translate, opacity", // not "transform"
  transitionDuration: "150ms",
})
```

**Animate the property you actually set.** `translate`, `scale` and `rotate` are
separate properties from `transform`, and a transition on it does not interpolate
them. This is one of the most common reasons an animation silently
does nothing.

## Animating a custom property

A custom property does not interpolate unless the browser knows its type. Register
it by giving the token a syntax, and it becomes animatable:

```tsx
import { defineTokens } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const fade = defineTokens("fade", {
  stop: { value: "0%", syntax: "<length-percentage>", inherits: false },
})
```

That emits an `@property` rule, so a transition or keyframe on `--fade-stop`
animates smoothly instead of jumping. A registered token may also be a keyframe
key, and a frame takes a custom property by its name, as `css()` does:

```tsx
const reveal = keyframes({
  from: { "--scroll-fade-t": "0px" },
  to: { "--scroll-fade-t": "24px" },
})
```

## Respecting motion preferences

`prefers-reduced-motion` is a condition like any other, and it ranks above width
queries:

```tsx
const item = css({
  transitionDuration: {
    base: "150ms",
    "@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)": "0s",
  },
})
```

## Entry and exit states

Libraries that animate elements in and out usually expose attributes for the two
edges, such as `[data-starting-style]` and `[data-ending-style]`. Those are
plain attribute conditions. Because they never appear at the same time but the
selectors cannot prove it, declare them as exclusive once in
[`conditions.exclusive`](/docs/reference/config), and the compiler stops asking
which of the two wins.
---
# Values known at runtime
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/dynamic
# Values known at runtime

Kirana compiles styles, but some values are only known when the component runs: a
progress width, a colour from data, a variant from props. Those are fine to write
where you write everything else: the compiler classifies each one and picks a
representation.

## Three classes of value

**Static.** Known at build time. Compiles to a class. Nothing else happens.

**Finite dynamic.** A choice between a known set of static values:

```tsx
<div sx={css({ color: tone === "danger" ? "crimson" : "black" })} />
```

Both values are compiled to classes, and the element gets a class _expression_, a
ternary between two class strings. Still no CSS at runtime.

**Open dynamic.** A value the compiler cannot enumerate:

```tsx
<div sx={css({ inlineSize: `${percent}%` })} />
```

The declaration becomes `inline-size: var(--k…)`, and the element gets that custom
property in its `style` attribute. One rule, any value, and the browser does the
rest. The compiler reports it as `dynamic-bridged` (informational), so you can see
where runtime values enter your styles.

<!-- ::figure-dynamic -->

## The branch budget

A finite dynamic value with too many branches would multiply classes, so there is
a budget: 16 branches by default, configurable as
[`dynamic.branchBudget`](/docs/reference/config). Past it, the compiler stops and
reports `branch-budget-exceeded` rather than emitting a combinatorial explosion.
Usually that is a sign the value should be a bridge, or a
[recipe](/docs/styling/recipes).

## What ships

A module that needs runtime merging or a bridge imports a private helper that is
under 1.1 kB minified and gzipped. It merges class strings and sets custom
properties. It never parses styles and never generates CSS.

Modules with only static styles import nothing.

## What is not allowed

Two things the compiler refuses, because they would mean generating styles at
runtime:

```tsx
css({ [key]: value }) // error: dynamic-key
css({ ...someObject }) // error: dynamic-spread
```

A style built from data is refused too. Some calls only ever build a plain object,
never a handle, and a merge cannot apply an object:

- `Object.fromEntries`, `Object.assign` and `Object.create`;
- `JSON.parse` and `structuredClone`.

Passing what one returns to `css()`, `cx()` or `sx` is `not-evaluable`:

```tsx
css(Object.fromEntries(entries)) // error: not-evaluable
```

Write the declarations out instead. A value the compiler cannot read in a handle
position is otherwise taken as a handle known at runtime, which is what lets
`css(base, props.sx)` merge a caller's style.

A style's _shape_ is fixed at build time; its _values_ may vary. If you need a
different property depending on state, write both and choose between handles:

```tsx
<div sx={vertical ? styles.vertical : styles.horizontal} />
```

## Keeping runtime values honest

- Prefer a finite set when there is one: a class expression costs nothing in the
  browser, a bridge costs a custom property.
- Bridge lengths, colours and numbers: values that vary continuously.
- If a page reports many `dynamic-bridged` values you did not expect, something
  that could be static is not: usually a token read through an intermediate
  variable the evaluator cannot follow.
- A helper that builds a value per key folds when its inputs do. Inside a helper,
  the `Object` functions over entries, keys and values, and `.map()` with a
  callback written in place, run at build time:

  ```tsx
  const END = { base: radius.lg, [vega]: radius.md }
  const perStyle = (value: (r: string) => string) =>
    Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(END).map(([key, r]) => [key, value(r)]))

  css({ borderRadius: { ":first-child": perStyle((r) => `${r} 0 0 ${r}`) } })
  ```
---
# Fallback values
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/fallbacks
# Fallback values

A browser drops a declaration whose value it does not understand and keeps the
one before it. `firstThatWorks()` uses that: you list the values a property
should try, the preferred first, and Kirana writes the property once per value.

```tsx
import { css, firstThatWorks } from "@kirana-style/core"

const screen = css({
  minHeight: firstThatWorks("100dvh", "100vh"),
  position: firstThatWorks("sticky", "-webkit-sticky"),
})
```

```css
.k7U_ulId {
  min-height: 100vh;
  min-height: 100dvh;
}
```

The preferred value is written last because the last declaration a browser
understands is the one it keeps. The arguments go in reading order (the value
you want, then what to fall back to), the same order as StyleX's helper and as
`var(--x, fallback)`.

## Where it works

Anywhere a property takes a value: inside conditions, recipes, `keyframes()`
frames, [`positionTry()`](/docs/styling/anchor-positioning) blocks and
[`viewTransition()`](/docs/styling/view-transitions) parts. Every value goes
through the same checks as a value written alone, so tokens resolve, units are
checked and shorthands expand:

```tsx
const ink = css({ color: firstThatWorks(brand.ink, "#334") })
const pad = css({
  padding: firstThatWorks("max(1rem, env(safe-area-inset-top))", "1rem"),
})
```

The run is one atom. Its class name covers every value in order, so two styles
with the same run share one class, and swapping the order is a different style.
Hover, `kirana-style trace` and `kirana-style analyze` show it as `firstThatWorks(100dvh, 100vh)`.

## What it refuses

| Written                                            | Diagnostic                                                            |
| -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `firstThatWorks()`                                 | `invalid-fallback`: it needs at least one value                       |
| `firstThatWorks(firstThatWorks(a, b), c)`          | `invalid-fallback`: runs do not nest                                  |
| `firstThatWorks(value, "100vh")`, value at runtime | `invalid-fallback`: every value must be known at build time           |
| `padding: firstThatWorks("1rem 2rem", "var(--p)")` | `invalid-fallback`: the values must set the same longhands            |
| `"--gap": firstThatWorks("1rem", "16px")`          | `fallback-on-variable` (warning): a custom property accepts any value |

The longhand rule exists because a shorthand with a `var()` cannot be split at
build time: one value would set four longhands and the other the shorthand, and a
browser would keep a fallback for some sides and the preferred value for others.
A custom property never falls back, because the browser accepts any text for it;
put the fallback where the variable is read, `var(--gap, 16px)`.

One value is that value: `firstThatWorks("grid")` is `"grid"`, which keeps code
migrated from StyleX working.

## When to use `supports()` instead

`firstThatWorks()` fits one property whose newer value a browser either parses or
drops. When several properties have to change together, or the old browser parses
the new value but renders it wrongly, use a [`supports()`](/docs/styling/conditions)
condition instead.
---
# Anchor positioning
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/anchor-positioning
# Anchor positioning

CSS anchor positioning places an element against another one, and
`position-try-fallbacks` lists where to put it when the first place overflows.
The built-in fallbacks (`flip-block`, `flip-inline`) mirror the position;
`positionTry()` defines your own.

```tsx
import { css, positionTry } from "@kirana-style/core"

const below = positionTry({
  positionArea: "bottom span-right",
  marginTop: "4px",
})
const above = positionTry({ positionArea: "top", marginBottom: "4px" })

export const tooltip = css({
  position: "absolute",
  positionAnchor: "--trigger",
  positionArea: "top",
  positionTryFallbacks: `${below}, ${above}, flip-inline`,
})
```

`positionTry()` returns a dashed ident, `--kp…`, and emits an `@position-try`
rule with that name:

```css
@layer kirana.tokens {
  @position-try --kp9KfV {
    position-area: bottom span-right;
    margin-top: 4px;
  }
}
```

The name is hashed from the declarations, like a keyframes name, so the same
block defined in two modules is one rule. The rule ships only when something
refers to it: a `positionTryFallbacks` value, a template string, or an export
another module reads.

## What a fallback may set

An `@position-try` block accepts the properties that place and size the box:

| Group          | Properties                              |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Inset          | `top`, `insetInline`, …                 |
| Margin         | the margin properties                   |
| Sizing         | `width`, `maxInlineSize`, …             |
| Self-alignment | `alignSelf`, `justifySelf`, `placeSelf` |
| Anchoring      | `positionAnchor`, `positionArea`        |

A browser ignores anything else without a word, so Kirana reports it instead:

```tsx
positionTry({ color: "red" })
// invalid-position-try: color has no effect in @position-try
```

Values are plain: a fallback has no hover state or breakpoint of its own, so a
conditional value is `invalid-position-try` too. Tokens and
[`firstThatWorks()`](/docs/styling/fallbacks) work as they do in a style.

## Anchors

Kirana does not manage `anchor-name` for you. An anchor name must be unique on
the page, the same as an `id`, so name it where you know the element is unique:
a `css()` style on that element, or an inline `style` when the name depends on
data.
---
# View transitions
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/styling/view-transitions
# View transitions

During a view transition the browser draws an element's old and new states in
four pseudo-elements, and `viewTransition()` styles them for every element of one
transition class:

- `::view-transition-group`
- `::view-transition-image-pair`
- `::view-transition-old`
- `::view-transition-new`

```tsx
import { css, keyframes, media, viewTransition } from "@kirana-style/core"

const fadeOut = keyframes({ to: { opacity: 0 } })
const slideIn = keyframes({ from: { translate: "0 1rem" } })

export const slide = viewTransition({
  old: { animationName: fadeOut, animationDuration: "150ms" },
  new: {
    animationName: slideIn,
    animationDuration: {
      base: "250ms",
      [media("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)")]: "0s",
    },
  },
})
```

The result is a class, `kw…`, that names itself as the element's
`view-transition-class`. The parts select every element of that class:

```css
@layer kirana.tokens {
  .kwBm2s {
    view-transition-class: kwBm2s;
  }
  ::view-transition-old(*.kwBm2s) {
    animation-name: kfBcwa;
    animation-duration: 150ms;
  }
  ::view-transition-new(*.kwBm2s) {
    animation-name: kfWkJE;
    animation-duration: 250ms;
  }
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    ::view-transition-new(*.kwBm2s) {
      animation-duration: 0s;
    }
  }
}
```

## Using it

The value is a style handle and a class name at the same time. Put it in `sx`
next to the element's other styles:

```tsx
<li sx={[card, slide]} style={{ viewTransitionName: `item-${item.id}` }} />
```

or pass it where a framework asks for a transition class, such as React's
`<ViewTransition share={slide}>`.

Kirana does not set `view-transition-name`. The browser needs it to be unique
among the elements taking part in one transition, so it usually comes from data
(an id, a slug) and belongs where that data is.

## The parts

| Key         | Pseudo-element                   | Typical use                                 |
| ----------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `group`     | `::view-transition-group()`      | the size and position animation, its timing |
| `imagePair` | `::view-transition-image-pair()` | isolation and blending of the two images    |
| `old`       | `::view-transition-old()`        | how the old state leaves                    |
| `new`       | `::view-transition-new()`        | how the new state arrives                   |

Each part is a style object. A property may be conditional on `media()` or
`supports()`; the pseudo-elements have no hover or attribute state, so other
conditions are `invalid-view-transition`, as is a key other than these four.
Values take tokens, keyframes and [`firstThatWorks()`](/docs/styling/fallbacks).

Like keyframes, the class is hashed from its parts, so the same transition
defined twice is one rule, and it ships only where something uses it.
---
# Tokens
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tokens/overview
# Tokens

A token is a named value your styles refer to. In Kirana it is an ordinary
imported constant, so your editor shows the value, "go to definition" works, and
nothing needs code generation.

```tsx
import { defineTokens } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const space = defineTokens("space", {
  1: "0.25rem",
  2: "0.5rem",
  4: "1rem",
})

css({ gap: space[2] })
```

The first argument is the **namespace**. It has to be unique in a package: two
groups claiming one namespace is an error (`token-namespace-collision`).

A token's identity carries its package, so packages may each have a `theme` group
and compile to different variables, which keeps libraries from overwriting each
other's. Because they then read alike, the compiler points such a pair out with an
info (`token-namespace-shared`), and `kirana-style export` names each token's
package.

## Inlined or a custom property

By default a token is **inlined**: `gap: space[2]` compiles to `gap: 0.5rem`. The
token costs nothing, and unreferenced tokens emit nothing at all.

Ask for a custom property when the value must be _overridable at runtime_, for a
theme, a mode, or a value a parent hands down:

```tsx
export const theme = defineTokens(
  "theme",
  { surface: "white", text: "black" },
  { variable: true }
)
```

Now `theme.surface` compiles to `var(--k…)`, the defaults are declared once in the
`kirana.tokens` layer, and anything below can override them.

|                        | Inlined                      | `variable: true`                  |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Compiles to            | the literal value            | `var(--k…)`                       |
| Overridable at runtime | no                           | yes                               |
| Cost                   | none                         | one declaration per token used    |
| Use for                | scales: spacing, radii, type | themes, modes, values handed down |

## Per-mode values

A token can carry a light and a dark value:

```tsx
export const theme = defineTokens(
  "theme",
  { surface: { light: "white", dark: "oklch(0.21 0 0)" } },
  { variable: true }
)
```

Colours are usually better written as one `light-dark()` value, which needs no
variable at all and no mode plumbing. Use `{ light, dark }` for values
`light-dark()` cannot express, such as a shadow's opacity, a blend mode or an
image filter. [Themes and modes](/docs/tokens/themes-and-modes) covers the difference.

## Registered tokens

Give a token a syntax and it becomes a real registered property, which means the
browser can animate it:

```tsx
export const fade = defineTokens("fade", {
  stop: { value: "0%", syntax: "<length-percentage>", inherits: false },
})
```

This emits `@property`, and the token may then be used as a keyframe key.

With the universal syntax a token may have no value at all. It starts unset, and
every reference to it falls back to nothing (`var(--k…,)`), so a chain of such
tokens lists only the parts an element sets. That is how Tailwind composes
`filter`:

```tsx
export const step = defineTokens("step", {
  blur: { syntax: "*", inherits: false },
  grey: { syntax: "*", inherits: false },
})

css({
  [step.grey]: "grayscale(100%)",
  filter: `${step.blur} ${step.grey}`, // grayscale(100%)
})
```

## Tokens nothing uses

A production build writes a variable token's declaration only when something uses
it. That means a rule that reads it, or the finished JavaScript still naming it, as
`el.style.gap = space.lg` does. A design system can define a hundred variable
tokens, and a page that reads ten ships ten.

A token read by code the compiler never sees needs saying so. Examples: a plain
script, a server-only template, a third party. Declare it `runtime: true`, for one
token or the whole group, and it is always written:

```tsx
export const brand = defineTokens(
  "brand",
  { accent: "oklch(0.7 0.15 150)" },
  { runtime: true }
)
```

`runtime: true` implies `variable: true`. If code rendered after the stylesheet
names a token it left out, as a server-only component can, the build stops and
names the token, so a missing declaration never reaches a page.

The dev server, `kirana-style check` and bundlers other than Vite and Rolldown
write every variable token, as before.

## A token as a style key

A variable token can be the _key_ of a declaration, which sets that custom
property for the subtree:

```tsx
css({ [ctx.iconSize]: "0.875rem" })
```

That is how a control tells the icons inside it how big to be, without either side
knowing the other's class names.

## What the compiler checks

- A token that does not exist: `unknown-token`.
- A token reference computed at runtime: `dynamic-token`, since tokens are
  build-time values by design.
- `defineTheme` on a token that is not a custom property: `token-not-variable`.

## Next

- [Using the scales preset](/docs/tokens/preset-scales): Tailwind's vocabulary,
  ready to import.
- [Semantic tokens](/docs/tokens/semantic-tokens): building your own layer on
  top.
---
# Starting with no preset, then scales
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tokens/preset-scales
# From no preset, to scales

Kirana has no opinion about what your spacing scale is. There is no default theme
to override and nothing to reset. You start with plain CSS, and adopt a vocabulary
when you want one.

## Level 1: no tokens at all

Perfectly valid, and the right way to start a small thing:

```tsx
const card = css({
  borderRadius: "0.75rem",
  padding: "1rem",
  backgroundColor: "white",
})
```

Nothing to install, nothing to learn. The compiler is already doing its job:
atoms, merge rules, diagnostics.

## Level 2: the scales preset

When repeating raw values gets old, `@kirana-style/preset-scales` gives you a
vocabulary: the palette, spacing, type ramp, radii, shadows, blurs, durations,
easings and breakpoints of Tailwind CSS v4, generated from its own theme, as
typed tokens.

```tsx
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { color, space, radius, breakpoint } from "@kirana-style/preset-scales"

const card = css({
  borderRadius: radius.xl,
  padding: { base: space[4], [breakpoint.md]: space[6] },
  backgroundColor: color.zinc50,
})
```

There is no configuration step: you import what you use, and the bundler adapter
compiles the preset from `node_modules` as it compiles your own modules. A token
nothing references emits nothing, so importing the package costs nothing in the
output.

### What is in it

| Export                                                                           | Contents                                                        |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `color`                                                                          | 26 hues × 11 steps in `oklch`, plus `black` and `white`         |
| `space`, `spacing()`                                                             | `0`, `px`, `0.5` … `96`, in rem; any quarter step               |
| `fontFamily`, `fontSize`, `lineHeight`, `fontWeight`, `letterSpacing`, `leading` | the type ramp, with line heights paired to sizes                |
| `radius`, `shadow`, `blur`                                                       | the radii, shadows and blurs                                    |
| `duration`, `easing`                                                             | motion values                                                   |
| `zIndex`, `screen`, `containerSize`                                              | layering, and raw widths                                        |
| `breakpoint`, `containerQuery`                                                   | ready-made conditions: `[breakpoint.md]`, `[containerQuery.lg]` |

`space` names the steps Tailwind lists. For a step between them, as shadcn/ui
writes `pl-9.5`, `spacing(9.5)` gives `2.375rem`: a quarter of a rem per unit. The
compiler folds the call into the value, so it costs nothing at runtime.

`breakpoint.*` and `containerQuery.*` are separate because they share step names
and mean different things: one queries the viewport, the other a container.

> [!NOTE] It is data, not a design system
> The preset deliberately stops at scales. It has no `primary`, `muted` or
> `background`: those are decisions about _your_ product, and they belong in your
> own semantic layer.

## Level 3: your own semantic layer

The next step is naming the decisions: what `primary` is, what a card's surface
is, what a border looks like in dark mode. That is
[semantic tokens](/docs/tokens/semantic-tokens), and it is where a design system
starts.

## Level 4: packaging a preset of your own

A preset is a module that exports token groups. To share yours, export them from a
package and import them like any other module:

```tsx
// @acme/tokens
export const brand = defineTokens("brand", { … }, { variable: true })

// an app
import { brand } from "@acme/tokens"
```

No registration and no plugin. Inside a workspace the package is compiled with
your own modules. Installed from npm, list it in [`libraries`](/docs/reference/config#libraries),
so its `defineTokens()` calls are compiled too; a token the app reads at runtime
would otherwise throw in the browser.

## The utility grammar

`@kirana-style/preset-scales/preset` declares Tailwind v4's utility names over these
scales, so `sx="px-4 text-sm"` works once the preset is listed:

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
import scales from "@kirana-style/preset-scales/preset"

export default defineConfig({ presets: [scales()] })
```

The `/preset` entry holds only data and imports no tokens, because a
configuration file runs uncompiled. See [utility strings](/docs/styling/utilities).

The grammar composes some utilities through `compose`, a group of registered,
non-inheriting tokens mirroring Tailwind's `--tw-*` properties, such as
`compose.shadow` and `compose["translate-x"]`. A style object can set them too,
and then combines with those utilities on the same element:

```tsx
import { compose } from "@kirana-style/preset-scales"

css({ [compose.shadow]: "0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.05)" })
```

`animation` holds the keyframes the animation utilities play:

| From                                                   | Keyframes                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tailwind                                               | `spin`, `ping`, `pulse`, `bounce`                              |
| `tw-animate-css` (MIT, credited in the package README) | `enter`, `exit`, and the accordion, collapsible and caret ones |

A style reads them by name:

```tsx
import { animation } from "@kirana-style/preset-scales"

css({ animationName: animation.spin, animationDuration: "1s" })
```

## How the grammar behaves

The grammar is data, but a few of its rules decide results you will notice. Each
matches what Tailwind v4 renders, and a property test checks every one of the
7,391 utilities it generates against the equivalent style object.

**A font size carries its line height.** `text-sm` sets the font size and the line
height paired with it. The pair is a default, not a declaration of its own:

- `text-sm leading-6` keeps `leading-6`, whichever comes first;
- `text-sm/relaxed` replaces the pair with `leading-relaxed`.

The paired line heights are Tailwind's ratios written as numbers rounded up at five
decimals (`lineHeight.sm` is `1.42858` for `1.25 / 0.875`). A CSS minifier would
round a `calc()` down and cost 14px text a fraction of a pixel per line; rounded up,
a line is never short.

**Uniform box utilities are logical axes.** `p-4` sets the block and the inline
padding, so:

- a later `p-0` replaces an earlier `py-4`, as `cn()` did;
- a later `px-2` replaces only the inline axis.

**Composed utilities combine instead of replacing.** Each pair below ends up in
one property:

| Utilities                        | One property |
| -------------------------------- | ------------ |
| `ring-2`, `shadow-sm`            | `box-shadow` |
| `translate-x-4`, `translate-y-2` | `translate`  |
| `blur-sm`, `brightness-75`       | `filter`     |

Each utility sets a layer, a registered, non-inheriting custom property such as
`compose.translate-x` (as Tailwind's `--tw-*` ones are), and the property reads
all of them. So class order does not change the result.

**Transitions read their timing from layers too.** `transition` sets the list of
properties and reads the duration and easing utilities from their layers, so
`duration-200 transition` and `transition duration-200` agree.

Without either, the timing is Tailwind's: 150 ms, `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)`.
`transition-none` also resets the duration and timing function, so it removes a
component's transition entirely, as `cn()` did by deleting the utility.

**`border` keeps a style you set.** `border` sets a 1 px width and reads the
border style from a layer that starts as `solid`; `border-dashed` sets that
layer. A component that is dashed stays dashed when a caller adds a plain border.

**A colour with an opacity is a mix.** `bg-primary/80` is
`color-mix(in oklab, <primary> 80%, transparent)`, as in Tailwind v4, so it works
on a `light-dark()` token and follows the colour scheme.

**Some names are not utilities.** They have no string form:

| Name                                                        | Write instead                                               |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `!important`                                                | Nothing: the [ladder](/docs/styling/precedence) replaces it |
| `group-*`, `peer-*`                                         | A declared [relation](/docs/styling/relations)              |
| An arbitrary property, such as `[mask-type:luminance]`      | An object entry                                             |
| Gradients (`bg-linear-*`, `from-*`, `to-*`) and `container` | A value; they are not in the preset yet                     |
---
# Semantic tokens
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tokens/semantic-tokens
# Semantic tokens

Scales tell you what values exist. Semantic tokens say what they _mean_: what a
card's surface is, what "primary" is, what a border looks like. This is the layer
that makes a component readable: `backgroundColor: theme.card` says something
`color.zinc50` does not.

```tsx
import { defineTokens } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { color } from "@kirana-style/preset-scales"

export const theme = defineTokens(
  "theme",
  {
    background: `light-dark(${color.white}, ${color.zinc950})`,
    foreground: `light-dark(${color.zinc950}, ${color.zinc50})`,
    card: `light-dark(${color.white}, ${color.zinc900})`,
    border: `light-dark(${color.zinc200}, ${color.zinc800})`,
    primary: `light-dark(${color.amber500}, ${color.amber400})`,
  },
  { variable: true }
)
```

Two decisions in that snippet, and both matter.

## Every colour is one `light-dark()` pair

`light-dark()` resolves against the element's `color-scheme`, so one declaration
covers both schemes. There is no dark variant, no `.dark` class, no duplicated
block, and no way for the two halves to drift apart: they are written on the same
line.

```tsx
// the whole story of this colour, in one place
card: `light-dark(${color.white}, ${color.zinc900})`
```

The application sets `color-scheme` once, at the root
([themes and modes](/docs/tokens/themes-and-modes)).

## Semantic tokens are variables

`variable: true`, because these are the values a theme overrides. Scales stay
inlined: nobody re-themes `space[4]`.

## Intent tokens for the things `light-dark()` cannot hold

Sometimes the two schemes differ in something that is not a colour: a shadow's
strength, an image filter, a blend mode. Those get per-mode values:

```tsx
export const surface = defineTokens(
  "surface",
  {
    imageDim: { light: "none", dark: "brightness(0.8)" },
  },
  { variable: true }
)
```

The same idea covers pairs where light and dark want _different roles_ rather than
different shades, such as a control that is a tint in light and a solid in dark. Naming
that intent once (`surface.control`) beats repeating a conditional in every
component that needs it.

## Deriving values

Tokens are constants, so deriving one from another is just an expression:

```tsx
export const radius = defineTokens(
  "radius",
  {
    base: "0.625rem",
    sm: "calc(0.625rem * 0.6)",
    lg: "0.625rem",
    xl: "calc(0.625rem * 1.4)",
  },
  { variable: true }
)

export const alpha = defineTokens("alpha", {
  primary20: `color-mix(in oklab, ${theme.primary} 20%, transparent)`,
})
```

`color-mix` with a variable token keeps the relationship live: re-theme
`theme.primary` and every tint follows.

## Where to put it

One module, exported, imported by every component. In this repository it is
`packages/ui/src/theme/semantic.ts`, and adding a colour is one line there rather
than a decision in each component.
---
# Themes and modes
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tokens/themes-and-modes
# Themes and modes

## Modes

`mode` gives you three handles that set `color-scheme`:

```tsx
import { mode } from "@kirana-style/core"

<html sx={mode.system} />   // color-scheme: light dark - follows the OS
<html sx={mode.light} />
<html sx={mode.dark} />
```

Put it on the **root element**, not the body: the root decides the page's canvas
and scrollbars, and an iframe whose root scheme differs from its frame gets an
opaque backdrop.

With every colour written as a [`light-dark()` pair](/docs/tokens/semantic-tokens),
that single declaration is the whole dark-mode implementation. `system` needs no
JavaScript at all.

A three-way switch is then ordinary state:

```tsx
const [scheme, setScheme] = useState<"system" | "light" | "dark">("system")

<html sx={mode[scheme]}>
```

## Themes

`defineTheme` overrides variable tokens for a subtree:

```tsx
import { defineTheme } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { theme } from "./tokens"

export const brand = defineTheme(theme, {
  primary: `light-dark(${color.violet500}, ${color.violet400})`,
})

<section sx={brand}>…</section>
```

Everything inside the section reads the new value; everything outside is
untouched. Themes nest, and a theme may override some tokens and leave the rest.

<!-- ::figure-themes -->

Only **variable** tokens can be overridden: overriding an inlined one is an error
(`token-not-variable`), because there is no variable to change. If a token needs a
theme, declare its group with `variable: true`.

### Per-mode overrides

A theme can set both halves of a token:

```tsx
export const brand = defineTheme(theme, {
  surface: { light: "white", dark: "oklch(0.24 0 0)" },
})
```

## Where the values live

- Token defaults go in the `kirana.tokens` layer, on `:root`.
- Theme overrides go in `kirana.themes`, as a class.

Both sit below your component styles, so a component that sets a colour directly
always wins over a theme that suggests one.

## Remembering the reader's choice

A switch that only sets state forgets the choice on a reload, and another open tab
keeps its own. Keeping it takes three things, whatever the framework:

1. **Store the choice in a cookie**, not in `localStorage`. The server can read a
   cookie, so it renders the page in the saved mode and nothing flashes.
2. **Render the root in it on the server**: read the cookie, and put the matching
   handle on `<html>`.
3. **Tell the other tabs**: write the cookie in the browser when the reader
   chooses, and post the new mode on a `BroadcastChannel` the other tabs listen to.

`system` needs none of this: it is `color-scheme: light dark`, which follows the
operating system without JavaScript. A reader who never chooses gets no cookie.

<!-- ::figure-theme-flow -->

### In TanStack Start

The code below is for TanStack Start with server rendering; it is what this site
runs. Other frameworks follow the same three steps (see the table after it).

The cookie, read on the server from the request and in the browser from
`document.cookie`, so a client-side navigation sends no request:

```ts file="src/lib/theme.ts"
import { createIsomorphicFn } from "@tanstack/react-start"
import { getCookie } from "@tanstack/react-start/server"

export type Scheme = "system" | "light" | "dark"
export const COOKIE = "theme"

export const isScheme = (value: unknown): value is Scheme =>
  value === "system" || value === "light" || value === "dark"

export const readScheme = createIsomorphicFn()
  .server((): Scheme => {
    const value = getCookie(COOKIE)
    return isScheme(value) ? value : "system"
  })
  .client((): Scheme => {
    const value = document.cookie.match(/(?:^|; )theme=(\w+)/)?.[1]
    return isScheme(value) ? value : "system"
  })
```

A provider that writes the cookie and keeps the tabs in step:

```tsx file="src/components/theme.tsx"
import { createContext, use, useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react"

import { COOKIE, isScheme } from "@/lib/theme"
import type { Scheme } from "@/lib/theme"

const ThemeContext = createContext<{
  scheme: Scheme
  setScheme: (scheme: Scheme) => void
} | null>(null)

export function ThemeProvider({
  initial,
  children,
}: {
  initial: Scheme
  children: React.ReactNode
}) {
  const [scheme, setState] = useState(initial)
  const channel = useRef<BroadcastChannel | null>(null)

  // Another tab chose: follow it.
  useEffect(() => {
    const tabs = new BroadcastChannel(COOKIE)
    tabs.onmessage = (event) => {
      if (isScheme(event.data)) setState(event.data)
    }
    channel.current = tabs
    return () => tabs.close()
  }, [])

  const setScheme = (next: Scheme) => {
    setState(next)
    document.cookie = `${COOKIE}=${next}; path=/; max-age=31536000; samesite=lax`
    channel.current?.postMessage(next)
  }

  return <ThemeContext value={{ scheme, setScheme }}>{children}</ThemeContext>
}

export const useTheme = () => use(ThemeContext)!
```

The root route reads the cookie before the document renders, and `<html>` takes
the handle:

```tsx file="src/routes/__root.tsx"
import { mode } from "@kirana-style/core"

import { ThemeProvider, useTheme } from "@/components/theme"
import { readScheme } from "@/lib/theme"

export const Route = createRootRoute({
  beforeLoad: () => ({ scheme: readScheme() }),
  shellComponent: RootDocument,
})

function RootDocument({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const { scheme } = Route.useRouteContext()
  return (
    <ThemeProvider initial={scheme}>
      <Html>{children}</Html>
    </ThemeProvider>
  )
}

function Html({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const { scheme } = useTheme()
  return (
    <html lang="en" sx={mode[scheme]}>
      <head>
        <HeadContent />
      </head>
      <body>
        {children}
        <Scripts />
      </body>
    </html>
  )
}
```

The switch is then any control that calls `setScheme`:

```tsx file="src/components/theme-switch.tsx"
const { scheme, setScheme } = useTheme()

<select value={scheme} onChange={(event) => setScheme(event.target.value as Scheme)}>
  <option value="system">System</option>
  <option value="light">Light</option>
  <option value="dark">Dark</option>
</select>
```

Two more details:

- **The back-forward cache.** A page the browser restores from its cache missed the
  messages sent while it was away. Read the cookie again on `pageshow` when
  `event.persisted` is true.
- **No shortcut on Ctrl or Cmd+D.** It is the browser's bookmark key.

### In other frameworks

The provider and the switch stay the same; what changes is where the server reads
the cookie and where the root element is rendered.

| Framework                  | Read the cookie on the server, then render the root with it |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Next.js (App Router)       | `(await cookies()).get("theme")` in the root layout         |
| Nuxt                       | `useCookie("theme")` in `app.vue`                           |
| SvelteKit                  | `cookies.get("theme")` in the root `+layout.server.ts`      |
| Astro                      | `Astro.cookies.get("theme")` in the layout                  |
| Laravel, Symfony, Rails, Phoenix and AdonisJS | the request's cookie, in the layout template                |

A site with no server (a static build) cannot read a cookie before the page is
sent. Keep the choice in `localStorage` instead, and apply it with a small inline
script at the top of `<head>`, which runs before the first paint:

```html
<script>
  const scheme = localStorage.getItem("theme")
  if (scheme === "light" || scheme === "dark")
    document.documentElement.style.colorScheme = scheme
</script>
```

Every colour is a `light-dark()` pair, so setting `color-scheme` is enough to
switch them all.

## What not to do

- **Do not put the mode on `<body>`.** The canvas belongs to the root.
- **Do not write a `dark:` variant.** There is no dark variant; the pair is in the
  token.
- **Do not theme scales.** Re-theming `space[4]` makes a layout unpredictable;
  theme the semantic layer instead.
---
# The configuration file
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/config/file
# The configuration file

Configuration is optional. Every key has a default, and a project with no
`kirana.config.ts` compiles.

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"

export default defineConfig({
  layers: { before: ["reset", "base"] },
  targets: { chrome: 123, safari: "17.5" },
})
```

`defineConfig` is an identity function: it exists for the types.

## How it is found

The compiler looks in the project root, in this order, and takes the first match:

1. `kirana.config.ts`
2. `kirana.config.mts`
3. `kirana.config.js`
4. `kirana.config.mjs`
5. `kirana.config.json`

TypeScript and JavaScript files are imported natively; the default export is the
configuration.

A TypeScript configuration written as an ES module loads as one even when your
`package.json` says `"type": "commonjs"`, as `npm init` writes, and so do the
TypeScript files it imports.

Node.js loads the file as it is, without a bundler, and so its imports: a relative
import in the configuration, or in a module it imports, needs its extension
(`./states.ts`, not `./states`). When the file fails to load, the command says which
file and which module it could not find, and exits with 2.

### In a workspace

The CLI's `check`, `trace` and `export` read, for each path you give them, the
nearest configuration file above it, as TypeScript finds its own configuration. Run from
the workspace root, they check each app with the app's own configuration. A path
with no configuration above it reads the working directory's, and a `--config`
option makes every path read one file. See
[the CLI](/docs/tooling/cli#which-configuration).

## What overrides what

Options passed to the adapter override the file, key by key:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
kirana({ config: { names: { prefix: "app" } } })
```

The project root comes from the adapter (Vite's `root`; for the CLI, the directory
of the configuration a path reads, or the working directory) and cannot be set in
the file.

## Unknown keys are errors

The validator rejects keys it does not know (`invalid-config`), rather than
ignoring them. A typo fails the build instead of silently doing nothing, and a
key from a future version fails loudly rather than pretending to work.

## Sharing configuration

A configuration is a plain object, so a shared one is a plain export:

```ts file="packages/ui/src/kirana.ts"
export const uiConfig = {
  conditions: {
    exclusive: [["[data-starting-style]", "[data-ending-style]"]],
  },
} satisfies KiranaConfig
```

```ts file="apps/web/kirana.config.ts"
export default defineConfig({ ...uiConfig, layers: { before: ["reset"] } })
```

That is how a component library tells every app what its attributes guarantee;
see [`conditions.exclusive`](/docs/reference/config).
---
# Layers and global CSS
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/config/layers
# Layers and global CSS

Kirana writes every rule inside a layer, and declares the order in one statement
at the top of the stylesheet:

```css
@layer reset, base, kirana;
@layer kirana.tokens, kirana.themes, kirana.contextual, kirana.atoms;
```

<!-- ::figure-layers -->

The first line is yours: the names from `layers.before` and `layers.after`. The
second is Kirana's own, and its order is fixed.

| Layer               | Holds                                                            |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `kirana.tokens`     | Variable token defaults on `:root`, and their per-mode overrides |
| `kirana.themes`     | `defineTheme` overrides                                          |
| `kirana.contextual` | `select.*` styles                                                |
| `kirana.atoms`      | Element styles: everything you write with `css()`                |

Nothing Kirana emits is unlayered, custom-property assignments included. That is
what lets a reset stay a reset: it cannot accidentally outrank a component style,
and a component style cannot accidentally outrank a theme.

## Your own layers

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
export default defineConfig({
  layers: { before: ["reset", "base"] },
})
```

Then write your global CSS into those layers:

```css file="globals.css"
@layer reset {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    box-sizing: border-box;
  }
  body {
    margin: 0;
  }
}

@layer base {
  a {
    color: inherit;
  }
}
```

Because `reset` and `base` come before `kirana` in the order statement, every
Kirana rule wins over them, whatever their selectors look like.

## Load order matters once

Import Kirana's stylesheet **before** your global CSS. Its `@layer` statement is
what fixes the order, and a layer first seen inside `globals.css` would otherwise
be ordered by where it appeared.

```tsx
<link rel="stylesheet" href={kiranaCss} />   {/* first */}
<link rel="stylesheet" href={globalCss} />
```

## Third-party CSS

A package's stylesheet you cannot edit (a date picker, a carousel) goes into a
layer you name, so your styles beat it without `!important`:

```ts
layers: {
  before: ["reset", "vendor", "base"]
}
```

```css
@import "some-package/dist/style.css" layer(vendor);
```

When the package imports its CSS from JavaScript, as a theme does, there is no
`@import` line to give a layer: on Vite, `cssLayer("vendor", "some-package/dist/")`
from `@kirana-style/vite` wraps those stylesheets in the layer as they load
([the Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite#a-dependency-s-css-in-a-layer)).

## When to write global CSS at all

Rarely. Two cases hold up:

- **A reset**, and base element styles that must apply to bare tags.
- **Markup you do not render**, where no component can carry a class, scoped by
  an attribute the library sets, as narrowly as you can manage.

Everything else belongs in `css()`, where the compiler can see it, check it and
tell you when two declarations fight.
---
# Choose a framework
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/overview
# Choose a framework

Kirana compiles the styles you write next to your components into class names
and one static stylesheet, with no styling runtime left in the page. It works
with every major framework and bundler, and with server-rendered templates
through the command line.



## Framework guides

Guides for each framework, covering the recommended way to install Kirana in it.
Each is complete on its own: install, configure, import the stylesheet, type
`sx`, write a component.

- [React](/docs/frameworks/react): The library for web and native user interfaces, on Vite.
- [Next.js](/docs/frameworks/nextjs): The React framework, with server components, on Turbopack.
- [React Router](/docs/frameworks/react-router): A standards-focused router and framework you can deploy anywhere.
- [TanStack Start](/docs/frameworks/tanstack-start): Full-stack React powered by TanStack Router. This site runs on it.
- [Gatsby](/docs/frameworks/gatsby): Static sites with React and GraphQL, built by webpack.
- [Remix](/docs/frameworks/remix): Remix 3: web standards, server-rendered components and client entries.
- [Waku](/docs/frameworks/waku): The minimal React framework, built on React Server Components.
- [Vike](/docs/frameworks/vike): The framework you assemble: your renderer, your server, on Vite.
- [Docusaurus](/docs/frameworks/docusaurus): Documentation websites with React, built by webpack.
- [Preact](/docs/frameworks/preact): A fast 3 kB alternative to React with the same API.
- [Solid](/docs/frameworks/solid): Simple, performant reactivity for user interfaces.
- [SolidStart](/docs/frameworks/solid-start): Solid's full-stack framework: routes, server rendering and server functions.
- [Vue](/docs/frameworks/vue): The progressive framework, with :sx in single-file components.
- [Nuxt](/docs/frameworks/nuxt): The intuitive Vue framework for universal applications.
- [VitePress](/docs/frameworks/vitepress): The Vite and Vue static site generator for documentation.
- [Svelte](/docs/frameworks/svelte): Cybernetically enhanced web apps, with sx on elements.
- [SvelteKit](/docs/frameworks/sveltekit): The fastest way to build apps of all sizes with Svelte.
- [Astro](/docs/frameworks/astro): The web framework for content-driven sites, sx in .astro files.
- [Qwik](/docs/frameworks/qwik): Instantly interactive apps, rendered on the server and resumed.
- [Angular](/docs/frameworks/angular): The platform for web apps, with an [sx] directive in templates.
- [Ember.js](/docs/frameworks/ember): A framework for ambitious web apps, on Embroider and Vite.
- [Meteor](/docs/frameworks/meteor): The full-stack JavaScript platform for web and mobile apps.
- [No framework](/docs/frameworks/vanilla): Plain TypeScript and web components: handles are class strings.

- [Laravel](/docs/frameworks/laravel): The PHP framework for web artisans: @kirana in Blade.
- [Symfony](/docs/frameworks/symfony): The PHP framework for websites and apps: kirana() in Twig.
- [Ruby on Rails](/docs/frameworks/rails): The full-stack Ruby framework: a kirana helper in ERB views.
- [Phoenix](/docs/frameworks/phoenix): Rich, interactive Elixir apps: kirana/1 in HEEx templates.
- [AdonisJS](/docs/frameworks/adonisjs): The fully featured Node.js framework: kirana() in Edge.

> [!NOTE] Don't see your framework?
> Most frameworks build with Vite: use [the Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite).
> Otherwise, pick [your bundler](/docs/integrations/bundlers), or let
> [the Kirana CLI](/docs/tooling/cli#kirana-style-dev) write the stylesheet and a
> [class map](/docs/frameworks/server-templates) for your templates.

## Using Vite

Kirana's Vite plugin compiles styles as Vite loads each module and keeps the
stylesheet live in development. Every Vite-based framework uses it.

### 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

### 2. Add the plugin

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [kirana(), react()] })
```

### 3. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

### 4. Write a component

```tsx file="src/card.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })

export const Card = () => <div sx={card} />
```

The [Vite guide](/docs/integrations/vite) has the options, and each framework's
guide its own line in `vite.config.ts`.

## Bundlers

One adapter for each bundler. Every one hands the modules that carry styles to
the same compiler, so the class names and the stylesheet are the same whichever
one builds them.

- [Vite](/docs/integrations/vite): The build tool most frameworks run on, with hot style updates.
- [Rolldown](/docs/integrations/rolldown): The Rust bundler under Vite, on its own.
- [webpack](/docs/integrations/webpack): A pre loader for sx and a plugin that writes the stylesheet.
- [Rspack and Rsbuild](/docs/integrations/rspack): The fast Rust-based web bundler, and its build tool.
- [Parcel](/docs/integrations/parcel): The zero-configuration build tool for the web.
- [Bun](/docs/integrations/bun): Bun's bundler and its dev server, from one plugin.
- [esbuild](/docs/integrations/esbuild): An extremely fast bundler, in watch and serve modes too.
- [PostCSS](/docs/integrations/postcss): The project's stylesheet wherever @kirana; stands.
- [Jest](/docs/integrations/jest): A transformer, so tests see the class names you ship.
- [Storybook](/docs/integrations/storybook): Stories built with your project's Vite config, styled as the app is.

## Kirana CLI

For server-rendered templates (Blade, ERB, HEEx, Twig, Edge) and anything else
without a bundler. You write styles in TypeScript modules; the CLI writes the
stylesheet, and a class map your templates read the class names from.

### 1. Install

```bash
npm install -D kirana-style @kirana-style/core
```

### 2. Name the modules templates use

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"

export default defineConfig({
  classes: { modules: ["styles"], out: "public/kirana/classes.json" },
})
```

### 3. Write styles

```ts file="styles/app.styles.ts"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
```

### 4. Run it

```bash
npx kirana-style dev styles --out public/kirana/kirana.css
```

`kirana-style dev` watches and rewrites both files; `kirana-style build` writes them once,
minified with `--minify`. Your template helper then turns `card` into its class
names; see [server templates](/docs/frameworks/server-templates).



## Every guide is a test

Every example lives in `packages/kirana/examples/`. On every change, CI packs the
packages, installs each example from the tarballs, builds it, and checks a styled
element's computed style and hover in a browser. It also starts each dev server
and checks that a style edit reaches the page in place, without a reload, where
the framework updates components that way. A row in this table is a test that
passes, not a claim.

| Guide                                             | Runs on                    | `sx` becomes                     | Tested example                   |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| [React](/docs/frameworks/react)                   | Vite                       | `className` and `style`          | `vite-react`                     |
| [Next.js](/docs/frameworks/nextjs)                | Turbopack, webpack         | `className` and `style`          | `next-turbopack`, `next-webpack` |
| [React Router](/docs/frameworks/react-router)     | Vite                       | `className` and `style`          | `react-router`                   |
| [TanStack Start](/docs/frameworks/tanstack-start) | Vite                       | `className` and `style`          | this site                        |
| [Gatsby](/docs/frameworks/gatsby)                 | webpack                    | `className` and `style`          | `gatsby`                         |
