| [Preact](/docs/frameworks/preact)                 | Vite                       | `class` and `style`              | `vite-preact`                    |
| [Solid](/docs/frameworks/solid)                   | Vite                       | `class` and `style`              | `vite-solid`                     |
| [Vue](/docs/frameworks/vue)                       | Vite                       | `:sx` → `class` and `style`      | `vite-vue`                       |
| [Nuxt](/docs/frameworks/nuxt)                     | Nuxt (Vite)                | `:sx` → `class` and `style`      | `nuxt`                           |
| [Svelte](/docs/frameworks/svelte)                 | Vite                       | `sx` → `class` and `style`       | `vite-svelte`                    |
| [SvelteKit](/docs/frameworks/sveltekit)           | Vite                       | `sx` → `class` and `style`       | `sveltekit`                      |
| [Astro](/docs/frameworks/astro)                   | Astro (Vite)               | `sx` → `class` and `style`       | `astro`                          |
| [Qwik](/docs/frameworks/qwik)                     | Qwik Router (Vite)         | `class` and `style`              | `qwik`                           |
| [Angular](/docs/frameworks/angular)               | Angular CLI, Analog (Vite) | `[sx]` directive (runtime merge) | `angular-cli`, `analog-angular`  |
| [Ember.js](/docs/frameworks/ember)                | Embroider (Vite)           | `cx` in templates                | `ember`                          |
| [Meteor](/docs/frameworks/meteor)                 | Meteor (Rspack)            | `className` and `style`          | `meteor`                         |
| [No framework](/docs/frameworks/vanilla)          | Vite                       | a class string you assign        | `vite-vanilla`                   |
| [Laravel](/docs/frameworks/laravel)               | Kirana CLI, Vite           | `@kirana(…)` in Blade            | `laravel`                        |
| [Symfony](/docs/frameworks/symfony)               | Kirana CLI, AssetMapper    | `kirana(…)` in Twig              | `symfony`                        |
| [Ruby on Rails](/docs/frameworks/rails)           | Kirana CLI, Propshaft      | `kirana` in ERB                  | `rails`                          |
| [Phoenix](/docs/frameworks/phoenix)               | Kirana CLI                 | `kirana/1` in HEEx               | `phoenix`                        |
| [AdonisJS](/docs/frameworks/adonisjs)             | Kirana CLI, Vite           | `kirana(…)` in Edge              | `adonisjs`                       |

The bundlers have their own examples, listed on [each page](/docs/integrations/bundlers).

# React
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/react
# React

`sx` compiles to `className` (and `style` for values known only at runtime).
Tested by `examples/vite-react`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

Kirana goes before the React plugin, so React only ever sees compiled JSX:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [kirana(), react()] })
```

## 3. Import the stylesheet

Once, in your entry, before your own global CSS:

```tsx file="src/main.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 4. Type `sx`

```json file="tsconfig.json"
{ "compilerOptions": { "types": ["@kirana-style/core/react"] } }
```

## 5. Write a component

```tsx file="src/button.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const styles = {
  button: css({
    paddingInline: "1rem",
    borderRadius: "0.5rem",
    backgroundColor: { base: "#111", ":hover": "#333" },
    color: "white",
  }),
}

export function Button(props: React.ComponentProps<"button">) {
  return <button {...props} sx={styles.button} />
}
```

Run `vite`: the page is styled, and editing a value updates it without a reload.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions): what
  goes inside `css()`.
- [The Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite): its options and what it does in
  development and in a build.
- Not on Vite? [Other bundlers](/docs/integrations/bundlers).
---
# Next.js
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/nextjs
# Next.js

Kirana works with both of Next.js's bundlers: **Turbopack**, the default for
development and production builds, and webpack (`--webpack`). Server components work
unchanged. Tested on every change by `examples/next-turbopack` and
`examples/next-webpack`, with npm and pnpm, in a production build and on the dev
server.



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It detects Next.js and its bundler, shows every change below as a diff, writes
them once you say yes, and prints the install command (`--install` runs it). Then
`npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result. The steps it takes are the ones this page
shows, so you can also do them by hand.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/next @kirana-style/postcss postcss
```

## 2. Wrap the configuration

```ts file="next.config.ts"
import type { NextConfig } from "next"
import { withKirana } from "@kirana-style/next"

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  // your Next.js configuration
}

export default withKirana(nextConfig)
```

`withKirana` configures both bundlers: a Turbopack rule that compiles your
scripts, and the webpack plugin for `next build --webpack`. Rules you already have
for the same files are kept.

## 3. Add the PostCSS plugin

```js file="postcss.config.mjs"
export default {
  plugins: {
    "@kirana-style/postcss": {},
    // Tailwind CSS, autoprefixer and the rest stay as they are.
  },
}
```

## 4. Put the stylesheet in your global CSS

```css file="app/globals.css"
@kirana;
```

The root layout already imports `globals.css`. The PostCSS plugin replaces
`@kirana;` with the whole stylesheet: one file, every atom once.

## 5. Type `sx`

```ts file="kirana.d.ts"
/// <reference types="@kirana-style/core/react" />
```

## 6. Write a component

```tsx file="app/page.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const styles = {
  title: css({ fontSize: "2rem", color: { base: "#111", ":hover": "#555" } }),
}

export default function Page() {
  return <h1 sx={styles.title}>Hello</h1>
}
```

That is a server component: `sx` compiles to a class string at build time, so
nothing of Kirana runs at request time. In your editor, the line shows what the
element gets; see [editor support](/docs/tooling/editor).

## How the stylesheet gets built

Turbopack runs loaders, not bundler plugins, so no single step sees every module.
Kirana splits the work the way Tailwind CSS v4 does: the loader rewrites each
module's styles into class names, and the PostCSS plugin compiles the project into
the stylesheet. The two never talk: they agree because a class name is a hash of
what it styles, never of the order modules were built in. In development the
plugin tells Next.js which folders to watch, so an edit to a component reaches the
page without a restart.

The cost is measured in the design note
`packages/kirana/design-notes/turbopack.md`: 53 ms to compile the 104 scripts of this documentation site the first time, 5 ms
after an edit. One difference from the other adapters: the stylesheet holds the
atoms of every script in the project, imported or not.

## With webpack only

A project that always builds with `--webpack` can skip PostCSS and use the webpack
adapter on its own:

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/webpack
```

```js file="next.config.js"
import { withKirana } from "@kirana-style/webpack/next"

export default withKirana({})
```

```jsx file="app/layout.jsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

Next runs a server and a client compiler over the same app, and a server
component is only seen by the server one. Every compiler of a project shares one
compiler session, which is how those atoms reach the stylesheet the client writes.
Details in [other bundlers](/docs/integrations/bundlers#nextjs).

With webpack, a style change in `next dev --webpack` shows after a reload: CSS
hot updates are not implemented for webpack.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
---
# React Router
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/react-router
# React Router

React Router's framework mode builds with Vite, so Kirana's Vite plugin is all it
needs: `sx` compiles to `className`, on the server render and in the browser
alike. Tested on every change by `examples/react-router`, built and on its dev
server. A Remix 2 app is a React Router app; [Remix 3](/docs/frameworks/remix) has
a guide of its own.



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It detects the project, shows every change below as a diff, writes them once you
say yes, and prints the install command (`--install` runs it). Then
`npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

Kirana goes before React Router's plugin, so routes reach it as source:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import { reactRouter } from "@react-router/dev/vite"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [kirana(), reactRouter()],
})
```

## 3. Import the stylesheet

In the root route, which renders the document:

```tsx file="app/root.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 4. Type `sx`

```json file="tsconfig.json"
{
  "compilerOptions": { "types": ["@kirana-style/core/react"] }
}
```

## 5. Write a route

```tsx file="app/routes/home.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const title = css({ fontSize: "2rem", fontWeight: 600 })

export default function Home() {
  return <h1 sx={title}>Hello</h1>
}
```

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).
- [The Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite).

# TanStack Start
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/tanstack-start
# TanStack Start

This site, and the three applications of our shadcn/ui port, are TanStack
Start apps; this page is the setup they use. Tested on every change by
`examples/tanstack-start`, prerendered and on its dev server.



## Install and add the plugin

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import { tanstackStart } from "@tanstack/react-start/plugin/vite"
import viteReact from "@vitejs/plugin-react"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
  // Kirana ahead of the framework plugins, so modules reach them compiled; route
  // splitting re-emits modules under a query, and those are compiled too.
  plugins: [kirana(), tanstackStart(), viteReact()],
})
```

## The root document

Two things belong at the root: the stylesheets, in order, and the colour scheme.

```tsx file="src/routes/__root.tsx"
import kiranaCss from "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css?url"
import appCss from "./globals.css?url"

export const Route = createRootRoute({
  head: () => ({
    links: [
      // First: its `@layer` statement fixes the layer order before your CSS
      // opens the reset and base layers.
      { rel: "stylesheet", href: kiranaCss },
      { rel: "stylesheet", href: appCss },
    ],
  }),
  shellComponent: RootDocument,
})

function RootDocument({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en" sx={mode.system}>
      <head>
        <HeadContent />
      </head>
      <body sx={styles.body}>{children}</body>
    </html>
  )
}
```

`color-scheme` goes on `<html>`, not `<body>`: the root owns the page canvas and
the scrollbars.

`mode.system` follows the operating system. To let readers choose Light or Dark
and keep the choice across reloads and tabs, see
[remembering the reader's choice](/docs/tokens/themes-and-modes#remembering-the-reader-s-choice).

## Typing `sx`

One reference, anywhere your `tsconfig.json` includes:

```ts
/// <reference types="@kirana-style/core/react" />
```

## Server rendering

There is nothing to do. Styles are in a stylesheet the document links, and class
names are in the markup, so server-rendered HTML is already styled, with no style
collection step, no flash and no double render.

Server components work the same way: the compiler runs at build time, so nothing
of Kirana has to run on the server at request time.

To render on Cloudflare Workers, add Cloudflare's Vite plugin before `kirana()`:
[Cloudflare Workers](/docs/building/cloudflare-workers) has the setup.

## Other setups

Every other framework has its own guide in [supported frameworks](/docs/frameworks/overview),
and React on other bundlers is in [other bundlers](/docs/integrations/bundlers).

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
---
# Gatsby
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/gatsby
# Gatsby

Gatsby builds with webpack in stages: the browser bundle, and the server render
that writes each page's HTML. `@kirana-style/gatsby` adds Kirana's webpack plugin to
every stage, and the stages share one compiler session, so the HTML and the
browser agree on every class. Tested on every change by `examples/gatsby`, built
and on its dev server.



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It detects the project, shows every change below as a diff, writes them once you
say yes, and prints the install command (`--install` runs it). Then
`npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/gatsby
```

## 2. Add the plugin

```js file="gatsby-config.js"
module.exports = {
  jsxRuntime: "automatic",
  plugins: ["@kirana-style/gatsby"],
}
```

`jsxRuntime: "automatic"` is Gatsby's own option, and the one its starters use;
without it every component needs `import React`.

## 3. Import the stylesheet

```js file="gatsby-browser.js"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 4. Write a page

```tsx file="src/pages/index.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const title = css({ fontSize: "2rem", fontWeight: 600 })

export default function Home() {
  return <h1 sx={title}>Hello</h1>
}
```

Type `sx` with `"types": ["@kirana-style/core/react"]` in `tsconfig.json`.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [The webpack plugin](/docs/integrations/webpack), which does the work.
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles).
---
# Remix
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/remix
# Remix

Remix 3 has no bundler. `node-tsx` compiles TypeScript and JSX as Node loads the
server, and the asset server compiles client entries as the browser asks for
them. Both hand on only the JavaScript that comes out, so Kirana compiles after
them, on the compiled JSX calls: `sx` becomes `className` in the server render and
in the browser alike. The server's compiler session has seen every module, client
entries included, and serves the stylesheet. Tested on every change by
`examples/remix`, on its server and its dev server.

This page is about Remix 3. A Remix 2 app is a [React Router](/docs/frameworks/react-router)
app now; follow that guide.



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It adds the hook to your scripts (step 2) and tells you the lines to add to the
router and the asset server (steps 3 and 4). Then `npx kirana-style doctor` checks
the result.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core @kirana-style/remix
```

`@kirana-style/remix` is a dependency, not a dev dependency: the hook, the loader
and the middleware run in your server.

## 2. Load Kirana after `node-tsx`

In every script that starts the server, after `--import remix/node-tsx`:

```json file="package.json"
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "node --watch --import remix/node-tsx --import @kirana-style/remix/node server.ts",
    "start": "node --import remix/node-tsx --import @kirana-style/remix/node server.ts"
  }
}
```

Node runs the hook registered last first, so Kirana's hook asks `node-tsx` for the
compiled module and compiles its styles.

## 3. Serve the stylesheet

`stylesheet()` answers `/kirana.css` from the server's compiler session:

```ts file="app/router.ts"
import { stylesheet } from "@kirana-style/remix"

export const router = createRouter({
  middleware: [stylesheet(), staticFiles("./public"), renderMiddleware],
})
```

Link it from the document:

```tsx file="app/actions/document.tsx"
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/kirana.css" />
```

It is minified when `NODE_ENV` is `production`; `stylesheet({ path, minify })`
changes either.

## 4. Compile client entries

Client entries reach the browser through the asset server. Add Kirana's loader to
its scripts, and allow `@kirana-style/core`, whose runtime a compiled module may
import:

```ts file="app/assets.ts"
import { kiranaLoader } from "@kirana-style/remix"

export const assets = createAssetServer({
  allowPackages: ["remix", "@kirana-style/core"],
  scripts: { loaders: [kiranaLoader] },
})
```

## 5. Type `sx`

```json file="tsconfig.json"
{
  "compilerOptions": { "types": ["node", "@kirana-style/core/remix"] }
}
```

## 6. Write a component

A server-rendered component and a client entry style themselves the same way:

```tsx file="app/actions/public/notice.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { clientEntry } from "remix/component"

const styles = {
  notice: css({
    paddingInline: "1rem",
    color: { base: "black", ":hover": "blue" },
  }),
}

export const Notice = clientEntry(import.meta.url, function Notice() {
  return () => <p sx={styles.notice}>Hello</p>
})
```

## Diagnostics

The hook and the loader see compiled JavaScript, so a diagnostic they print points
at the compiled module. `npx kirana-style check app` reads your source and points
at the line you wrote.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).
---
# Waku
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/waku
# Waku

Waku builds with Vite, and takes Vite plugins under `vite` in `waku.config.ts`.
Kirana compiles server components and client components alike, so a page
rendered at build time (`render: "static"`) has the class names in its HTML, and
the browser has the same ones. Tested on every change by `examples/waku`, built
and on its dev server.



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It detects the project, shows every change below as a diff, writes them once you
say yes, and prints the install command (`--install` runs it). Then
`npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

```ts file="waku.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import { defineConfig } from "waku/config"

export default defineConfig({
  vite: { plugins: [kirana()] },
})
```

## 3. Import the stylesheet

In the root layout, which wraps every page:

```tsx file="src/pages/_layout.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 4. Type `sx`

```json file="tsconfig.json"
{
  "compilerOptions": { "types": ["@kirana-style/core/react"] }
}
```

## 5. Write a page

A server component styles itself the way a client component does; there is no
runtime to keep out of it, because the styles are compiled away:

```tsx file="src/pages/index.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const title = css({ fontSize: "2rem", fontWeight: 600 })

export default async function Home() {
  return <h1 sx={title}>Hello</h1>
}

export const getConfig = async () => ({ render: "static" }) as const
```

## Next

- [React](/docs/frameworks/react): `sx` in React components.
- [Next.js](/docs/frameworks/nextjs), the other framework with server
  components that Kirana supports.
- [The Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite).

# Vike
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/vike
# Vike

Vike builds with Vite, so Kirana's Vite plugin compiles every page, layout and
`+` file before the renderer's plugin sees it, and prerendered HTML carries the
class names. Tested on every change by `examples/vike`, built and on its dev
server.

This page uses React. With Vue or Solid as the renderer, the steps are the same,
with the `sx` types of [Vue](/docs/frameworks/vue) or
[Solid](/docs/frameworks/solid).



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It detects the project, shows every change below as a diff, writes them once you
say yes, and prints the install command (`--install` runs it). Then
`npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

Kirana goes first, so pages reach the renderer's plugin and Vike's with `sx`
already a class name:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react"
import vike from "vike/plugin"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [kirana(), react(), vike()],
})
```

## 3. Import the stylesheet

In a file every page shares, `+Layout` or `+Head`:

```tsx file="pages/+Head.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"

export function Head() {
  return <meta charSet="utf-8" />
}
```

## 4. Type `sx`

```json file="tsconfig.json"
{
  "compilerOptions": { "types": ["@kirana-style/core/react"] }
}
```

## 5. Write a page

```tsx file="pages/index/+Page.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const title = css({ fontSize: "2rem", fontWeight: 600 })

export default function Page() {
  return <h1 sx={title}>Hello</h1>
}
```

## Next

- [React](/docs/frameworks/react): `sx` in React components.
- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component).
- [The Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite).

# Docusaurus
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/docusaurus
# Docusaurus

Docusaurus builds with webpack, twice: the browser bundle, and the server render
that writes each page's HTML. A plugin of a few lines adds Kirana's webpack
plugin to both, and the two share one compiler session, so a class name is the
same in the HTML and in the browser. Tested on every change by
`examples/docusaurus`, built and on its dev server.



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It writes the configuration and the stylesheet's import, and tells you the
plugin to add (step 2). Then `npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/webpack
```

## 2. Add the plugin

```ts file="docusaurus.config.ts"
import type { Config, Plugin } from "@docusaurus/types"
import { KiranaPlugin } from "@kirana-style/webpack"

function kirana(): Plugin {
  return {
    name: "kirana",
    configureWebpack: () => ({ plugins: [new KiranaPlugin()] }),
  }
}

export default {
  // …
  plugins: [kirana],
} satisfies Config
```

Kirana's loader runs ahead of Docusaurus's own, so it reads `sx` before JSX is
compiled away.

## 3. Declare Docusaurus's aliases

`@theme/Layout`, `@docusaurus/Link` and the rest are webpack aliases that
Node.js resolution cannot follow. Listed as externals, imports from them are
runtime values, without an `unresolved-import` warning on every page:

```ts file="kirana.config.mts"
import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"

export default defineConfig({
  externals: [
    "@theme/",
    "@theme-original/",
    "@theme-init/",
    "@site/",
    "@generated/",
    "@docusaurus/",
  ],
})
```

## 4. Import the stylesheet

In the theme's `Root`, which wraps every page (create it if the site has none):

```tsx file="src/theme/Root.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"

export default function Root({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return <>{children}</>
}
```

## 5. Write a page

```tsx file="src/pages/index.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"
import Layout from "@theme/Layout"

const title = css({ fontSize: "2rem", fontWeight: 600 })

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <Layout>
      <h1 sx={title}>Hello</h1>
    </Layout>
  )
}
```

Infima, the classic theme's CSS framework, is unlayered: on an element it
styles itself (a link's colour, a heading's margin), its rule beats yours.
Style your own elements, or wrappers around Infima's, and it does not come up.

## Next

- [React](/docs/frameworks/react): `sx` in React components.
- [The webpack plugin](/docs/integrations/webpack).
- [Layers](/docs/config/layers).
---
# Preact
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/preact
# Preact

`sx` compiles to `class` (and a style attribute for values known only at
runtime). Kirana picks that up from the JSX import source in your `tsconfig.json`,
so there is nothing to configure. Tested by `examples/vite-preact`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

Kirana goes before the Preact plugin, so Preact only ever sees compiled JSX:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import preact from "@preact/preset-vite"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [kirana(), preact()] })
```

## 3. Point `jsxImportSource` at Preact, and type `sx`

```json file="tsconfig.json"
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "jsxImportSource": "preact",
    "types": ["@kirana-style/core/preact"]
  }
}
```

Without a `tsconfig.json`, set [`jsx: "preact"`](/docs/reference/config) in
`kirana.config.ts` instead.

## 4. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 5. Write a component

```tsx file="src/card.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
const wide = css({ width: "100%" })

export const Card = (props: { wide: boolean }) => (
  <div class="card" sx={[card, props.wide && wide]} />
)
```

A `class` already on the element is merged with the styles into the one `class`
it ends up with, and so is a `className`.

`props()` follows the same rule: it returns `{ class, style }`, so its result
spreads onto an element as it is, and the type entry types it that way. Read its
`class`, never its `className`.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).
- [The Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite).
---
# Solid
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/solid
# Solid

`sx` compiles to `class` (and a style attribute for values known only at
runtime). Kirana picks that up from the JSX import source in your `tsconfig.json`,
so there is nothing to configure. Tested by `examples/vite-solid`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

Kirana goes before the Solid plugin, so Solid only ever sees compiled JSX:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import solid from "vite-plugin-solid"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [kirana(), solid()] })
```

## 3. Point `jsxImportSource` at Solid, and type `sx`

```json file="tsconfig.json"
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "preserve",
    "jsxImportSource": "solid-js",
    "types": ["@kirana-style/core/solid"]
  }
}
```

Without a `tsconfig.json`, set [`jsx: "solid"`](/docs/reference/config) in
`kirana.config.ts` instead.

## 4. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 5. Write a component

```tsx file="src/card.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
const wide = css({ width: "100%" })

export const Card = (props: { wide: boolean }) => (
  <div class="card" sx={[card, props.wide && wide]} />
)
```

A `class` already on the element is merged with the styles into the one `class`
it ends up with, and so is a `className`.

`props()` follows the same rule: it returns `{ class, style }`, so its result
spreads onto an element as it is, and the type entry types it that way. Read its
`class`, never its `className`.

  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.

# SolidStart
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/solid-start
# SolidStart

SolidStart 2 builds with Vite, with its configuration in `vite.config.ts`, so
Kirana's Vite plugin is all it needs: `sx` compiles to `class`, on the server
render and after hydration alike. Tested on every change by
`examples/solid-start`, built and on its dev server.



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It detects the project, shows every change below as a diff, writes them once you

`npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result.


## 2. Add the plugin

Kirana goes before SolidStart's plugin, so routes reach Solid's compiler with
`sx` already a class:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import { solidStart } from "@solidjs/start/config"
import { nitro } from "nitro/vite"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [kirana(), solidStart(), nitro()],
```

```tsx file="src/app.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

```json file="tsconfig.json"
  "compilerOptions": { "types": ["@kirana-style/core/solid"] }
}
```

```tsx file="src/routes/index.tsx"

  return <h1 sx={title}>Hello</h1>
```

# Vue
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/vue
# Vue

Declare styles in `<script setup>` and apply them with `:sx`. Kirana compiles the
component as it is read, before Vue does. Tested by `examples/vite-vue`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import vue from "@vitejs/plugin-vue"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [kirana(), vue()] })
```

## 3. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.ts"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 4. Type `:sx`

For `vue-tsc` and the Vue language tools:

```ts file="src/env.d.ts"
/// <reference types="@kirana-style/core/vue" />
```

## 5. Write a component

```vue file="src/Card.vue"
<script setup lang="ts">
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

defineProps<{ wide: boolean }>()

const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
const full = css({ width: "100%" })
</script>

<template>
  <div class="card" :sx="[card, wide && full]"><slot /></div>
</template>
```

`:sx` takes what `sx` takes anywhere: a style, a list, conditionals. Vue merges
the result with the element's own `class` and `style`.

## A component that takes `:sx`

On a component, a caller's `:sx` arrives as the `class` Vue falls through to its
root, where Vue adds it beside the root's own classes: two classes for one
property, and the stylesheet's order picks one. To let the caller's styles win,
property by property, turn the fallthrough off and put them last in the root's own
`:sx`, with `useSx()`:

```vue file="src/Button.vue"
<script setup lang="ts">
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { useSx } from "@kirana-style/core/vue"

defineOptions({ inheritAttrs: false })
const { sx, attrs } = useSx()

const button = css({ height: "2rem", backgroundColor: "black" })
</script>

<template>
  <button v-bind="attrs" :sx="[button, sx]"><slot /></button>
</template>
```

`sx` is the caller's classes, and `attrs` every other attribute it passed:
listeners, `aria-*` and its inline style, bound on the same element. Then
`<Button :sx="tall">` gives the button one class per property, the caller's where
both set one.

## How it compiles

The script compiles like any module: `css()` becomes class strings, and the
stylesheet gets the atoms. Each `:sx` becomes
`v-bind="…"` with a call to Kirana's small runtime, which merges the styles when
the component renders. Keep `css()` calls in the script: one written inside the
template is not compiled, and says so when it runs.

An element takes one object binding, so an element's own `v-bind` object is
merged into the compiled one with Vue's `mergeProps`.

A component imported from a workspace package, outside the app's root, compiles
and hot-reloads like one inside it.

## Nuxt

On Nuxt, follow the [Nuxt guide](/docs/frameworks/nuxt): the plugin goes in
`nuxt.config.ts` instead.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
---
# Nuxt
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/nuxt
# Nuxt

Nuxt compiles Vue components with Vite, so Kirana works as it does in
[Vue](/docs/frameworks/vue): styles in `<script setup>`, `:sx` in the template.
Pages rendered on the server and hydrated in the browser are styled from the first
byte. Tested by `examples/nuxt`, built as a static site and run on the dev
server.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Configure Nuxt

Add the plugin to Nuxt's Vite configuration, and the stylesheet to its global CSS:

```ts file="nuxt.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"

export default defineNuxtConfig({
  css: ["@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"],
  vite: { plugins: [kirana()] },
})
```

## 3. Type `:sx`

```ts file="app/kirana.d.ts"
/// <reference types="@kirana-style/core/vue" />
```

## 4. Write a component

```vue file="app/components/Card.vue"
<script setup lang="ts">
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

defineProps<{ wide: boolean }>()

const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
const full = css({ width: "100%" })
</script>

<template>
  <div class="card" :sx="[card, wide && full]"><slot /></div>
</template>
```

In `nuxt dev`, editing a style updates the page in place, without a reload.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Vue](/docs/frameworks/vue): how `:sx` compiles, and what to keep in the script.
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).

# VitePress
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/vitepress
# VitePress

VitePress builds with Vite, and takes Vite plugins under `vite` in
`.vitepress/config`. Kirana compiles your theme's components and the components
pages use, written with `:sx` as in any [Vue](/docs/frameworks/vue) component.
One thing is particular to it: the default theme's CSS. Tested on every change
by `examples/vitepress`, built and on its dev server, on VitePress 2.



VitePress 2 builds on Vite 8, which Kirana's plugin needs. VitePress 1 is on
Vite 5 and is not supported.

## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It finds the source directory (`docs/`, or the root), shows every change below
as a diff, and writes them once you say yes. Then `npx kirana-style doctor`
checks the result.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin, and layer the theme

```ts file="docs/.vitepress/config.ts"
import kirana, { cssLayer } from "@kirana-style/vite"
import { defineConfig } from "vitepress"

export default defineConfig({
  vite: {
    plugins: [
      kirana(),
      cssLayer("vitepress", "vitepress/dist/client/theme-default/"),
    ],
  },
})
```

Most of the default theme's CSS is unlayered, and its reset
(`* { padding: 0 }`) sits in a layer declared after Kirana's. Either one beats
every style you write with `css()`, whatever its selector: an unlayered rule
outranks all layered ones. `cssLayer` puts the theme's stylesheets in a
`vitepress` layer as Vite loads them, and the configuration orders it before
Kirana's ([layers](/docs/config/layers)).

## 3. Order the layer

Kirana reads its configuration from Vite's root, which VitePress makes its
source directory, so the file goes beside `.vitepress`:

```ts file="docs/kirana.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"

export default defineConfig({ layers: { before: ["vitepress"] } })
```

## 4. Import the stylesheet

In the theme's entry, before the default theme's styles:

```ts file="docs/.vitepress/theme/index.ts"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
import DefaultTheme from "vitepress/theme"

export default DefaultTheme
```

## 5. Write a component

```vue file="docs/.vitepress/theme/Note.vue"
<script setup lang="ts">
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const note = css({ borderLeftWidth: "3px", paddingInline: "1rem" })
</script>

<template>
  <aside :sx="note"><slot /></aside>
</template>
```

Register it in the theme's `enhanceApp`, and use `<Note>` in any page.

## Next

- [Vue](/docs/frameworks/vue): `:sx` in single-file components.
- [Layers](/docs/config/layers): where third-party CSS goes.
- [The Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite), and `cssLayer`.
---
# Svelte
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/svelte
# Svelte

Declare styles in the component's `<script>` and apply them with `sx`. Kirana
compiles the component as it is read, before Svelte does. Tested by
`examples/vite-svelte`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

Kirana goes before Svelte's plugin:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import { svelte } from "@sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [kirana(), svelte()] })
```

## 3. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.ts"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 4. Type `sx`

For `svelte-check`:

```ts file="src/env.d.ts"
/// <reference types="@kirana-style/core/svelte" />
```

## 5. Write a component

```svelte file="src/Card.svelte"
<script lang="ts">
  import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

  let { wide, children } = $props()

  const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
  const full = css({ width: "100%" })
</script>

<div class="card" sx={[card, wide && full]}>
  {@render children?.()}
</div>
```

The element's own class and style attributes are merged into what `sx` produces,
in order, and `class:` and `style:` directives keep working beside it.

## A component that takes `sx`

On a component, a caller's `sx` arrives as its `class` and `style` props. Take them
and put the class last in the root's own `sx`, so the caller's styles win,
property by property:

```svelte file="src/Button.svelte"
<script lang="ts">
  import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

  let { class: sx, style, children, ...rest } = $props()

  const button = css({ height: "2rem", backgroundColor: "black" })
</script>

<button {...rest} {style} sx={[button, sx]}>
  {@render children?.()}
</button>
```

Svelte passes nothing through on its own, so there is no fallthrough to turn off.

## How it compiles

The script compiles like any module: `css()` becomes class strings, and the
stylesheet gets the atoms. Each `sx` becomes a spread of a call to Kirana's small
runtime, which merges the styles as the component renders, so a condition like
`wide && full` stays reactive. Keep `css()` calls in the script: one written
inside the markup is not compiled, and says so when it runs.

## SvelteKit

On SvelteKit, follow the [SvelteKit guide](/docs/frameworks/sveltekit): the
plugin goes before `sveltekit()`, and the stylesheet in the root layout.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
---
# SvelteKit
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/sveltekit
# SvelteKit

SvelteKit compiles Svelte components with Vite, so Kirana works as it does in
[Svelte](/docs/frameworks/svelte): styles in `<script>`, `sx` on elements. Pages
rendered on the server, or prerendered, are styled from the first byte. Tested by
`examples/sveltekit`, built with the static adapter and run on the dev server.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

Before SvelteKit's, so every component reaches Svelte compiled:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import { sveltekit } from "@sveltejs/kit/vite"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [kirana(), sveltekit()] })
```

SvelteKit 3 reads its options there too, such as `sveltekit({ adapter: adapter() })`,
and no longer reads `svelte.config.js`.

## 3. Import the stylesheet

In the root layout:

```svelte file="src/routes/+layout.svelte"
<script lang="ts">
  import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"

  let { children } = $props()
</script>

{@render children()}
```

## 4. Type `sx`

```ts file="src/app.d.ts"
/// <reference types="@kirana-style/core/svelte" />
```

## 5. Write a component

```svelte file="src/lib/Card.svelte"
<script lang="ts">
  import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

  let { wide, children } = $props()

  const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
  const full = css({ width: "100%" })
</script>

<div class="card" sx={[card, wide && full]}>
  {@render children?.()}
</div>
```

In `vite dev`, editing a style updates the page in place, without a reload.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Svelte](/docs/frameworks/svelte): how `sx` compiles, and what to keep in the
  script.
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).

# Astro
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/astro
# Astro

Declare styles in the frontmatter and apply them with `sx`. Kirana compiles the
component as it is read, before Astro does. Tested by `examples/astro`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/astro
```

## 2. Add the integration

```js file="astro.config.mjs"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/astro"
import { defineConfig } from "astro/config"

export default defineConfig({ integrations: [kirana()] })
```

Use the integration rather than `@kirana-style/vite` directly: Astro inlines small
stylesheets into its pages and links larger ones by names it records early, and
the integration is what renames the finished stylesheet by its content after Astro
has written every page.

## 3. Import the stylesheet

In your layout's frontmatter:

```astro file="src/layouts/Base.astro"
---
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
---
```

## 4. Type `sx`

For `astro check`:

```ts file="src/env.d.ts"
/// <reference types="@kirana-style/core/astro" />
```

## 5. Write a component

```astro file="src/components/Card.astro"
---
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const { wide } = Astro.props
const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
const full = css({ width: "100%" })
---

<div class="card" sx={[card, wide && full]}>
  <slot />
</div>
```


The element's own `class` and `style` are merged into what `sx` produces. Islands
written in React, Preact, Solid, Vue or Svelte go through the same integration and
follow their own guides for `sx` (islands are not in the test matrix yet).

## How it compiles

The frontmatter compiles like any module, and each `sx` becomes a spread of a call
to Kirana's small runtime, evaluated when the page renders, which is at build time
for a static page. Keep `css()` calls in the frontmatter: one written inside the markup
is not compiled, and says so when it runs.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.

# Qwik
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/qwik
# Qwik

`sx` compiles to `class` (and a style attribute for values known only at
runtime). Kirana picks that up from the JSX import source in your `tsconfig.json`,
so there is nothing to configure.

Kirana supports **Qwik 2** (`@qwik.dev/core`): Qwik 1 runs only on
Vite 7 and older, and Kirana's Vite plugin needs Vite 8. Tested on every change
by `examples/qwik`, a Qwik Router app built and served with npm and pnpm.



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It detects Qwik, shows every change below as a diff, writes them once you say
yes, and prints the install command (`--install` runs it). Then
`npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

Kirana goes first, so Qwik's optimizer splits components that are already
compiled:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import { qwikVite } from "@qwik.dev/core/optimizer"
import { qwikRouter } from "@qwik.dev/router/vite"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [kirana(), qwikRouter(), qwikVite()],
})
```

One Kirana session serves the server render and the client build, so both name
the same classes.

## 3. Point `jsxImportSource` at Qwik, and type `sx`

```json file="tsconfig.json"
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "jsxImportSource": "@qwik.dev/core",
    "types": ["@kirana-style/core/qwik"]
  }
}
```

Without a `tsconfig.json`, set [`jsx: "qwik"`](/docs/reference/config) in
`kirana.config.ts` instead.

## 4. Import the stylesheet

In the root component, which every page renders:

```tsx file="src/root.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 5. Write a component

```tsx file="src/components/card.tsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { component$ } from "@qwik.dev/core"

const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
const wide = css({ width: "100%" })

export const Card = component$((props: { wide: boolean }) => (
  <div class="card" sx={[card, props.wide && wide]} />
))
```

Keep the handles at module level, as here: the optimizer moves each `$` function
into a module of its own, which imports them. A `class` already on the element is
merged with the styles into the one `class` it ends up with.

`props()` follows the same rule: it returns `{ class, style }`, so its result
spreads onto an element as it is, and the type entry types it that way. Read its
`class`, never its `className`.

## In development

Qwik updates the page from the server render, so run the dev server in its SSR
mode (`vite --mode ssr`, which a Qwik Router app's `dev` script already does). A
style edit then reaches the page like any other edit.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).
- [The Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite).
---
# Angular
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/angular
# Angular

Kirana works with both ways of building Angular: the **Angular CLI**, through two
builders that replace Angular's own for building and serving, and **Analog** on
Vite, through a Vite plugin. Templates style elements with an `[sx]` directive.
Tested on every change by `examples/angular-cli` and `examples/analog-angular`,
with npm and pnpm, in a production build and on the dev server.



## How Angular differs

Everywhere else, `sx` is compiled away: the build writes the class names into the
element. An Angular template reaches only its component's members, so there the
build compiles your `css({...})` calls into class strings, and the `[sx]`
directive merges them in the browser with Kirana's runtime, which is under 1.1 kB gzipped.
The stylesheet is still built ahead of time, and the classes are the same ones a
JSX app would get. What moves to the browser is only the merge: which entry wins
when two handles set the same property.

## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It detects Angular and whether it builds with the CLI or Analog, shows every
change below as a diff, writes them once you say yes, and prints the install
command (`--install` runs it). Then `npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result.

## With the Angular CLI

### 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core @kirana-style/angular
```

### 2. Use Kirana's builders

In `angular.json`, swap the `build` and `serve` builders. Every option stays as
it is:

```json file="angular.json"
{
  "projects": {
    "app": {
      "architect": {
        "build": {
          "builder": "@kirana-style/angular:application",
          "options": { "browser": "src/main.ts" }
        },
        "serve": {
          "builder": "@kirana-style/angular:dev-server"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Angular compiles TypeScript from disk and has no hook to change a file first. So
the builders keep a compiled copy of `src/` in `.kirana/`, and hand Angular:

- that copy, through `fileReplacements`;
- the stylesheet, `.kirana/kirana.css`, in `styles`.

The dev server and watch builds update the copy as you edit. Ignore the folder:

```bash file=".gitignore"
.kirana/
```

There is no stylesheet import to add: the builders add it.

## With Analog

### 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core @kirana-style/angular
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

### 2. Add the plugin

Kirana goes after Analog. Angular compiles each file from disk, and Kirana
compiles the JavaScript it emitted:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import analog from "@analogjs/platform"
import { kiranaAngular } from "@kirana-style/angular/vite"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [analog(), kiranaAngular()],
})
```

### 3. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.ts"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## Write a component

Import `SxDirective`, and expose the handles as a member with the same name, so
the template can reach them:

```ts file="src/app/card.ts"
import { Component, input } from "@angular/core"
import { SxDirective } from "@kirana-style/angular"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const styles = {
  card: css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" }),
  wide: css({ width: "100%" }),
}

@Component({
  selector: "app-card",
  imports: [SxDirective],
  template: `<div
    class="card"
    [sx]="[styles.card, wide() && styles.wide]"
  ></div>`,
})
export class Card {
  readonly wide = input(false)
  protected readonly styles = styles
}
```

`[sx]` takes what `sx` takes anywhere: one handle, or an array with falsy guards.
Angular type-checks it against `Sx`. The element's own class and style attributes stay;
the directive adds and removes only what it set. Templates in a `templateUrl`
file work the same way.

A value known only at runtime, such as `css({ marginLeft: offset })`, is bridged
through a custom property, as in [dynamic styles](/docs/styling/dynamic).

### Another class-name prefix

If `kirana.config` sets [`names.prefix`](/docs/reference/config), tell the
directive:

```ts file="src/main.ts"
import { provideKirana } from "@kirana-style/angular"

bootstrapApplication(App, { providers: [provideKirana({ prefix: "app" })] })
```

## In the editor

The [editor extensions](/docs/tooling/editor) read `[sx]` in inline templates and
in `templateUrl` files: colour hints, the style card on hover, go to definition
and diagnostics, as in JSX.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [merging](/docs/styling/merging).
- [The Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite), for Analog.
---
# Ember.js
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/ember
# Ember.js

Ember's template-tag components (`.gjs`, `.gts`) hold a `<template>` next to
their JavaScript. Kirana's plugin runs after Embroider has turned them into
JavaScript, so `css()` works in them as anywhere else, and templates reach the
handles in scope.

The `sx` helper merges them, later ones winning. Tested on
every change by `examples/ember`, built and on its dev server.



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It detects the project, shows every change below as a diff, writes them once you
say yes, and prints the install command (`--install` runs it). Then
`npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core @kirana-style/ember
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

Kirana goes last, after Embroider's plugins:

```js file="vite.config.mjs"
import { kiranaEmber } from "@kirana-style/ember/vite"
import { classicEmberSupport, ember, extensions } from "@embroider/vite"
import { babel } from "@rollup/plugin-babel"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    classicEmberSupport(),
    ember(),
    babel({ babelHelpers: "runtime", extensions }),
    kiranaEmber(),
  ],
})
```

The Ember plugin also tells the compiler that `@ember/`, `@glimmer/` and
`@embroider/virtual/` are modules only Embroider resolves
([`externals`](/docs/reference/config)).

## 3. Import the stylesheet

```js file="app/app.js"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 4. Write a component

```js file="app/components/card.gjs"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { sx } from "@kirana-style/ember"

const styles = {
  card: css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" }),
  active: css({ outline: "2px solid" }),
}

<template>
  <div class={{sx styles.card (if @active styles.active)}}>{{yield}}</div>
</template>
```

`sx` is a plain function, which Ember calls as a helper. It merges the handles
with Kirana's runtime, the way an `sx` list does at build time elsewhere. A
value known only at runtime carries custom properties a class cannot hold; set it
from the component's code.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [merging](/docs/styling/merging).
- [The Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite).

# Meteor
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/meteor
# Meteor

Since Meteor 3.4 the `rspack` package bundles app code with Rspack, so Kirana's
Rspack plugin is Meteor's plugin too. Tested on every change by
`examples/meteor`, built with `meteor build` and on `meteor run`.



## The fast way

In the project's root:

```bash
npx kirana-style@latest init
```

It detects the project, shows every change below as a diff, writes them once you
say yes, and prints the install command (`--install` runs it). Then
`npx kirana-style doctor` checks the result.

## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/rspack
```

## 2. Add the plugin

```js file="rspack.config.js"
const { defineConfig } = require("@meteorjs/rspack")
const { KiranaPlugin } = require("@kirana-style/rspack")

module.exports = defineConfig(() => ({ plugins: [new KiranaPlugin()] }))
```

## 3. Tell Kirana about Meteor's modules

`meteor/meteor` and the other `meteor/` modules exist only in Meteor's bundler:

```json file="kirana.config.json"
{ "externals": ["meteor/"] }
```

## 4. Import the stylesheet

```jsx file="client/main.jsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 5. Write a component

```jsx file="imports/ui/App.jsx"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

const title = css({ fontSize: "2rem", fontWeight: 600 })

export const App = () => <h1 sx={title}>Hello</h1>
```

## Notes

- Meteor turns on Rspack's persistent cache, so a build can restore modules
  without running loaders. Kirana compiles those from disk before it writes the
  stylesheet, so a cached build is complete.
- Kirana resolves imports as Node.js does: Meteor's root-relative
  `/imports/ui/App` is a runtime value to it. Import styles relatively, or through
  `paths` in `tsconfig.json`.

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
- [Rspack and Rsbuild](/docs/integrations/rspack).
- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles).

# No framework
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/vanilla
# No framework

A style handle is a class string, and `cx` merges handles the way `sx` does. That
is all plain TypeScript, a web component or a server template needs. Tested by
`examples/vite-vanilla`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/vite
```

## 2. Add the plugin

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [kirana()] })
```

## 3. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.ts"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## 4. Style elements

```ts file="src/main.ts"
import { css, cx } from "@kirana-style/core"

const button = css({ paddingInline: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
const primary = css({ backgroundColor: "black", color: "white" })

const element = document.createElement("button")
element.className = String(cx(button, primary))
```

Later handles win, exactly as in an `sx` list, so `cx(button, primary)` is the
merge you want and `cx(primary, button)` the reverse.

## Without a bundler

`kirana-style build src --out styles.css` writes the stylesheet from the command line;
see the [CLI](/docs/tooling/cli).

## Next

- [Your first component](/docs/start/first-component): a button with a hover state
  and a variant, and the CSS it compiles to.
---
# Server templates
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/server-templates
# Server templates

A server-rendered template cannot call `css()`. So a server app keeps its styles
in TypeScript modules, Kirana's CLI compiles them, and the templates name them.

- [Laravel](/docs/frameworks/laravel): The PHP framework for web artisans: @kirana in Blade.
- [Symfony](/docs/frameworks/symfony): The PHP framework for websites and apps: kirana() in Twig.
- [Ruby on Rails](/docs/frameworks/rails): The full-stack Ruby framework: a kirana helper in ERB views.
- [Phoenix](/docs/frameworks/phoenix): Rich, interactive Elixir apps: kirana/1 in HEEx templates.
- [AdonisJS](/docs/frameworks/adonisjs): The fully featured Node.js framework: kirana() in Edge.

## How it works

1. **You write styles in modules** listed under `classes.modules` in
   `kirana.config`. Each exported handle, and each handle inside an exported
   object, is a style a template can name:

   ```ts file="resources/styles/app.styles.ts"
   import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

   export const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
   export const button = {
     base: css({ paddingInline: "1rem" }),
     primary: css({ backgroundColor: "black", color: "white" }),
   }
   ```

2. **The CLI writes two files**: the stylesheet, and a class map of every name
   with the classes it compiles to:

   ```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
   import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"

   export default defineConfig({
     classes: {
       modules: ["resources/styles"],
       out: "public/kirana/classes.json",
     },
   })
   ```

   ```bash
   npx kirana-style dev resources/styles --out public/kirana/kirana.css
   ```

   `kirana-style dev` rewrites both on every edit; `kirana-style build --minify` writes them
   once, for production.

3. **A template names styles** through its language's helper, which reads the
   class map and merges the names, later ones winning, as an `sx` list does:

   ```html
   <button class="@kirana('button.base', 'button.primary')">Save</button>
   ```

## Merging without a runtime

Kirana's class names carry their own merge rules: everything before the final `_`
says which property, target and conditions a class sets, so the last class for a
key wins. The helpers in PHP, Ruby and Elixir implement those rules in a few dozen
lines, and each passes the same 400 merge cases as the JavaScript runtime, on every
change. Nothing about a style is decided in the template.

## Limits

- **Only styles known at build time.** A recipe, an array, or a value from a
  variable has no class string a template can use; the build reports it as
  `classes-not-static`. Pick between variants in the template instead:
  `kirana('button.base', $primary ? 'button.primary' : null)`.
- **An unknown name fails loudly**: at runtime in the helper, and in the editor,
  where the [language server](/docs/tooling/editor) underlines it
  (`unknown-class-name`) and hovers a known one with its styles.
- **The stylesheet holds every style the modules export**, used or not: no
  template is read at build time.
---
# Laravel
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/laravel
# Laravel

Blade templates name styles with `@kirana(…)`; the Kirana CLI writes the
stylesheet and the class map into `public/kirana`. How it fits together:
[server templates](/docs/frameworks/server-templates). Tested on every change by
`examples/laravel`, served by `php artisan serve`, with a style edit checked on
reload. A React, Vue or Svelte front end (Inertia) uses [the Vite
plugin](/docs/integrations/vite) as usual.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D kirana-style
```

```bash
composer require kirana-style/kirana
```

Laravel discovers the package's service provider, which registers the directive.

## 2. Name the style modules

```json file="kirana.config.json"
{
  "classes": {
    "modules": ["resources/styles"],
    "out": "public/kirana/classes.json"
  }
}
```

## 3. Write styles

```ts file="resources/styles/app.styles.ts"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
export const active = css({ outline: "2px solid" })
```

## 4. Run the CLI beside the server

```bash
npx kirana-style dev resources/styles --out public/kirana/kirana.css
```

For production, `npx kirana-style build resources/styles --out public/kirana/kirana.css --minify`
in your deploy step.

## 5. Use it in Blade

```html file="resources/views/home.blade.php"
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ asset('kirana/kirana.css') }}" />

<div class="@kirana('card', $active ? 'active' : null)">…</div>
```

The class map is read from `public/kirana/classes.json`; set `kirana.classes` in
your configuration to read it from elsewhere.


```bash

```

## 2. Register the Twig function

```yaml file="config/services.yaml"
services:
  Kirana\Twig\KiranaExtension:
    arguments: ["%kernel.project_dir%/public/kirana/classes.json"]
```

Autoconfiguration tags it as a Twig extension. It reads the class map on first
use, so `cache:clear` works before the first `kirana-style build`.

## 3. Name the style modules and write styles

```json file="kirana.config.json"
{
  "classes": {
    "modules": ["resources/styles"],
    "out": "public/kirana/classes.json"
  }
}
```

```ts file="resources/styles/app.styles.ts"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
```

## 4. Run the CLI

```bash
npx kirana-style dev resources/styles --out public/kirana/kirana.css
```

`kirana-style build --minify` writes both files once, for production.

## 5. Use it in Twig

```twig file="templates/home.html.twig"
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ asset('kirana/kirana.css') }}">

<div class="{{ kirana('card', active ? 'active') }}">…</div>
```

# Ruby on Rails
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/rails
# Ruby on Rails

ERB views name styles with the `kirana` helper, which the gem's Railtie puts in
every view; the Kirana CLI writes the stylesheet and the class map. How it fits
together: [server templates](/docs/frameworks/server-templates). Tested on every
change by `examples/rails`, served by Puma, with a style edit checked on reload.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D kirana-style
```

```ruby file="Gemfile"
gem "kirana"
```

## 2. Name the style modules and write styles

```json file="kirana.config.json"
{
  "classes": { "modules": ["app/styles"], "out": "public/kirana/classes.json" }
}
```

```ts file="app/styles/app.styles.ts"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
```

## 3. Run the CLI with the server

```bash file="Procfile.dev"
web: bin/rails server
kirana: npx kirana-style dev app/styles --out public/kirana/kirana.css
```

For production, run `npx kirana-style build app/styles --out public/kirana/kirana.css --minify`
before `assets:precompile`.

## 4. Use it in a view

```erb file="app/views/home/index.html.erb"
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/kirana/kirana.css">

<div class="<%= kirana :card, active && :active %>">…</div>
```

The helper reads the class map again whenever `kirana-style dev` rewrites it. Set
`config.kirana.classes` to read it from somewhere other than
`public/kirana/classes.json`.

# Phoenix
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/frameworks/phoenix
# Phoenix

HEEx templates name styles with `kirana/1`; the Kirana CLI writes the stylesheet
and the class map into `priv/static/kirana`. How it fits together:
[server templates](/docs/frameworks/server-templates). Tested on every change by
`examples/phoenix`, with a style edit checked on reload.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D kirana-style
```

```elixir file="mix.exs"
defp deps do
  [
    # …
    {:kirana, "~> 0.1"}
  ]
end
```

## 2. Import the helper

```elixir file="lib/my_app_web.ex"
defp html_helpers do
  quote do
    # …
    import Kirana, only: [kirana: 1]
  end
end
```

## 3. Name the style modules and write styles

```json file="kirana.config.json"
{
  "classes": {
    "modules": ["assets/styles"],
    "out": "priv/static/kirana/classes.json"
  }
}
```

```ts file="assets/styles/app.styles.ts"
import { css } from "@kirana-style/core"

export const card = css({ padding: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" })
```

## 4. Run the CLI as a watcher

```elixir file="config/dev.exs"
config :my_app, MyAppWeb.Endpoint,
  watchers: [
    kirana: {System, :cmd, ["npx", ~w(kirana-style dev assets/styles --out priv/static/kirana/kirana.css)]}
  ]
```

Add `kirana` to the `only:` list of `Plug.Static` (in `static_paths/0`).

In your deploy, run `npx kirana-style build … --minify` before `mix phx.digest`.

## 5. Use it in HEEx

```heex file="lib/my_app_web/components/layouts/root.html.heex"
<link rel="stylesheet" href={~p"/kirana/kirana.css"} />

<div class={kirana(["card", @active && "active"])}>…</div>
```

# Choose a bundler
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/bundlers
# Choose a bundler

Every adapter does the same small job: it hands modules that carry styles to the
compiler, and puts the finished stylesheet where the bundler expects it. None of
them interprets a style, so the atoms, the class names and the stylesheet are
byte-for-byte the same whichever bundler built them.

- [Vite](/docs/integrations/vite): The build tool most frameworks run on, with hot style updates.
- [Rolldown](/docs/integrations/rolldown): The Rust bundler under Vite, on its own.
- [webpack](/docs/integrations/webpack): A pre loader for sx and a plugin that writes the stylesheet.
- [Rspack and Rsbuild](/docs/integrations/rspack): The fast Rust-based web bundler, and its build tool.
- [Parcel](/docs/integrations/parcel): The zero-configuration build tool for the web.
- [Bun](/docs/integrations/bun): Bun's bundler and its dev server, from one plugin.
- [esbuild](/docs/integrations/esbuild): An extremely fast bundler, in watch and serve modes too.
- [PostCSS](/docs/integrations/postcss): The project's stylesheet wherever @kirana; stands.
- [Jest](/docs/integrations/jest): A transformer, so tests see the class names you ship.
- [Storybook](/docs/integrations/storybook): Stories built with your project's Vite config, styled as the app is.

## Development servers


Every host updates the stylesheet while you work. Vite, webpack, Rspack, Rsbuild
and Next.js send it as a CSS hot update; Bun and esbuild as their reload. Each is
checked on every change: the dev server starts, a style is edited, and the page
must show it.

## Same styles on every host

Kirana's adapters only hand modules to one compiler and put its stylesheet where
the bundler expects it, so the same source gives the same CSS whichever bundler
builds it. CI checks exactly that: one React example, built with every bundler,
must produce the same set of classes as with Vite.
---
# Vite
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/vite
# Vite

`@kirana-style/vite` is the adapter for Vite 8 and Rolldown. It owns a compiler session,
compiles the modules that carry styles, serves the stylesheet in development and
writes it in a build.

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [kirana(), react()],
})
```

**Order matters.** Kirana runs `pre`, before the framework plugin, so React (or
anything else) only ever sees compiled JavaScript.

## Options

```ts
kirana({
  // Overrides kirana.config.ts, key by key.
  config: { names: { prefix: "app" } },
  // Surface info-level diagnostics (bridged values, lowered targets) in the terminal.
  reportInfo: true,
  // Shorter class names in a production build (below).
  names: "dense",
})
```

All are optional, and most projects pass nothing: the plugin finds
`kirana.config.*` in the Vite root on its own.

## Dense names

With `names: "dense"`, a production build replaces the two hashes in every
class name with codes of one or two characters, assigned from the whole build:
`k50-KFHz_D9ur` becomes something like `k50-b_a`.

- **The development server keeps the hashed names.** So do the language
  server and `kirana-style trace`.
- **Only names the compiler wrote are renamed.** A string that merely looks like
  a class name, such as an example on a documentation page, is left alone.
- **The client and server bundles agree.** Both are renamed from one map, and
  the stylesheet with them.

It is off by default: names can change between deploys in chunks whose source
did not, so those chunks are downloaded again. See
[dense names](/docs/building/output#dense-names) for what it saves and why. It cannot be
combined with a [class map](/docs/frameworks/server-templates), whose server-side
helpers read hashed names, and the build says so.

## Which modules it compiles

Script files only (TypeScript and JavaScript, with or without JSX, ES modules
included) outside `node_modules`, and only when the text contains one of:

- `@kirana-style/`;
- an `sx` attribute;
- a call of a relation's read (`.within(`, `.parent(`, `.after(` or `.before(`),
  which a module that imports a relation from another may hold alone.

That prefilter is why adding Kirana to a large application does not slow the build
down in proportion to its size.

Markdown, HTML and other assets are never compiled, so `sx` written there does
nothing. Neither are the modules a plugin generates rather than reads from a file
(`virtual:` ids, and Rollup's null-prefixed ones), even when their id ends in a
script extension: they hold that plugin's code, never your styles.

## A dependency's CSS in a layer

`cssLayer(name, include)` puts a dependency's stylesheets in a cascade layer as
Vite loads them: every stylesheet whose path contains `include`, or matches it
when it is a regular expression. It is for a package that imports unlayered CSS
from JavaScript, where there is no import line to give a layer. Unlayered, a
theme's reset would beat every style you write.

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana, { cssLayer } from "@kirana-style/vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [kirana(), cssLayer("vendor", "some-theme/dist/")],
})
```

Then order the layer before Kirana's, `layers: { before: ["vendor"] }`
([layers](/docs/config/layers)). `@charset` and `@import` stay at the top of a
wrapped file, and an import without a layer of its own takes the same one.
[VitePress](/docs/frameworks/vitepress) uses it for its default theme.

## The stylesheet

Import the entry once, in your entry; a framework that renders the document as a
component imports it as a URL for its `<link>`:

```tsx
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
// or, for <link rel="stylesheet" href={kiranaCss} /> in a document component:
import kiranaCss from "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css?url"
```

- **In development** the plugin serves the live stylesheet and pushes updates
  over Vite's hot channel, so a style change restyles the page without a reload.
- **In a build** it replaces the placeholder rule with the real stylesheet and
  renames the asset to a content hash.

`kirana()` returns two plugins, which Vite flattens, so it is still one entry in
`plugins`. The second, `kirana:late`, runs at the end of a build for a stylesheet
asset a framework adds after the first has filled the others (Qwik does).

`?url`, `?raw` and `?inline` behave the way they do for any other Vite asset.

## A stylesheet of your own

Kirana's stylesheet keeps `light-dark()` as written. A stylesheet you write goes
through Vite's CSS minifier instead, and Vite's default `build.cssTarget` predates
that function, so the minifier rewrites it into switches on two custom properties
that nothing sets: colours that work in development vanish in production. Set the
target to Kirana's floor, Chrome 123, Safari 17.5, Firefox 120, the first browsers with it:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
export default defineConfig({
  build: { cssTarget: ["chrome123", "safari17.5", "firefox120"] },
})
```

## Diagnostics in the terminal

Errors fail the build; warnings print with their file, line and help text. Info
diagnostics are quiet unless you pass `reportInfo: true`, which is useful when you
want to see every runtime bridge in an application.

## Rolldown

Vite 8 is Rolldown-backed, and the plugin uses Rolldown's filters, so a
Rolldown-only setup works the same way.
---
# Rolldown
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/rolldown
# Rolldown

Rolldown on its own does not bundle CSS, so the adapter writes the stylesheet
itself and your HTML links it. On Vite, which is Rolldown-backed and does bundle
CSS, use [the Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite) instead. Tested by
`examples/rolldown-react`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/rolldown
```

## 2. Add the plugin

```ts file="rolldown.config.mjs"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/rolldown"
import { defineConfig } from "rolldown"

export default defineConfig({
  input: "src/main.tsx",
  output: { dir: "dist" },
  plugins: [kirana()],
})
```

## 3. Link the stylesheet

Importing `@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css` from a module gives you the stylesheet's
file name, `kirana.css` by default (`kirana({ fileName })` changes it); the
build writes it as `dist/kirana.css`.

```html file="index.html"
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/kirana.css" />
```

## Next

- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).
- [Every bundler](/docs/integrations/bundlers).

# webpack
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/webpack
# webpack

The plugin adds its loader in front of your own (`enforce: "pre"`), so it reads
`sx` before your JSX compiler (swc or Babel) compiles it away, and writes the
finished stylesheet once every module is built. Tested by
`examples/webpack-react`. Next.js has [its own guide](/docs/frameworks/nextjs),
and Gatsby, which runs webpack, [its own too](/docs/frameworks/gatsby).



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/webpack
```

## 2. Add the plugin

```js file="webpack.config.js"
import { KiranaPlugin } from "@kirana-style/webpack"

export default {
  // Webpack's native CSS, or css-loader with mini-css-extract-plugin.
  experiments: { css: true },
  plugins: [new KiranaPlugin()],
}
```

## 3. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

The stylesheet entry is ordinary CSS to webpack: it names, links and minifies it
like any other. The plugin fills it in before the minifier runs and before
`realContentHash` names the file after its real content, which is on by default
in production; turn it off and the file name stops tracking the styles.

## Next

- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).
- [Every bundler](/docs/integrations/bundlers).
---
# Rspack and Rsbuild
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/rspack
# Rspack and Rsbuild

Rspack runs webpack's plugins unchanged, so Kirana's webpack plugin is its
plugin too; Rsbuild gets a one-line `pluginKirana`. Tested by
`examples/rsbuild-react` and `examples/rspack-react`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/rspack
```

## 2. Add the plugin



### Rsbuild

```ts file="rsbuild.config.ts"
import { pluginKirana } from "@kirana-style/rspack"
import { defineConfig } from "@rsbuild/core"
import { pluginReact } from "@rsbuild/plugin-react"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [pluginReact(), pluginKirana()],
})
```

### Rspack

```ts file="rspack.config.ts"
import { KiranaPlugin } from "@kirana-style/rspack"
import { defineConfig } from "@rspack/cli"

export default defineConfig({
  entry: { main: "./src/main.tsx" },
  // Rsbuild does this for you: CSS needs a module type.
  module: { rules: [{ test: /\.css$/, type: "css" }] },
  plugins: [new KiranaPlugin()],
})
```



## 3. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## Next

- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).
- [Every bundler](/docs/integrations/bundlers).
