# Parcel
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/parcel
# Parcel

Parcel runs transformers in worker processes, with no step that sees every
module. So the work is split as for Next.js on Turbopack: a transformer rewrites
the styles in each script into class names, and the PostCSS plugin compiles the
whole project into the stylesheet. Tested on every change by `examples/parcel`,
built and on `parcel serve`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/parcel-transformer @kirana-style/postcss postcss
```

## 2. Add the transformer

```json file=".parcelrc"
{
  "extends": "@parcel/config-default",
  "transformers": {
    "*.{js,mjs,jsx,ts,tsx}": ["@kirana-style/parcel-transformer", "..."]
  }
}
```

## 3. Add the PostCSS plugin and mark the stylesheet

```json file=".postcssrc"
{ "plugins": { "@kirana-style/postcss": {} } }
```

```css file="src/kirana.css"
@kirana;
```

Link that stylesheet from your HTML, as any other.

## Next

- [PostCSS](/docs/integrations/postcss), and its options.
- [Every bundler](/docs/integrations/bundlers).
---
# Bun
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/bun
# Bun

Bun writes CSS imported from an entry next to it (`main.css`), and the plugin
finishes it once every module has loaded. Tested by `examples/bun-react`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core
npm install -D @kirana-style/bun
```

## 2. Add the plugin

```ts file="build.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/bun"

await Bun.build({
  entrypoints: ["./src/main.tsx"],
  outdir: "./dist",
  plugins: [kirana()],
})
```

For Bun's dev server (`bun ./index.html`), register it in `bunfig.toml`; there
the stylesheet follows every edit:

```ts file="kirana.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/bun"

export default kirana()
```

```toml file="bunfig.toml"
[serve.static]
plugins = ["./kirana.ts"]
```

## 3. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

## Limits

A `naming` pattern that hashes CSS assets keeps the placeholder's hash, and a
build with `write: false` keeps the placeholder, because there is no file to
finish.

- [Styles](/docs/styling/styles) and [conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).
- [Every bundler](/docs/integrations/bundlers).

# esbuild
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/esbuild
# esbuild

esbuild writes CSS imported from an entry beside it (`main.css`), and the plugin
finishes it once every module has loaded, on disk or in `outputFiles` with
`write: false`. Tested by `examples/esbuild-react`.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install @kirana-style/core

```

```js file="build.mjs"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/esbuild"
import * as esbuild from "esbuild"

await esbuild.build({
  entryPoints: ["src/main.tsx"],
  bundle: true,
  outdir: "www",
  plugins: [kirana()],
})
```

With `context().watch()` and `serve()` the stylesheet follows every edit,
delivered by esbuild's live reload.

## 3. Import the stylesheet

```ts file="src/main.tsx"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
```

# PostCSS
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/postcss
# PostCSS

`@kirana-style/postcss` replaces `@kirana;` (or the stylesheet entry's placeholder) with
the project's stylesheet. It compiles every script of the project, incrementally
by modification time, and reports project-wide diagnostics as PostCSS warnings.

It writes the stylesheet only: the scripts still need Kirana's compiler to turn
`css()` into class names. That is why it comes with a script step wherever it is
used: the loader in [Next.js on Turbopack](/docs/frameworks/nextjs), the
transformer in [Parcel](/docs/integrations/parcel).



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install -D @kirana-style/postcss postcss
```

## 2. Add the plugin

```js file="postcss.config.mjs"
export default { plugins: { "@kirana-style/postcss": {} } }
```

## 3. Mark where the stylesheet goes

```css file="app/globals.css"
@kirana;
```

## Options

| Option       | Default               | What it does                                          |
| ------------ | --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `root`       | the working directory | Where `kirana.config.*` and the project are.          |
| `minify`     | on in production      | Write minified CSS.                                   |
| `reportInfo` | `false`               | Report info diagnostics (bridged values) as warnings. |

## Next

- [Next.js](/docs/frameworks/nextjs), which uses it with Turbopack.
- [Every bundler](/docs/integrations/bundlers).
---
# Jest
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/jest
# Jest

Jest runs no bundler, so Kirana is a transformer: it compiles a module's styles,
then hands it to the transformer you already use. Tests see the class names your
app ships; no stylesheet is written. Tested by `examples/jest-react`. With
Vitest, [the Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite) does this already.



## 1. Install

```bash
npm install -D @kirana-style/jest
```

## 2. Add the transformer

```js file="jest.config.js"
export default {
  transform: {
    "\\.[jt]sx?$": ["@kirana-style/jest", { transformer: "babel-jest" }],
  },
}
```

## Caching

Jest caches a module by its own source. After changing tokens another module
reads, run Jest once with `--no-cache`.

## Next

- [Every bundler](/docs/integrations/bundlers).

# Storybook
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/integrations/storybook
# Storybook

Storybook's Vite builders (`@storybook/react-vite`, `@storybook/vue3-vite` and
the rest) read your project's `vite.config`, so a project already set up for
Kirana needs no Storybook configuration of its own for the styles: stories
compile with the same plugin, to the same class names. Tested on every change by
`examples/storybook`, built and on its dev server.

## 1. Kirana in `vite.config`

As for the app ([the Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite)):

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [kirana(), react()] })
```

## 2. The stylesheet in the preview

Stories render in the preview's frame, which has a document of its own:

```ts file=".storybook/preview.ts"
import "@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css"
import type { Preview } from "@storybook/react-vite"

export default {} satisfies Preview
```

## 3. Write a story

```tsx file="src/button.stories.tsx"
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from "@storybook/react-vite"

import { Button } from "./button"

export default { component: Button } satisfies Meta<typeof Button>

export const Primary: StoryObj<typeof Button> = { args: { tone: "primary" } }
```

A story for each variant of a [recipe](/docs/styling/recipes) shows every class
the variant compiles to, and editing a style updates the story on the dev server.

## Next

- [Recipes](/docs/styling/recipes): variants worth a story each.
- [Themes and modes](/docs/tokens/themes-and-modes): a toolbar switch for
  `mode.light` and `mode.dark` in the preview.

# Migrating from Tailwind
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/migration/from-tailwind
# Migrating from Tailwind

We have done this migration at full scale (every shadcn/ui component, three
applications) twice: once by hand (by way of the StyleX port), and once with
`kirana-style migrate tailwind`, until the result matched the Tailwind original with zero computed-style differences.
So this page is what it costs, not what it should cost in theory.

## The shift, in four lines

1. **A property, not a class.** `px-4` becomes `paddingInline: space[4]`.
2. **Conditions nest inside values.** `hover:bg-black` becomes
   `backgroundColor: { ":hover": … }`.
3. **A ladder, not specificity.** No `!important`, no arbitrary-variant ordering
   games. [Precedence](/docs/styling/precedence).
4. **Merging replaces entries.** `cn()` deleted a whole utility; Kirana replaces
   the entries you name. [Merging](/docs/styling/merging).

## The mapping

| Tailwind                      | Kirana                                                                      |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `flex items-center gap-2`     | `{ display: "flex", alignItems: "center", gap: space[2] }`                  |
| `px-4 py-2`                   | `{ paddingInline: space[4], paddingBlock: space[2] }`                       |
| `text-sm`                     | `{ fontSize: fontSize.sm, lineHeight: lineHeight.sm }`, always both         |
| `bg-primary/80`               | `{ backgroundColor: alpha.primary80 }`, a `color-mix` token                 |
| `hover:underline`             | `{ textDecorationLine: { ":hover": "underline" } }`                         |
| `md:grid-cols-2`              | `{ gridTemplateColumns: { [breakpoint.md]: "repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr))" } }` |
| `dark:bg-zinc-900`            | nothing: the token is a `light-dark()` pair                                 |
| `group-hover:opacity-100`     | `{ opacity: { [group.within(":hover")]: 1 } }`                              |
| `peer-checked:text-black`     | `{ color: { [peer.after(":checked")]: "black" } }`                          |
| `[&_svg]:size-4`              | `{ [select.descendant("svg")]: { width: …, height: … } }`                   |
| `cn(a, b)`                    | `cx(a, b)`, or `sx={[a, b]}`                                                |
| `cva({ variants })`           | [`recipe({ variants })`](/docs/styling/recipes)                             |
| `data-[state=open]:rotate-90` | `{ rotate: { '[data-state="open"]': "90deg" } }`                            |

The vocabulary itself carries over: `@kirana-style/preset-scales` is generated from
Tailwind v4's own theme, so `space[4]`, `color.zinc500` and `breakpoint.md` are
the values you already know.

## The four that do not translate directly

**`text-sm` sets two properties.** Tailwind's type utilities set a size _and_ a
line height. Write both, every time: a size without its line height is the most
common visual drift in a port.

**`border` sets a colour.** Tailwind's preflight gives every element a default
border colour, so `border` alone is visible. Kirana has no preflight: `border`
sets widths only, and you name the colour.

**`cn()` conflict resolution is gone, and that is the point.** `cn("p-2", "p-4")`
kept the last. Kirana merges per entry, so the same intent is `padding: space[4]`
written once. But a _conditional_ value you did not name survives. Read
[merging](/docs/styling/merging) before porting a component with states.

**Arbitrary variants that read classes** (`[&:not([class*='size-'])]`) have no
equivalent, because Kirana's class names are hashes. Use
[`select`](/docs/styling/contextual): contextual styles sit in a lower layer, so
the child's own style wins without a guard.

## The codemod

> [!TIP] Porting with a coding agent
> The [`kirana-migrate` skill](/docs/project/agent-skills) gives an agent this
> page's process: the codemod and its report, the traps, and how to prove the
> port renders the same.

`kirana-style migrate tailwind` rewrites Tailwind's constructs into Kirana's:

| Tailwind        | Kirana                               |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| class strings   | `css()` objects                      |
| `cn(…)`         | `sx` arrays                          |
| `cva`           | [`recipe`](/docs/styling/recipes)    |
| `group`, `peer` | [relations](/docs/styling/relations) |
| `[&_svg]:`      | [`select`](/docs/styling/contextual) |

It uses the same [utility grammar](/docs/styling/utilities) as utility strings, so
the object it writes compiles to exactly the atoms of the class string it replaces.

<!-- ::figure-codemod -->

First give the project the vocabulary, and point the colour scale at your theme:

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"
import scales from "@kirana-style/preset-scales/preset"

export default defineConfig({
  presets: [scales()],
  utilities: {
    scales: {
      color: [
        { module: "@kirana-style/preset-scales", export: "color" },
        { module: "./src/theme.ts", export: "theme" },
      ],
    },
    // shadcn's `@custom-variant`s, as conditions
    variants: { "data-horizontal": '[data-orientation="horizontal"]' },
  },
})
```

Then run it over your sources and your CSS. The CSS is read for `@custom-variant`
and `@utility`, so a custom variant nobody declared is reported instead of
silently getting Tailwind's default meaning:

```bash
kirana-style migrate tailwind src src/globals.css            # read the diff and the report
kirana-style migrate tailwind src src/globals.css --write
kirana-style check src
```

A colour's `dark:` value becomes a `light-dark()` pair. Any other property's
becomes a `{ light, dark }` token in a small group at the top of the file, which
follows the colour scheme and Kirana's [`mode`](/docs/tokens/themes-and-modes)
handles.

So where your theme switch sets `.dark`, set `mode.dark` too.

A Base UI part rendering one of your components (`render={<Button />}`) hands
its styles to that component as `sx`, since both are one element and a class
merged into the component's props would replace the component's own.

`space-x-2` and `divide-y` become a `select.child(":not(:last-child)")` block,
which, like Tailwind's `:where()` rule, loses to a child's own margin or border.

Where a class goes:

- A component's `className` prop becomes `sx`, in its props type too.
- A component from an installed package (Base UI parts) gets `{...props(…)}`
  instead, because it does not read `sx`.
- A class string known only at runtime stays in `className`, where the compiler
  merges it with `sx`.

A class string that stays on one of your own components is reported too: once
migrated, the component reads `sx`, so the class lands in its props and their
spread replaces its styles. A library that hands your component a `className`
(react-day-picker's `components`) does the same without any file showing it; take
`className` out of the props there.

A `select` block ranks below the target's own styles, where Tailwind's parent
rule usually won. When the parent and the target both carry a `data-slot`, the
codemod moves the rule onto the target, as a condition on its position
(`':is([data-slot="field"] > [data-slot="field-label"])'`), so the result is the
same. When it cannot (no `data-slot` on the parent, a recipe variant) and the
target sets the property itself, it says so, and the fix is to read the parent
from the target by hand.

What it reports rather than guesses:

- `!important` under a variant;
- custom variants and utilities nobody declared;
- a contextual target under a condition (`focus:**:text-x`);
- targets that are class names;
- `in-*` on anything but a `data-slot` (`in-data-[slot=x]:` becomes a relation
  every `data-slot="x"` element anchors);
- a colour's `dark:` with no value at rest;
- relations anchored in no migrated file;
- a dropped `w-`/`h-` guard;
- dynamic class strings.

Each report item is also left as a `// tailwind:` comment beside the style it
concerns, so the diff shows where to look.

A tool that only needs to know what one class string becomes, to draft a value in
a report rather than rewrite a file, calls the same lowering from code:
`driver.lowerTailwind(classes, file)` on `@kirana-style/compiler` returns the
`css()` call, the module that declares what it reads, and what it left out (see
[the same answers from code](/docs/tooling/cli#the-same-answers-from-code)).

## Measured: the Tailwind original of our shadcn/ui port

We ran the codemod over the whole Tailwind original (`packages/ui`, the shared
shell, and the demo, blocks and examples applications) and compared the result
with the original, element by element.

| Step                            | Result                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The codemod, unedited           | 199 report items                                                                        |
| Hand fixes                      | 38 patches, each resolving report items or a difference conformance found               |
| Conformance, at rest            | **0 differences** on 1 + 64 + 124 routes, three widths, light and dark                  |
| Conformance, interactive states | **0 differences**: dialogs, menus with a highlighted row, selects, tabs, hover, focus … |

"Conformance" is the computed style of every `[data-slot]` element, including
`::before` and `::after`, diffed against the Tailwind build. What it does not
prove: right-to-left layouts, focus rings and states outside the harness's list,
and elements without a `data-slot`. Check those by reading or by hand.

The 199 items, by reason: 39 `!important` under a variant, 35 class strings built
at runtime (they stay classes), 33 contextual targets under a condition, 20
targets that are class names or siblings, 16 contextual rules the target
outranks, 13 arbitrary selectors, 12 utilities the preset lacks (gradients,
`container`, and a few misspelt classes that render nothing in Tailwind either),
9 `dark:` values on non-colours, and 22 informational. Most need no change; the
38 patches are the ones that did.

## Pitfalls we hit

Every one of these compiled cleanly and rendered differently. They are listed
roughly by how often they cost us time.

**A parent's rule no longer beats the child's own.** In Tailwind,
`*:data-[slot=label]:w-full` on a field beat the label's own `w-fit`, because a
variant's rule is printed after plain utilities, or is more specific. In Kirana a
`select` block ranks below the target's own styles. That is what lets an icon keep
its own size without a `:not([class*='size-'])` guard.

The codemod moves such rules onto the target when both ends carry a `data-slot`;
when it cannot, it reports "sets `width` itself, which outranks a contextual
rule". Fix it by letting the target read the parent, with a relation
(`inGroup.within()`) or a condition on its own position
(`':is([data-slot="field"] > *)'`). It was our most common hand fix.

**`!important` has no equivalent.** Without a variant, `p-0!` becomes
`{ "*": null, base: 0 }`, which removes every other padding entry, as the
important flag did. Under a variant (`hover:size-3!`) it is reported: decide
where the value belongs, usually as a condition on the element that must win.

**A class name passed to a migrated component replaces its styles.** A migrated
component reads `sx`; a `className` that still reaches it lands in the props
spread, after the component's own class, and replaces it. Look for libraries that
hand your components a class you never see: react-day-picker's `components` gave
its day button one, and every day button lost its styles. Take the class name out
of those props.

**A guard that was an escape hatch.** `*:[div:not([class*='w-'])]:w-full` let a
child opt out by carrying any class starting with `w-`, including `max-w-*`.
Class names are hashes in Kirana, so the guard is dropped and reported; a child
that relied on it needs `width: auto` of its own.

**Selectors that read class names.** `[.border-b]:pb-6` on a card header asked
whether the header had a bottom border class. There is no such class after the
migration: set the padding where the border is set.

**A `light-dark()` pair is replaced whole.** Tailwind's `bg-background` over
`bg-transparent dark:bg-input/30` left the dark rule in place, and it still won
in dark mode.
In Kirana the override replaces the pair, so an override that must keep the dark
value carries both halves: `light-dark(var(--background), <input/30>)`.

**Variant order used to decide.** Where Tailwind's stylesheet order made
`dark:hover:bg-muted/50` beat `aria-expanded:bg-muted`, Kirana's ladder decides
instead: an attribute outranks `:hover`. The codemod already lets a colour's
`dark:` value outrank the states it encloses; the rest you nest (hover inside the
attribute, since two conditions beat one).

**`sr-only` and margins.** Tailwind printed the screen-reader class's
`margin: -1px` before a legend's own `mb-1.5`, which won. The migrated `sr-only`
style leaves the bottom margin alone, so the element's own margin still applies.

**Suffix selectors cannot be moved.** `**:data-[slot$=-item]:…` matches every
slot ending in `-item`; the codemod cannot know which elements those are. We
moved the rules into a shared style that each item applies.

**Custom variants must be declared.** shadcn's `data-open:` and
`data-horizontal:` are `@custom-variant`s, not Tailwind's defaults. Pass your CSS
to the codemod so it reads them; an undeclared one is reported instead of getting
the wrong meaning.

## Utility strings or objects?

The codemod writes objects, because an object is what the rest of these docs
describe and what the [language server](/docs/project/roadmap) will explain. But
with the scales preset, `sx="flex items-center gap-2"` is valid Kirana too, and
compiles to the same atoms. A reasonable split: strings for short layout lines,
objects for anything with states or tokens of your own. See
[why vertical styles read well](/docs/start/why-kirana#it-doubles-the-code).

## Migrating by hand

Without the codemod (a handful of components, or a codebase whose class strings
are mostly dynamic), work component by component with the mapping above, and:

1. Give every component `sx?: Sx` in place of `className`, and replace
   `cn(base, className)` with `sx={[styles.base, sx]}`.
2. Turn each `cva` into a [`recipe`](/docs/styling/recipes); `defaultVariants`
   carry over.
3. Replace each `group`/`peer` with a declared [relation](/docs/styling/relations);
   the compiler errors on a read nobody anchors.
4. Replace `[&_svg]:` and `*:` with [`select`](/docs/styling/contextual), and
   delete the `:not([class*='size-'])` guards: the child's own size wins anyway.
5. Delete every `dark:` on a colour; write the colour as a `light-dark()` token.
6. Run `kirana-style check` and resolve every diagnostic before moving on.

## The process that worked

1. **Port leaf components first.** They have the fewest conditions and teach you
   the shape.
2. **Port structure verbatim.** Keep the same elements and attributes; change only
   how the styles are expressed. Then a visual diff means something.
3. **Run `kirana-style check` after each component.** `sx-on-external-component` and
   `unused-sx` catch the two mistakes everyone makes with wrapper components.
4. **Compare computed styles, not screenshots.** We kept the
   Tailwind build alongside the Kirana one and diffed the computed styles of every
   element in both schemes at three widths. Eyes miss a 1 px border; a diff does
   not.
5. **Check interactive states too.** Open every overlay, highlight a menu row,
   hover a button and focus an input, then diff again. Some differences exist
   only in a state: a hovered, expanded ghost button in dark mode was one.
6. **Keep hand fixes as patches.** We kept each fix as a patch applied over a
   fresh run of the codemod, so the codemod could improve and be re-run without
   losing work. A patch that stops applying is a sign the codemod now does that
   fix itself.
7. **Fix the original when it is the one that is wrong.** Several "differences"
   we found this way were bugs in the Tailwind original.

## What you get for the trouble

Type checking on every property and value, a stated answer to "which style wins",
diagnostics for the mistakes that used to be silent, and a stylesheet that grows
with distinct declarations instead of with markup.
---
# Migrating from StyleX
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/migration/from-stylex
# Migrating from StyleX

If you write StyleX today, most of your styles are already Kirana styles: both
systems put typed style objects next to components and conditions inside values,
so the mapping below is close to mechanical. The differences that matter are in
merge semantics and in what the compiler checks.

## The mapping

Four names carry most of a StyleX codebase; the table after them has the rest.

<!-- ::figure-stylex -->

| StyleX                               | Kirana                                                    |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `stylex.create({ … })`               | `css({ … })` per style, or an object of handles           |
| `stylex.props(a, b)`                 | `props(a, b)`, or `sx={[a, b]}` on your own elements      |
| `stylex.defineVars({ … })`           | `defineTokens(namespace, { … }, { variable: true })`      |
| `stylex.defineConsts({ … })`         | `defineTokens(namespace, { … })`                          |
| `stylex.createTheme(vars, { … })`    | `defineTheme(tokens, { … })`                              |
| `stylex.keyframes({ … })`            | `keyframes({ … })`                                        |
| `stylex.firstThatWorks(a, b)`        | [`firstThatWorks(a, b)`](/docs/styling/fallbacks)         |
| `stylex.positionTry({ … })`          | [`positionTry({ … })`](/docs/styling/anchor-positioning)  |
| `stylex.viewTransitionClass({ … })`  | [`viewTransition({ … })`](/docs/styling/view-transitions) |
| `stylex.when.hover` and markers      | [`relation()`](/docs/styling/relations)                   |
| `default:` inside a value            | `base:`                                                   |
| `@media (…)` as a key inside a value | the same, or `[media("…")]`                               |

## The difference that bites

In StyleX, `default: null` inside a variant means **"this variant sets nothing
here"**. In Kirana, `base: null` **removes** a base value an earlier style set.

```tsx
// StyleX: "no default value for this variant"
{ color: { default: null, ":hover": "blue" } }

// Kirana: "delete any base colour that was set before me"
{ color: { base: null, ":hover": "blue" } }
```

A codemod cannot tell which you meant, so it does not try. Port these by hand:
if the intent was "nothing here", **omit the key**.

## What Kirana has that StyleX does not

The mapping above is close to one-to-one because both systems share a premise.
These are the things that have no StyleX counterpart, and between them they are
most of the reason Kirana exists.

**A stated precedence ladder, and a tool that reads it back.** StyleX offers two
modes (later-wins and property-specificity), and neither reproduced what the
Tailwind components needed. Kirana has one ladder, and `kirana-style trace file:line
property` prints every candidate declaration, the winner, and the step that
decided it.

**Ambiguity is reported.** When two values could both apply and nothing orders
them, the compiler says so (`ambiguous-precedence`) instead of silently picking.
`conditions.exclusive` is how you tell it that a library never sets two
attributes together.

**A diagnostics catalogue.** 50 codes with stable names, severities and help
text, and a configuration key to re-level the non-errors. StyleX reports
compilation failures; it does not have a catalogue you can suppress, raise, or
look up.

**Relations are declared and checked.** `relation("field")` gives you an anchor
and four reads, and the compiler errors when a relation is read but never
anchored (`relation-without-anchor`) or anchored in a position that cannot match
(`relation-placement`). StyleX's `when.*` with marker classes compiles either
way, and a mis-placed marker is a rule that silently never fires.

**Contextual styles have a layer of their own.** `select.descendant("svg")` lands
below element styles, so the target's own style always wins, with no hand-down
custom properties and no `:not([class*='size-'])` guards.

**`sx` is checked where it is used.** Passing it to a component that does not read
it is reported (`sx-on-external-component`), including one module away through a
rest spread, and a component that takes it and drops it gets `unused-sx`.

**Colour modes without plumbing.** Every colour is one `light-dark()` pair and
`mode.system` needs no JavaScript at all. StyleX needs a theme per mode and a
mechanism to switch it.

**Registered tokens.** A token declared with a `syntax` emits `@property`, so a
custom property can be animated and used as a keyframe key.

**Layers you control.** `layers.before` / `layers.after` place your reset and
vendor CSS around Kirana's own layers, and nothing is emitted unlayered, including
custom-property assignments, which StyleX leaves outside any layer.

**A branch budget for dynamic values.** A finite set of runtime values compiles
to a class expression, an open value to a custom-property bridge, and exceeding
the budget is an error rather than a combinatorial explosion.

**Tailwind's vocabulary, if you want it.** [`@kirana-style/preset-scales`](/docs/tokens/preset-scales)
is Tailwind v4's scales as tokens, and [utility strings](/docs/styling/utilities)
(`sx="px-4 text-sm"`) compile to the same atoms as the object form. StyleX
leaves the vocabulary to you.

**Hosts and frameworks.** Adapters for Vite, Rolldown, webpack, Rspack, Rsbuild, Parcel, Bun and esbuild; `sx` in
React, Preact, Solid, Qwik, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Angular and Ember and every framework built on them (React, Next.js, React Router, TanStack Start, Gatsby, Remix, Waku, Vike, Docusaurus, Preact, Solid, SolidStart, Vue, Nuxt, VitePress, Svelte, SvelteKit, Astro, Qwik, Angular, Ember and Meteor); and
templates in Laravel, Symfony, Rails, Phoenix and AdonisJS, each with an example CI builds and checks. See
[frameworks](/docs/frameworks/overview).

The longer argument, with the StyleX port's problems and what answers each, is
[Why Kirana](/docs/start/why-kirana#what-stylex-got-right-and-what-kirana-adds).

## What StyleX has that Kirana does not

Fairness matters more than a feature list:

- **It is published, versioned and used in production** at Meta scale. Kirana is
  at a 0.x version.
- **A larger ecosystem**: community plugins, documentation, examples, articles and people who have
  already hit your problem.
- **A few helpers** have no direct equivalent, `stylex.when.descendant` and
  `stylex.when.anySibling` among them; write a `:has()` condition.
  `kirana-style migrate stylex` names each one it meets in its report.

If you need a styling compiler in production this quarter, StyleX is the
defensible choice. Kirana is worth it when predictability and diagnostics are the
thing you are missing.

## What else is different

**Precedence.** StyleX has two modes (later-wins and property-specificity), and
neither reproduced what the Tailwind components needed. Kirana has one
[ladder](/docs/styling/precedence), and reports the cases it cannot order instead
of picking silently.

**Relations are declared.** StyleX's `when.*` and marker classes become a
`relation()` with an `anchor`, which the compiler then _checks_: a read with no
anchor is an error rather than a rule that never matches.

**Contextual styles have a layer.** `select.descendant("svg")` lands below element
styles, so a child that sets its own size keeps it, with no hand-down custom
properties and no guards.

**Everything is layered.** StyleX left custom-property assignments unlayered;
Kirana emits nothing outside its layers.

## The codemod

> [!TIP] Porting with a coding agent
> The [`kirana-migrate` skill](/docs/project/agent-skills) gives an agent this
> page's process: the codemod and its report, the traps, and how to prove the
> port renders the same.

```bash
kirana-style migrate stylex src          # print the diff and the report
kirana-style migrate stylex src --write  # apply it
```

It makes the mechanical rewrites, renames `*.stylex.ts` files, and prints a report
of everything it would not decide:

| StyleX                | Kirana         |
| --------------------- | -------------- |
| `create`              | `css`          |
| `defineVars`          | `defineTokens` |
| `createTheme`         | `defineTheme`  |
| markers               | `relation`     |
| `{...stylex.props()}` | `sx`           |

Two follow-up passes still live as scripts in the compiler's repository:

- `{...props(a, b)}` on an element you own becomes `sx={[a, b]}`;
- `sx` on a component from a package becomes `{...props(…)}`, because those never
  read `sx`.

## After the codemod

Work through the report, then let the compiler finish the job: `kirana-style check`
will find the relations without anchors, the components that swallow `sx`, and the
ambiguous pairs. Fix those and the port is done.
---
# Verifying a migration
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/migration/conformance
# Verifying a migration

When you rewrite an application's styling, the question is not "does it look
about right" but "is any computed value different, anywhere, in any state".
Screenshots answer that badly: they miss a 1 px border, and they fail loudly over
a font that loaded a frame late.

This project compares **computed styles**.

<!-- ::figure-conformance -->

## The method

1. Serve the same application twice: the build you came from and the new one.
2. Open the same route in both, at several widths, in both colour schemes.
3. Walk every element and read the same property list from `getComputedStyle`,
   including the things that usually hide, like `text-wrap`, `border-style` and
   the geometry of pseudo-elements.
4. Diff, per element and per property.
5. Anything that differs is either a bug in the new build, a bug in the old one,
   or a difference you list explicitly with a reason.

That last point is the discipline: an expected difference is written down, with
why. A file of exceptions that nobody reads is the same as no test.

## Things worth knowing if you build one

- **Normalise colours.** Read them through a probe element rather than comparing
  strings, or `oklch()` and `color-mix()` values compare unequal for silly
  reasons.
- **Wait for a stable DOM**, not a fixed timeout, and stop animations before
  reading.
- **Confirm a difference on a second read.** A late render is not a regression.
- **Check states too**: open a menu, focus a field, hover a row, because that is
  where precedence bugs live.

## How it runs

The harness builds the Kirana app and the two baselines, serves all three, crawls
every route and diffs. It is how 60+ blocks
and every component were verified, and it is what caught the merge-order bugs
that a human review had passed.

The harness runs in a separate repository beside the StyleX port and the
Tailwind original, which this one does not carry.
---
# Habits for a new project
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/building/tips
# Habits for a new project

Fifteen habits from building every shadcn/ui component on Kirana and migrating
the same three applications from StyleX and from Tailwind. Each one is here
because skipping it cost us a bug.

<!-- ::figure-habits -->

## Structure

### 1. One `styles` object per module, named by part

Declare the styles after the imports, one per part. The element's `data-slot` is
a good name: `card-header` becomes `styles.cardHeader`, and a search for it finds
both ends.

```tsx
const styles = {
  card: css({ display: "flex", flexDirection: "column", gap: space[6] }),
  cardHeader: css({ display: "grid", gap: space[2] }),
}
```

### 2. Components take `sx`, and put it last

An `sx` array is merge order, so the caller's styles go last and win. A
`className` prop for styles is never needed.

```tsx do
<div sx={[styles.card, sx]} />
```

```tsx dont
<div sx={[sx, styles.card]} />
```

**Checked by** `sx-last`, in the [lint plugin](/docs/tooling/lint).

### 3. Take `sx` out of the rest spread

A wrapper that spreads its props carries `sx` inside the spread, where nothing
compiles it.

```tsx do
function Trigger({ sx, ...props }: Props) {
  return <Button sx={[styles.trigger, sx]} {...props} />
}
```

```tsx dont
function Trigger(props: Props) {
  return <Button {...props} />
}
```

**Checked by** `unused-sx`, which reports a wrapper that drops it.

### 4. Installed components do not read `sx`

Base UI parts and anything else from `node_modules` take compiled props:
`props` from `@kirana-style/core` turns styles into them.

```tsx do
<Menu.Popup {...props(styles.popup, sx)} />
```

```tsx dont
<Menu.Popup sx={styles.popup} />
```

**Checked by** `sx-on-external-component`.

## Values

### 5. Start with plain values; adopt scales when they repeat

You do not need a preset to begin. When you want a vocabulary,
[`@kirana-style/preset-scales`](/docs/tokens/preset-scales) is Tailwind v4's, and a
token nothing references emits nothing.

### 6. Put product decisions in your own tokens

`primary`, `muted` and `border` are yours. Define each once as a
[semantic token](/docs/tokens/semantic-tokens), a `light-dark()` pair.

Set the theme's `color-scheme` on `<html>`: the root decides the scrollbars and an
iframe's canvas.

```tsx do
export const theme = defineTokens("theme", {
  primary: "light-dark(oklch(0.21 0 0), oklch(0.92 0 0))",
})
```

```tsx dont
const button = css({
  backgroundColor: "oklch(0.21 0 0)",
})
```

### 7. A font size comes with its line height

A size without its line height was the most common drift in our ports.

```tsx do
css({
  fontSize: fontSize.sm,
  lineHeight: lineHeight.sm,
})
```

```tsx dont
css({ fontSize: fontSize.sm })
```

### 8. Name the longhands you set

Logical properties make right-to-left work without a second style. To replace a
longhand a component's base sets, name that longhand: a shorthand sits beside it
instead.

```tsx do
css({ paddingInlineStart: 0 })
```

```tsx dont
css({ padding: 0 })
```

**Checked by** `mixed-logical-physical`.

## Overrides and states

### 9. Override under the same condition

Styles [merge per entry](/docs/styling/merging). A plain value replaces the base
entry only, and the component's conditional entries still win under their
conditions. Omitting a key keeps it; `null` removes it.

```tsx do
alignSelf: {
  '[data-orientation="vertical"]': "auto",
}
```

```tsx dont
alignSelf: "auto"
```

To clear every entry first: `alignSelf: { "*": null, base: "auto" }`.

**Checked by** `override-keeps-conditions`, in the lint plugin.

### 10. Nest the winner inside the other condition

When two conditions of the same kind can match together and set different values,
the compiler reports them rather than letting source order decide. Twice, turning
the report off hid a real bug.

```tsx do
backgroundColor: {
  '[aria-invalid="true"]': {
    base: red,
    "[data-checked]": blue,
  },
}
```

```ts dont
// kirana.config.ts
diagnostics: {
  "ambiguous-precedence": "off",
}
```

When a library never sets both, name the pair in
[`conditions.exclusive`](/docs/reference/config) instead.

**Checked by** `ambiguous-precedence`.

### 11. Put the relation anchor where the state lives

A [relation](/docs/styling/relations) reads the state of the element that carries
its anchor, so the anchor goes on that element, not on the one being styled.

```tsx do
<div
  data-state={state}
  sx={[menu.anchor, styles.root]}
>
```

```tsx dont
<div data-state={state}>
  <div sx={[menu.anchor, styles.inner]}>
```

**Checked by** `relation-placement`.

### 12. A parent's rule ranks below the child's own

A [`select`](/docs/styling/contextual) block styles children from a parent, below
their own styles, so an icon that sets its own size keeps it. When the parent must
win, let the child read the parent.

```tsx do
label: css({
  width: {
    base: "auto",
    ':is([data-slot="field"] > *)': "100%",
  },
})
```

```tsx dont
field: css({
  [select.child("label")]: { width: "100%" },
})
```

### 13. Animate the property you set

`translate`, `scale` and `rotate` are properties of their own, and a transition on
`transform` does not cover them.

```tsx do
css({
  translate: "0 4px",
  transitionProperty: "translate",
})
```

```tsx dont
css({
  translate: "0 4px",
  transitionProperty: "transform",
})
```

## Runtime values

### 14. Prefer a finite set

A choice between known values compiles to a choice between classes and costs
nothing. Bridge only what varies continuously, such as a width in percent; the
`dynamic-bridged` report shows where runtime values enter. See
[values known at runtime](/docs/styling/dynamic).

```tsx do
<div
  sx={css({
    color: tone === "danger" ? "crimson" : "black",
  })}
/>
```

```tsx dont
// "crimson" or "black", known only at runtime
<div sx={css({ color })} />
```

**Checked by** `finite-bridge`, in the lint plugin's `strict` config.

## Checking

### 15. Let the tools answer "why"

`kirana-style check` reports every diagnostic with an exit code, for CI.
`kirana-style trace` answers when a value is not the one you expected: every
entry, the winner, and the step of the ladder that decided it.

```console
$ kirana-style check src
$ kirana-style trace src/card.tsx:12 minHeight
```

To verify a port or a refactor, compare **computed styles**, not screenshots, in
both colour schemes and at several widths. A 1 px border, an easing curve and a
missing hover state were all invisible in screenshots and obvious in a diff. See
[conformance](/docs/migration/conformance).
---
# Building a design system
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/building/design-system
# Building a design system

Kirana is a compiler, not a design system. This repository builds one on top of
it (the shadcn/ui component set, rebuilt), and its shape is worth copying.

## Six layers

<!-- ::figure-design-system -->

**1 · Scales.** Plain constants: the palette, spacing, type ramp, radii,
durations. Inlined, so they cost nothing.
[`@kirana-style/preset-scales`](/docs/tokens/preset-scales) gives you Tailwind's.

**2 · Semantic tokens.** What the scales _mean_, such as `background`,
`foreground` and `primary`, as variable tokens, every colour a `light-dark()`
pair. This is the layer a theme overrides.
[Semantic tokens](/docs/tokens/semantic-tokens).

**3 · Conditions.** The relations components share (a menu item reading its
menu's state), context tokens a parent hands down (`iconSize`, `sidebarWidth`),
and the keyframes. Declared once, in one module each.

**4 · Recipes.** Variant tables for the components that have variants, plus the
shared chrome (a focus ring, an overlay surface, a menu surface), so twelve
components do not each invent their own.

**5 · Primitives.** Thin elements such as `Box`, `Stack` and `Text` that carry
the system's defaults and nothing else.

**6 · Components.** The real thing. Each takes `sx` last, so callers can override
without forking.

## Rules that keep it from drifting

- **A colour is one `light-dark()` pair**, written once. No dark variant anywhere.
- **A parent hands values down through context tokens**, never through class
  names it hopes a child reads.
- **A component's variants live in its recipe**, not scattered through the JSX.
- **New things have one home**: a scale value goes to the scales, a per-mode
  colour to the semantic layer, a parent-to-child value to the context tokens, a
  group or peer to the relations.
- **Global CSS is the last resort**, for markup you do not render.

## What the compiler gives you here

A design system is mostly discipline, and the compiler enforces some of it for
you: `sx` that goes nowhere is a warning, a relation without an anchor is an
error, two conditions that could both apply are reported, and a mixed
logical/physical box is flagged. Those are precisely the mistakes that make a
system slowly stop being one.
---
# Publishing a library
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/building/libraries
# Publishing a library

A Kirana library publishes its styles **uncompiled**, and each app that uses it
compiles them together with its own. That is what lets an app override a
library's style property by property, keeps every declaration in the stylesheet
once, and applies the app's prefix, targets and layers to the library too.

Tested by `examples/vite-library`, which installs a packed library from a tarball.

<!-- ::figure-library -->

## In the library

Build your package without Kirana's plugin (with `tsc`, `tsdown` or any bundler),
so the `css()` calls stay in the published JavaScript, and ship no CSS:

```js file="acme-ui/index.js"
import { css, props } from "@kirana-style/core"
import { jsx } from "react/jsx-runtime"

const styles = {
  button: css({ paddingInline: "1rem", borderRadius: "0.5rem" }),
}

export function Button({ sx, ...rest }) {
  return jsx("button", { ...rest, ...props(styles.button, sx) })
}
```

Apply styles with `props()` (or `cx` into `className`): both compile in plain
JavaScript.

`sx` needs JSX, which a library's build usually compiles away; ship `.jsx` or
`.tsx` if you want to keep it.

Make `@kirana-style/core` a peer dependency, so the library and the app share one.

## In the app

List the package:

```ts file="kirana.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@kirana-style/core/config"

export default defineConfig({ libraries: ["acme-ui"] })
```

Its modules are now compiled from `node_modules` like your own, and its exported
tokens work in your styles. With Vite nothing else is needed: the adapter keeps
listed libraries out of dependency pre-bundling, in the browser and in a server
environment that pre-bundles (a Cloudflare Worker's), and out of server
externals. With Next.js, also add the package to `transpilePackages`.

## Why not ship compiled CSS

A library compiled on its own bakes its compiler version and configuration into
its class names. With a different prefix, an app's override can no longer replace
the library's value: both classes stay, and whichever rule comes later in the
stylesheet wins. With an older compiler, the same declaration ships twice. The
reasoning, with the measurements, is in the design note
`packages/kirana/design-notes/published-libraries.md`.

The one cost: an app that does not use Kirana cannot use a Kirana library.
---
# The output
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/building/output
# The output

## One declaration per rule

```css
@layer kirana.atoms {
  .k5O_23ai {
    display: flex;
  }
  .kJ_1O3s {
    gap: 0.75rem;
  }
  .k44_MaxI {
    background-color: light-dark(oklch(0.21 0 0), oklch(0.92 0 0));
  }
}
```

Every rule is one class with one declaration, at specificity (0,1,0), shared by
every module that writes that declaration ([why](/docs/start/how-it-works#the-pipeline)).

One declaration can still reach several rules (the same colour under `:hover`,
under an attribute and at rest), and there the writer gives one rule all three
selectors:

```css
.k5O_u3uh,
.k5O-KFHz_u3uh:where(:hover),
.k5O-Ikox_u3uh:where(:focus) {
  display: block;
}
```

It does that only when no rule in between decides the same property, because
inside the layer the order of the rules **is** the
[precedence ladder](/docs/styling/precedence). A merge that could move a rule past
a competing declaration is not taken.

## Class names

<!-- ::figure-class-name -->

A name is `{prefix}{property code}[-{target}][-{conditions}]_{value}`. The prefix is
[configurable](/docs/reference/config) and defaults to `k`; the property code is
an index into the property table; then come optional 3- and 4-character hashes for
a pseudo-element or contextual target and for the condition set; and after the `_`,
four characters of the value's hash.

Names are content-derived, so they are stable across builds and machines, and two
applications with different prefixes can share a page.

The widths are fixed and never grow. A name that depended on what else the project
contained would change as the project grew, which would break incremental builds;
so if two values on one property ever took the same name, the build stops with
`class-name-collision` instead of guessing. Four characters make that about one
build in two thousand for an application the size of the ones this compiler is
tested on.

### Dense names

A production build can go further with
[`names: "dense"`](/docs/integrations/vite#dense-names). After every module has
compiled, the compiler knows every condition set and every value in the
application, so it can number them instead of hashing them:

- **Each condition hash becomes a code of one or two characters**, never three, so
  it is never mistaken for a target.
- **Each value hash becomes a code of one or two characters** from one numbering
  shared by every property. A runtime merge that unfolds a shorthand builds a
  longhand's name from the shorthand's value, so a value has to mean the same
  thing under every key.
- **The property code and the target stay.** They are what the runtime reads to
  merge, so merging works exactly as before and no lookup table ships.

The most used segments get the shortest codes. A code, once given, never changes
for the rest of the build, so a chunk renamed early stays valid while later modules
compile. The stylesheet keeps its rules in the same order; only the names in it
change.

Measured on the three applications of
[the benchmarks](/docs/project/benchmarks), Kirana 0.3.4 with
dense names makes the CSS 12 % smaller in gzip, and the CSS and
JavaScript a page downloads 2 % smaller, with cold builds
8 % slower. On this site, the stylesheet is 12.7 % smaller in
gzip and brotli.

Dense names stay opt-in for one reason besides the build time: a code goes to the
most used segments first, so when a new segment outranks an old one between two
deploys, names change in chunks whose source did not, and those chunks get new
content hashes and are downloaded again. A names manifest that keeps codes
across deploys would remove that, and with it the reason to keep them off.

## Conditions in the selector

Conditions compile into the selector or the at-rule, and order inside the layer
carries the [ladder](/docs/styling/precedence), with no `!important`, no
specificity tricks and no sublayers per bucket.

## Determinism

The same sources produce byte-identical CSS: same rule order, same names,
independent of thread count or file-system order. Which means a content hash is
meaningful, a diff in CI means a real change, and two developers see the same
output.

## Minification and targets

The compiler's own writer minifies, so your values reach the browser as you wrote
them: a colour is never re-serialized into another colour space, and `calc()` is
never "simplified".

Lightning CSS runs only when your configured [`targets`](/docs/reference/config)
are below the default floor, and then only to lower what those browsers need.
Lowering is reported as `target-lowering` so you know a modern feature was
rewritten.

## Dead styles

A style nothing references emits nothing. Tokens, keyframes and recipes all follow
the same rule, so an imported preset costs nothing until it is used.

## What ships to the browser

- The stylesheet.
- Class strings in your JavaScript.
- The private runtime (under 1.1 kB, gzipped) **only** in modules that merge at
  runtime or bridge a value.

There is no style engine, no CSS-in-JS injection, and no rule generation at
runtime.
---
# Cloudflare Workers
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/building/cloudflare-workers
# Cloudflare Workers

Cloudflare's Vite plugin runs an app's server half inside workerd, the runtime
Workers use, during `vite dev` and `vite build` alike, so a Node-only API fails on
your machine rather than after deploying. Kirana's
`examples/tanstack-start-cloudflare` is checked on every change this way: built,
then served from a cold cache with its first request rendered in workerd.

## The plugins, in order

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
import { cloudflare } from "@cloudflare/vite-plugin"
import kirana from "@kirana-style/vite"
import { tanstackStart } from "@tanstack/react-start/plugin/vite"
import viteReact from "@vitejs/plugin-react"
import { defineConfig } from "vite"

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    cloudflare({ viteEnvironment: { name: "ssr" } }),
    kirana(),
    tanstackStart(),
    viteReact(),
  ],
})
```

Cloudflare's plugin comes first, so it owns the server environment before the
framework configures it. Kirana comes before the framework plugins, as with any
Vite app, so modules reach them compiled.

The Worker's entry is the framework's server entry:

```jsonc file="wrangler.jsonc"
{
  "name": "my-app",
  "compatibility_date": "2026-10-01",
  "compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"],
  "main": "@tanstack/react-start/server-entry",
}
```

## Development and preview

`vite dev` renders each request in workerd. `vite preview` serves the production
build in workerd too, the way Cloudflare will, and `wrangler deploy` ships it:

```bash
vite build && vite preview
```

## Workers and pre-bundling

Vite pre-bundles the Worker's dependencies apart from the browser's. Kirana's Vite
plugin names its runtime for pre-bundling and keeps its presets compiled in every
environment, so nothing needs configuring.

Kirana 0.3.1 did that for the browser only: the first request in development
discovered Kirana's runtime late, re-optimised and loaded React twice, and a
pre-bundled preset threw `defineTokens() ran without being compiled`. On 0.3.1, name
the runtime and keep the preset out of workerd's pre-bundling:

```ts file="vite.config.ts"
export default defineConfig({
  optimizeDeps: { include: ["@kirana-style/core/internal"] },
  environments: {
    ssr: {
      optimizeDeps: {
        include: ["@kirana-style/core/internal"],
        exclude: ["@kirana-style/preset-scales"],
      },
    },
  },
  // the plugins, as above
})
```

Remove it when you upgrade past 0.3.1.

## A stylesheet of your own

A stylesheet you write goes through Vite's CSS minifier, which lowers
`light-dark()` unless `build.cssTarget` is set to Kirana's floor:
[the Vite guide](/docs/integrations/vite#a-stylesheet-of-your-own) has the setting.
---
# API reference
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/reference/api
# API reference

Everything below is exported from `@kirana-style/core`, and every one of them is
compiled away. Calling one in a module the compiler never saw throws an error that
says exactly that.

## `css(...styles)`

```ts
css(...styles: readonly (Style | Sx)[]): StyleHandle
```

Compiles style objects, and handles you already have, into one handle. Arguments
merge left to right. [Writing styles](/docs/styling/styles).

## `cx(...handles)`

```ts
cx(...handles: readonly Sx[]): StyleHandle
```

Merges handles, skipping `null`, `undefined` and `false`.
[Merging](/docs/styling/merging).

## `props(...handles)`

```ts
props(...handles: readonly (Sx | string)[]): { className?: string; style?: Record<string, string> }
```

The compiled props for a component that does not read `sx`. Conventionally
imported as `props as styleProps`.

In Solid, Preact and Qwik it returns `{ class, style }`, the attribute their JSX
takes, and that framework's type entry types it so.
[Styling other people's components](/docs/styling/external-components).

## `recipe(config)`

```ts
recipe({ slots?, base?, variants?, compoundVariants?, defaultVariants? }): Recipe
```

Variants and slots. A call with static options compiles to a constant; with a
runtime option it resolves through the runtime and reports `dynamic-variant`.
[Recipes](/docs/styling/recipes).

## `relation(name)`

```ts
relation(name: string, options?: { optional?: boolean }): {
  name: string
  anchor: StyleHandle
  within(state?: string): Condition
  parent(state?: string): Condition
  after(state?: string): Condition
  before(state?: string): Condition
}
```

Styling by another element's state. `optional: true` lets a reader be installed
without the component that applies the anchor, where the read never matches,
instead of failing `relation-without-anchor`.
[Relations](/docs/styling/relations).

## `select.descendant(target)` · `select.child(target)`

```ts
select.descendant(target: string): SelectTarget
select.child(target: string): SelectTarget
```

Top-level keys that style elements below this one, in a layer their own styles
beat. Targets are element names or attribute selectors.
[Contextual styles](/docs/styling/contextual).

## `keyframes(frames)`

```ts
keyframes(frames: Record<string, Properties & { [property: `--${string}`]: string | number }>): Keyframes
```

A name usable as `animationName` from any module.
[Animation](/docs/styling/animation).

## `firstThatWorks(preferred, ...fallbacks)`

```ts
firstThatWorks<V>(...values: [V, ...V[]]): Fallbacks<V>
```

A property value written once per value, the preferred last, so a browser that
does not understand it keeps the one before. Values must be known at build time
and expand to the same longhands. [Fallback values](/docs/styling/fallbacks).

## `positionTry(block)`

```ts
positionTry(block: PositionTryBlock): PositionTry
```

An `@position-try` rule and its dashed ident, for `positionTryFallbacks`. The
block takes inset, margin, size, self-alignment, `positionAnchor` and
`positionArea`; anything else is reported.
[Anchor positioning](/docs/styling/anchor-positioning).

## `viewTransition(parts)`

```ts
viewTransition(parts: { group?, imagePair?, old?, new?: TransitionStyle }): ViewTransition
```

Styles for a view transition's pseudo-elements. The result is a style handle for
`sx` and, at once, the `view-transition-class` name a framework's transition API
takes. [View transitions](/docs/styling/view-transitions).

## `counterStyle(descriptors)`

```ts
counterStyle(descriptors: CounterStyleDescriptors): CounterStyle
```

An `@counter-style` rule and its name, for a list's marker or a counter. The
keys are the CSS descriptors, written as CSS text. An unknown descriptor, a
custom property or a system without the symbols it needs is reported.
[At-rules](/docs/styling/at-rules#counter-styles).

## `defineTokens(namespace, values, options?)`

```ts
defineTokens(namespace: string, values: TokenValues, options?: { variable?: boolean }): Tokens
```

A token group. Values may be a plain value, `{ light, dark }`, `{ value, variable }`,
or `{ value, syntax, inherits? }` to register an animatable custom property.
[Tokens](/docs/tokens/overview).

## `defineTheme(tokens, overrides)`

```ts
defineTheme(tokens: Tokens, overrides: ThemeOverrides): StyleHandle
```

A handle that overrides variable tokens for a subtree.
[Themes and modes](/docs/tokens/themes-and-modes).

## `mode.system` · `mode.light` · `mode.dark`

Handles that set `color-scheme`. Apply to the root element.

## `media(query)` · `container(query, name?)` · `supports(condition)`

```ts
media(query: string): Condition
container(query: string, name?: string): Condition
supports(condition: string): Condition
```

Condition values for computed keys. [Conditions](/docs/styling/conditions).

## Types

| Type                  | What it is                                                                              |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `StyleHandle`         | A compiled style. Opaque.                                                               |
| `Sx`                  | `StyleHandle \| null \| undefined \| false \| readonly Sx[]`: what `sx` and `cx` accept |
| `Style`               | A style object: CSS properties, custom properties, pseudo-elements, `select` targets    |
| `ConditionalValue<V>` | `{ base?: V, [condition]: V \| ConditionalValue<V> }`                                   |
| `Condition`           | A condition value, from `media`/`container`/`supports` or a relation read               |
| `SelectTarget`        | A contextual target, from `select.*`                                                    |
| `Token`, `Keyframes`  | A token's CSS text; a keyframes name                                                    |
| `PositionTry`         | An `@position-try` rule's dashed ident                                                  |
| `Fallbacks<V>`        | A `firstThatWorks()` run of values `V`                                                  |
| `ViewTransition`      | A `viewTransition()` class: a `StyleHandle` that is also its class name                 |

## Entry points

| Import                              | What it gives                                 |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `@kirana-style/core`                | the API above                                 |
| `@kirana-style/core/config`         | `defineConfig` for `kirana.config.ts`         |
| `@kirana-style/core/react`          | the `sx` prop's types                         |
| `@kirana-style/core/stylesheet.css` | the stylesheet entry                          |
| `@kirana-style/core/internal`       | the private runtime, not for application code |
---
# Configuration reference
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/reference/config
# Configuration reference

Every key there is, and what each one changes.

## `layers`

```ts
layers: { before?: string[], after?: string[] }   // default: { before: [], after: [] }
```

Layer names placed around Kirana's own layer, for your global CSS. Each must be a
valid CSS identifier, and none may be `kirana`. See [layers](/docs/config/layers).

## `targets`

```ts
targets: { chrome?: number | string, safari?: number | string, firefox?: number | string }
```

Browser versions to compile for, as a major number (`123`) or `"major.minor"`
(`"17.5"`). The default floor is **Chrome 123, Safari 17.5, Firefox 120**.

Setting a target below the floor makes Lightning CSS lower the output where it
can, and emits `target-lowering` (informational) so you know it happened. A minor
above 255, or a value that is not a number, is `invalid-config`.

## `names.prefix`

```ts
names: { prefix?: string }   // default: "k"
```

The prefix on every generated class and custom property. One to four lowercase
ASCII letters. Give two independently built applications different prefixes and
they can share a page without colliding.

## `dynamic.branchBudget`

```ts
dynamic: { branchBudget?: number }   // default: 16
```

How many branches a class expression may have before the compiler stops and
reports `branch-budget-exceeded`. Must be at least 1. See
[values known at runtime](/docs/styling/dynamic).

## `jsx`

```ts
jsx: "preact" // "react" | "preact" | "solid" | "qwik"
```

Which attribute `sx` compiles to. Leave it out and the compiler reads
`compilerOptions.jsxImportSource` from the project's `tsconfig.json`, so most
projects never set it:

| Value      | `sx` compiles to | Read when `jsxImportSource` is |
| ---------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `"react"`  | `className`      | anything not below             |
| `"preact"` | `class`          | `"preact"`                     |
| `"solid"`  | `class`          | `"solid-js"`                   |
| `"qwik"`   | `class`          | `"@qwik.dev/core"`             |

See [supported frameworks](/docs/frameworks/overview).

## `libraries`

```ts
libraries: ["@acme/design-system"] // default: []
```

Installed packages whose styles this app compiles as it compiles its own. A
published Kirana library ships its `css()` calls uncompiled; listing it here puts
its styles in your stylesheet, deduplicated with yours and under your prefix,
targets and layers. Leave a library out and its first `css()` throws with a message
naming this key. Kirana's own scales preset is compiled without being listed. See
[publishing a library](/docs/building/libraries).

## `presets`

```ts
import scales from "@kirana-style/preset-scales/preset"

presets: [scales()] // default: []
```

Presets contribute data to the configuration: today, a utility grammar that
turns on [utility strings](/docs/styling/utilities). A preset is
`{ name: string, utilities?: UtilityGrammar }`; later presets replace earlier ones
scale by scale, root by root and variant by variant.

## `utilities`

```ts
utilities: {
  scales: { color: [{ module: "./src/theme.ts", export: "theme" }] },
  utilities: { stack: [{ static: { display: "flex", flexDirection: "column" } }] },
  variants: { selected: '[aria-selected="true"]' },
}
```

The application's own grammar, merged after every preset. It has three parts:

| Part        | What it holds                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `scales`    | Where a scale's values come from: exports of modules, looked up as an `import` would be (relative modules from the project root), searched in order. |
| `utilities` | What each root sets, as rules tried in order.                                                                                                        |
| `variants`  | A name for any condition `css()` accepts; one starting with `::` is a pseudo-element block.                                                          |

A rule is one of three kinds:

| Rule                     | For                                   |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `{ static: {…} }`        | the root alone: `flex` sets `display` |
| `{ properties, scale }`  | values from a scale, or a number      |
| `{ properties, values }` | values from a fixed table of keywords |

A scale rule takes these options:

| Option        | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `number`      | `{ step, unit }`: a number that is not a key, as `w-50` is 50 × `0.25rem`. A rule may have `number` and no `scale`.                                                                                         |
| `pair`        | Properties set from other scales at the same key: `text-sm` also sets its line height. A utility that sets that property itself (`text-sm leading-6`) wins, and a modifier (`text-sm/relaxed`) replaces it. |
| `alpha`       | A colour: `/90` mixes it with `transparent`.                                                                                                                                                                |
| `negative`    | `-mt-2` negates the value.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `fractions`   | `w-1/2` is a percentage.                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `format`      | The value inside other text: `brightness({value})`.                                                                                                                                                         |
| `aliases`     | Utility keys spelled differently from the scale's: `in-out` reads `inOut`.                                                                                                                                  |
| `iconLibrary` | the library icons are drawn with: `lucide` (the default), `tabler`, `hugeicons`, `phosphor` or `remixicon`                                                                                                  |
| `design`      | the design system's values your project uses, such as `{ style: "vega" }`, which `kirana-style ui preset` writes                                                                                            |
| `also`        | Declarations set alongside, as written (a keyword rule takes it too).                                                                                                                                       |

In any text of a rule, `{scale.key}` is that token, and a property written
`{scale.key}` sets the token's custom property. That is how a ring and a shadow
share one `box-shadow`: its value is `"{compose.ring-shadow}, {compose.shadow}"`,
and each utility sets one of the two.

## `diagnostics`

```ts
diagnostics: Record<string, "off" | "info" | "warning" | "error">
```

Re-level a diagnostic by its kebab-case name:

```ts
diagnostics: {
  "sx-on-external-component": "error",   // stricter
  "dynamic-bridged": "off",              // quieter
}
```

**Errors cannot be re-levelled.** An error means the output would be wrong, so
turning it into a warning would only hide a broken build. Trying is
`invalid-config`, as is naming a diagnostic that does not exist. The
[diagnostics reference](/docs/tooling/diagnostics) lists which ones can move.

## `conditions.exclusive`

```ts
conditions: { exclusive?: string[][] }   // default: []
```

Groups of conditions that a library guarantees never hold together on one
element. Each group needs at least two entries, and each entry must be exactly one
attribute or pseudo-class selector.

```ts
conditions: {
  exclusive: [
    ["[data-starting-style]", "[data-ending-style]"],
    ["[data-open]", "[data-closed]"],
  ],
}
```

This is how you silence `ambiguous-precedence` for pairs the selectors cannot
prove are exclusive. The compiler already knows about two values of one attribute,
a selector and its negation, and fixed positions counted from the same end; you
only need to declare what a library promises.

## `conditions.exclusiveAcross`

```ts
conditions: { exclusiveAcross?: string[][] }   // default: []
```

One vocabulary per library a design system writes its components for: two
conditions that no vocabulary holds together are exclusive, since a component is
built on one library. At least two vocabularies, each entry exactly one attribute
or pseudo-class selector. `exclusiveAcross()` from `@kirana-style/states` builds
them from the library vocabularies; see
[one look for several libraries](/docs/styling/states#one-look-for-several-libraries).

## `conditions.ownAttributes`

```ts
conditions: { ownAttributes?: string[] }   // default: []
```

Attributes your own components write, by name (`"data-side"`), whatever library
they are built on. A vocabulary may name one too, as Base UI does for its popups'
side, but on your component the attribute is yours: `exclusiveAcross` keeps nothing
apart by it, so a sheet's side nested in React Aria's entering state is emitted
rather than left out. Two values of the attribute still never meet.

## `classes`

```ts
classes: { modules: ["resources/styles"], out: "public/kirana/classes.json" }
```

The class map for server templates. `modules` are files or folders, relative to
the root, whose exported handles Blade, Twig, ERB, HEEx and Edge templates name.
The build and dev commands write their class strings to `out`, and compile the
modules whatever paths they were given. A recipe or a runtime value among the
exports is `classes-not-static`. See [server templates](/docs/frameworks/server-templates).

## `externals`

```ts
externals: ["meteor/"] // default: []
```

Specifier prefixes the bundler provides and Node.js resolution cannot find. An
import from one is a runtime value, as an installed package's is, instead of an
`unresolved-import` warning.

Who sets them:

- the Ember adapter adds Ember's own: `@ember/`, `@glimmer/`, `@embroider/virtual/`;
- [Meteor](/docs/frameworks/meteor) sets `meteor/`;
- [Docusaurus](/docs/frameworks/docusaurus) sets its webpack aliases, such as
  `@theme/` and `@docusaurus/`.

## `ui`

```ts
ui: { framework: "react", preset: "k0" } // default: none
```

The component registry's settings, read by [`kirana-style ui`](/docs/tooling/cli#kirana-style-ui)
(`@kirana-style/registry`) and never by the compiler, which accepts the key and
leaves it out of every compile.

```ts
ui: {
  registries: {
    "@acme": "https://acme.dev/r/{name}.json",
    "@private": {
      url: "https://private.dev/r/{name}.json",
      headers: { Authorization: "Bearer ${PRIVATE_TOKEN}" },
    },
    "@local": "public/r/{name}.json",
  },
}
```

`registries` names registries by namespace:

- each is a template holding `{name}`: a URL, a path from the configuration's
  folder, or a `file:` URL;
- a header may read an environment variable as `${NAME}`. One that is not set
  stops the command, and a header's value is never printed;
- `@kirana`, Kirana UI's registry, is known without being named, and can be
  renamed to point elsewhere.

What `kirana-style ui add` installs, and where:

| Key         | Holds                                                                                                                             |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `framework` | whose markup to install; by default the framework your project depends on (`react`, `vue`, `svelte`, `solid-js`, `@angular/core`) |
| `base`      | which base's markup, such as `base` or `aria`; by default the only one an item has                                                |
| `aliases`   | the import specifier for each file type, `ui`, `lib`, `component`, `hook` and `page`                                              |

The aliases default to shadcn/ui's:

```ts
aliases: { ui: "@/components/ui", lib: "@/lib", component: "@/components", hook: "@/hooks" }
```

A file is written in the directory your `tsconfig.json`'s paths map its alias to:
with `"@/*": ["./src/*"]`, the ui files go to `src/components/ui`.

The settings are checked before anything is fetched.

## `root`

Set by the adapter, not by you: the project root, which scopes a build and makes
diagnostic paths relative.
---
# The CLI
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tooling/cli
# The CLI

The `kirana-style` command, by what it does:

| What it does                            | Commands                              |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Sets a project up, and checks the setup | `init`, `doctor`                      |
| Compiles without a bundler              | `build`, `dev`                        |
| Reports                                 | `check`, `analyze`, `export`, `trace` |
| Rewrites other styling systems          | `migrate`                             |
| Serves your editor                      | `lsp`                                 |
| Installs components from a registry     | `ui`                                  |

In a project without Kirana, run it without installing anything: your package
manager's runner fetches it for one run, as `npx shadcn@latest` does.

```bash
# npm
npx kirana-style@latest init
# pnpm
pnpm dlx kirana-style@latest init
# yarn
yarn dlx kirana-style@latest init
# bun
bunx --bun kirana-style@latest init
# deno
deno run -A npm:kirana-style@latest init
```

Once it is installed, the package manager runs the project's own copy:

```bash
# npm
npx kirana-style check
# pnpm
pnpm exec kirana-style check
# yarn
yarn kirana-style check
# bun
bunx kirana-style check
# deno
deno run -A npm:kirana-style check
```

`init` adds `kirana-style` to the project's dev dependencies, so every later run
uses the version the project pins, and the editor's language server comes from the
same install.

### A shorter name

The command is `kirana-style` everywhere: npm does not give out the plain name
`kirana`, so a bare `npx kirana` cannot run Kirana. For a shorter
name in your own project, add a script:

```json file="package.json"
{
  "scripts": {
    "kirana": "kirana-style"
  }
}
```

Then `npm run kirana -- check src`; pnpm, Yarn and Bun run scripts the same way. In your shell,
`alias kirana="npx kirana-style"` does the same for every project.

In this repository the binary runs through its entry script:

```bash
node packages/kirana/npm/cli/bin/kirana-style.ts <command>
```

## `kirana-style init`

Set a project up: the configuration file, the adapter in your bundler's
configuration, the stylesheet, and the types for `sx`.

```bash
kirana-style init             # show the changes, ask, write them
kirana-style init --dry-run   # only show them
kirana-style init --yes       # write without asking
kirana-style init --install   # also run the install command
kirana-style init --preset    # with the scales preset (utilities)
```

It reads `package.json` and the lockfile to find the framework, the bundler and
the package manager (npm, pnpm, Yarn, Bun, or Deno from a `deno.lock`), then prints
every change as a diff before it writes anything:

```console
$ kirana-style init --dry-run
Next.js · turbopack · npm · TypeScript

+ config: create kirana.config.mts
+ adapter: add @kirana-style/next to next.config.ts, add @kirana-style/postcss to postcss.config.mjs
+ stylesheet: add @kirana; to app/globals.css
+ types: create kirana.d.ts

--- next.config.ts
  import type { NextConfig } from "next";
+ import { withKirana } from "@kirana-style/next";
  …
- export default nextConfig;
+ export default withKirana(nextConfig);
```


It knows Next.js (Turbopack and webpack), Nuxt, SvelteKit, Astro, TanStack Start,
Qwik, Angular (the CLI, whose `angular.json` builders it swaps, and Analog), React
Router, Gatsby, Ember, Meteor and Parcel; React, Preact, Solid, Vue, Svelte or
plain DOM on Vite, Rsbuild, Rspack, webpack and Rolldown; and the server frameworks
Laravel, Symfony, Rails, Phoenix and AdonisJS, which get a class map and a starter
style module. Edits follow the file's own quotes and semicolons. Where a
configuration is not in a shape it can edit safely (`module.exports`, a function,
a plugin list built elsewhere), it prints the step to do by hand instead of
guessing. The install command is your package manager's own (Deno's takes each
package as `npm:…`), printed, never run unless you pass `--install`, so your
lockfile stays yours.

Its last line names the next command the way your package manager runs it, such
as `pnpm exec kirana-style doctor`.

Its setups were checked the way the examples are: sixteen examples, stripped of
Kirana and set up again by `kirana-style init`, built from packed tarballs and styled
exactly like the hand-written ones in a browser.

## `kirana-style doctor`

Check a project's setup, and say what is missing.

```bash
kirana-style doctor
kirana-style doctor --json
kirana-style doctor --report
kirana-style doctor --report bug.md --trace src/card.tsx:12 minHeight
```

```console
$ kirana-style doctor
✓ engine       native (linux-x64)
✓ packages     @kirana-style/core@0.3.4, @kirana-style/next@0.3.4, kirana-style@0.3.4
✓ config       kirana.config.mts, prefix "k"
✓ project      Next.js · turbopack · npm · TypeScript
✓ adapter      next.config.ts, postcss.config.mjs
✓ stylesheet   app/globals.css
✓ types        kirana.d.ts
✓ cache        none on disk: every build compiles from source

All good.
```

It reports the engine in use (native, or the WebAssembly fallback), every
installed `@kirana-style/*` version and whether they match, whether the configuration
loads, and whether the adapter, stylesheet and types are in place, which it learns
by running `kirana-style init`'s plan without writing. The exit code is 1 when something fails.
There is no cache to clear: Kirana keeps nothing on disk between builds.

In a monorepo, run it in the app. A setup the app takes from the workspace counts:

- the adapter, from a shared config package its own config imports
  (`vite.config.ts, through @workspace/vite-config`);
- the types for `sx`, from a shared UI package that imports them;
