- `kirana-style` and the adapter's package, listed at the workspace's root or in that
  shared package.

### A bug report

`--report` writes `kirana-report.md` (or the file after the flag): an issue body
with a place at the top for what happened and the smallest reproduction, then what
Kirana collected:

- the engine version, Node.js and OS, the framework and the bundler;
- every `@kirana-style/*` version, and the doctor's checks;
- each diagnostic code, how often it occurred and where first;
- the stylesheet's size and the resolved configuration.

`--trace <file>:<line> <property>` adds `kirana-style trace` output, and `--json` prints
the same data instead of writing the file.

```console
$ kirana-style doctor --report --trace src/card.tsx:12 minHeight
wrote kirana-report.md: describe what happened and add a reproduction at the top, read the rest, then paste it into an issue
```

The report is safe to paste. It contains no source code, the project directory
reads `<project>`, the home directory `~` and your user name `<user>`,
configuration values under keys that name a secret are masked, and no environment
variable is read. Read it before you post it anyway.

## `kirana-style dev`

Watch mode for projects without a bundler: plain HTML, web components, server
templates.

```bash
kirana-style dev src --out public/kirana.css
kirana-style dev --minify
```

It compiles every script under the paths (`src`, or the project when there is
none), writes the stylesheet (`kirana.css` unless `--out` says otherwise), and on
each change recompiles that file and the modules that read a value from it. The
stylesheet is rewritten only when it changed, and diagnostics print as they
appear:

```console
$ kirana-style dev src --out public/kirana.css
✓ public/kirana.css (4780 bytes, 8 file(s), 9 ms)
watching src
✓ public/kirana.css (4802 bytes, src/card.ts, 2 ms)
```

## `kirana-style check`

Report diagnostics without writing anything.

```bash
kirana-style check src
kirana-style check src --format json
kirana-style check src --format github --max-warnings 0
```

It walks the paths you give it, skipping `node_modules`, `dist`, dotfiles and
`.d.ts` files. Human output underlines the span and prints the help line:

```console
$ kirana-style check src
warning[KRN1703] sx-on-external-component: a component from "@base-ui/react"
receives `sx`, which it does not read (src/menu.tsx:14:7)
  help: spread the compiled props instead: {...props(styles.root, sx)}

1 diagnostic(s), 0 error(s)
```

`--format json` prints an array of `{ code, name, severity, file, span, message, help }`,
for an editor or a script. The exit code is 1 when anything is an error.

`--format github` prints one GitHub Actions workflow command per diagnostic, which
annotates the line in the pull request's diff: errors as errors, warnings as
warnings, infos as notices. Paths are relative to the project root, so run it from
the repository root or a project at the root.

`--max-warnings <n>` fails the run, exit code 1, when there are more than `n`
warnings; `0` makes every warning block a merge, without re-levelling them in the
configuration.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
- run: npx kirana-style check src --format github --max-warnings 0
```

### Which configuration

Each path reads the nearest `kirana.config.*` above it, so `check` at a workspace
root checks each app with its own configuration, as its build and the editor do.
Paths that share a configuration are checked together. When a group reads a
configuration other than the working directory's, or there are several, the human
output names which file each group read:

```console
$ kirana-style check apps/web/src packages/ui/src
apps/web/kirana.config.ts: apps/web/src
0 diagnostic(s), 0 error(s)
no kirana.config: packages/ui/src
1 diagnostic(s), 0 error(s)
```

Beside that:

- `--config <file>` makes every path read that file instead;
- `--format json` stays one array however many configurations are read;
- `trace` groups its locations the same way;
- `export` reads one configuration, and asks for `--config` when its paths would
  read several.

## `kirana-style build`

Compile files and write the stylesheet.

```bash
kirana-style build src --out dist/kirana.css
kirana-style build src --out dist/kirana.css --minify
```

Useful when a bundler is not in the picture: a library build, a check in CI, or
looking at the CSS for yourself. Applications normally let the
[Vite plugin](/docs/integrations/vite) do this.

## `kirana-style analyze`

What the stylesheet holds, and why.

```bash
kirana-style analyze src
kirana-style analyze src --json
kirana-style analyze src --html report.html
```

```console
$ kirana-style analyze src
58 module(s), 1607 site(s), 851 atom(s), 39.2 kB stylesheet

Stylesheet by layer
  order                      91 B
  kirana.tokens            1.7 kB
  kirana.atoms            37.3 kB

Atoms by the number of sites applying them
  1          86 atom(s)
  2–4       518 atom(s)
  5–9       103 atom(s)
  10+       144 atom(s)

Most reused
   477 site(s) in  42 module(s)  k5O_fqMV  display: grid
   263 site(s) in  44 module(s)  k50_6mrG  color: var(--kviZP2)
```

That is this documentation site. The report goes on with the largest modules (the
bytes of their rules, and of the rules only they use, which is what deleting them
would save), then values bridged to runtime, recipes resolved at runtime,
themes and the tokens they override, relation reads no anchor proves, and tokens
your project declares that nothing reads. `--json` prints all of it;
`--html` writes one self-contained page, readable in light and dark. The exit
code is the same as `check`'s.

## `kirana-style export`

The design system, as JSON: every token with its value (and both halves of a
`light-dark()` pair), each theme and the tokens it overrides, each recipe with
its variant groups, options and defaults, every relation and where it is
anchored and read, and the keyframes, `positionTry`, `viewTransition` and
`counterStyle` names.
Each comes with the file and line that declares it.

```bash
kirana-style export                       # print it
kirana-style export src --out design-system.json
```

```json file="design-system.json"
{
  "schema": 1,
  "engine": "0.3.4",
  "prefix": "k",
  "tokens": [
    {
      "identity": "color.brand",
      "package": "app",
      "value": "light-dark(#000, #fff)",
      "light": "#000",
      "dark": "#fff",
      "variable": true,
      "origin": "src/tokens.ts:2"
    }
  ],
  "themes": [
    {
      "name": "ocean",
      "origin": "src/design.ts:3",
      "class": "kt9fBs",
      "overrides": ["color.brand"]
    }
  ],
  "recipes": [
    {
      "name": "button",
      "origin": "src/design.ts:4",
      "variants": { "size": ["sm", "md"], "tone": ["quiet"] },
      "defaults": { "size": "md" },
      "compoundVariants": 1
    }
  ],
  "relations": [
    {
      "name": "field",
      "declaredIn": ["src/design.ts"],
      "anchoredIn": [],
      "readIn": []
    }
  ],
  "keyframes": [
    { "name": "spin", "origin": "src/design.ts:11", "css": "kfMMUp" }
  ],
  "positionTries": [
    { "name": "below", "origin": "src/design.ts:12", "css": "--kpd1Rq" }
  ],
  "viewTransitions": [
    { "name": "slide", "origin": "src/design.ts:13", "css": "kwTyjU" }
  ],
  "counterStyles": [
    { "name": "check", "origin": "src/design.ts:14", "css": "kcLn6a" }
  ]
}
```

It is what a coding agent should read before writing a style (the tokens and
recipes that exist, by their real names), and what a design tool or a review needs
to see what a change did to the system. Names, values and project-relative
locations only, never source text; everything is sorted, so the file diffs cleanly
when it is committed. `schema` changes only when a field does. The exit code is
1 when the project has errors, as for `check`.

A token's identity is what code writes (`color.brand`), and `package` names the
package that declares it, left out for a file outside any package. Packages may
each declare a group of one name: their tokens compile apart, and `package` tells
them apart here. The compiler points such a pair out with an info,
`token-namespace-shared`.

### Definitions

`--definitions` adds what each exported style and recipe evaluates to, for a tool
that would otherwise run a second evaluator of its own:

- `styles` lists every exported `css()` handle, and each one inside an exported
  object (as `styles.root`);
- each recipe gets its `parts`: the base first, then each variant option and
  compound variant, slot by slot.

```bash
kirana-style export src --definitions --out design-system.json
```

```json file="design-system.json"
{
  "styles": [
    {
      "name": "styles.root",
      "origin": "src/styles.ts:5",
      "entries": [
        {
          "property": "color",
          "value": "var(--kvMob9)",
          "conditions": [],
          "tokens": ["color.brand"],
          "class": "k50_sxqm"
        },
        {
          "property": "color",
          "value": "red",
          "conditions": [{ "kind": "pseudo", "text": ":hover" }],
          "class": "k50-KFHz_D9ur"
        }
      ],
      "anchors": ["field"]
    }
  ]
}
```

Each entry carries:

- its property and value;
- its conditions, each with its kind, and a relation by its name and where the
  reader sits;
- its `select` target or pseudo-element;
- the tokens it reads, constant ones included, and the token it assigns, by
  identity;
- the keyframes it names and the class it compiles to;
- its key path and its value as written.

The key path (`path`) lists the object keys from the top of the style down to the
value, in the order you wrote them, so a tool can write the style back as source.
The value as written (`written`) is the value before it is compiled.

| In your source                       | In the export                             |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| `color: { [lyra]: { ":hover": x } }` | `["color", "[data-base=lyra]", ":hover"]` |
| `color: { ":hover": { [lyra]: x } }` | `["color", ":hover", "[data-base=lyra]"]` |
| a condition as a key                 | `{ "conditions": [...] }`                 |
| `[select.child("svg")]`              | `{ "select": "> svg" }`                   |
| `[color.muted]`                      | `{ "token": "color.muted" }`              |
| `zIndex: 0`                          | `0`                                       |
| `padding: space[2]`                  | `{ "token": "space.2" }`                  |
| a template literal that reads tokens | `{ "template": [...] }`                   |
| `firstThatWorks("100dvh", "100vh")`  | `{ "firstThatWorks": [...] }`             |

A `null` that removes a property when styles merge is an entry whose value is
`null`, with no conditions when it removes the property under every condition.

A removal under every condition has no key path, and no removal has a value as
written. A template literal names its tokens when it is written in the module
that exports the style; one imported from another module reads as its text.

## `kirana-style trace`

Explain which declaration wins for a property, and why.

```bash
kirana-style trace src/components/card.tsx:24 padding-top
```

It prints one line per candidate: a marker for the winner, the value, the
conditions, the layer, and the ladder step that decided it.

```console
$ kirana-style trace src/components/card.tsx:24 padding-top
✓ 2px   base   kirana.atoms   step 5 (set 1 longhand < 4)
  1px   base   kirana.atoms
```

The property may be written the way you wrote it (`paddingTop`) or the way CSS
does (`padding-top`). Give it the line the style is on.

This is the tool for "why is this not applying". It answers from the compiled
result, not from reading the source.

On the line of a `recipe()`, each candidate says in brackets which part of the
recipe it comes from: `base`, a variant option (`size: sm`), or a compound variant,
after its slot when the recipe has slots. Where two parts of one slot set the same
entry, the recipe's merge decides rather than the cascade: the later part replaces
the earlier one.

```console
$ kirana-style trace src/components/button.ts:2 height
height at src/components/button.ts:2
  ✓ 1.5rem   base [size: sm]   kirana.atoms   merge (size: sm replaces base)
    2rem     base [base]       kirana.atoms
```

### For a tool

`--format json` prints an answer per question, and several `file:line property`
pairs are answered in one run, each file compiled once:

```bash
kirana-style trace src/button.ts:2 height src/card.tsx:9 color --format json
```

```json
[
  {
    "file": "src/button.ts",
    "line": 2,
    "property": "height",
    "entries": [
      {
        "value": "1.5rem",
        "conditions": [],
        "layer": "kirana.atoms",
        "class": "k6V_5QUl",
        "part": { "options": { "size": "sm" }, "compound": false },
        "step": 0,
        "reason": "merge (size: sm replaces base)"
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

Nothing has to be parsed out of a line of text:

- each condition comes with its kind: a pseudo-class, an attribute, a media,
  container or supports query, or a relation;
- a pseudo-element or `select` target is under `target`;
- `step` is the ladder step that ranks an entry above the next one, or 0 where a
  recipe's merge decides.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning                                                            |
| ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 0    | No errors                                                          |
| 1    | At least one error diagnostic, or a file could not be written      |
| 1    | `doctor`: something failed; `init`: you said no                    |
| 1    | `check --max-warnings n`: more than `n` warnings                   |
| 2    | Bad configuration, one that fails to load, or a malformed argument |

`kirana-style ui` exits with its package's code, or 1 when the project does not
have that package.

## `kirana-style migrate`

Rewrite another styling system's sources into Kirana, and report what it will
not decide for you.

```bash
kirana-style migrate tailwind src                    # print the diff and the report
kirana-style migrate tailwind src --write            # apply it
kirana-style migrate tailwind src --report todo.txt  # also save the report
kirana-style migrate stylex src --write
```

Nothing is written without `--write`. The report is printed either way: each
line is a file position and something a person has to do, and the utility it is
about is also left in a comment beside the style it belongs to.

`migrate tailwind` needs a [utility grammar](/docs/styling/utilities) (the preset
and your theme's scales), and reads `@custom-variant` and `@utility` from any CSS
file among its paths. See
[migrating from Tailwind](/docs/migration/from-tailwind#the-codemod).

## The same answers from code

`trace`, `export` and the Tailwind lowering are calls on the compiler's `Driver`
too, from `@kirana-style/compiler`, for a tool that asks many times and should
compile once:

```ts
import { Driver } from "@kirana-style/compiler"

const driver = await Driver.create({ root: process.cwd() })

const answers = driver.trace([
  { file: "src/button.ts", line: 2, property: "height" },
  { file: "src/card.tsx", line: 9, property: "color" },
])
const system = driver.export(["src"], { definitions: true })
const lowered = driver.lowerTailwind(
  "h-7 gap-1 px-2.5 text-xs",
  "src/report.tsx"
)
```

`trace` returns what `--format json` prints, and `export` what the command prints.
The Tailwind call lowers one class string the way `migrate tailwind` lowers a class
attribute in that file, and throws without a utility grammar. It returns:

- `style`, the `css()` call;
- `module`, a file holding it with the imports, relations and per-mode tokens it
  needs;
- `anchors`, the relations the element anchors;
- `left`, each utility it left out, with the reason.

## `kirana-style lsp`

Start the language server on stdin and stdout. Editors run it for you (see
[editor support](/docs/tooling/editor)), but any LSP client can:

```bash
kirana-style lsp
```

It loads `kirana.config.*` like every other command, indexes the project, and then
answers hover, colour, completion, inlay-hint, code-lens, definition, reference
and code-action requests from the same compiler session the build uses.

## `kirana-style ui`

The component registry's commands. They live in their own package,
`@kirana-style/registry`, so the compiler every project installs carries no
registry client: `kirana-style ui …` runs the project's copy of that package with
the arguments after `ui`.

```bash
npm install --save-dev @kirana-style/registry
```

Without it, the command says so and exits 1:

```console
$ kirana-style ui add button
kirana-style ui needs @kirana-style/registry, which this project does not have: add it as a development dependency, or start a new project with npx @kirana-style/registry init --template <example> <directory>
```

Where no project exists yet, run the package itself: `npx @kirana-style/registry`
takes the same commands as `kirana-style ui`.

| Command                                | Does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `kirana-style ui init`                 | Set a project up for a registry: Kirana where it is missing, the `ui` settings, the aliases in `tsconfig.json` (and Vite's `resolve.tsconfigPaths`) when there are none, and the registry's design system installed and wired in. `--framework`, `--base`, `--registry @acme=<template>`, `--design <item>`, `--template <example> [directory]` to start from one of Kirana's examples, `--preset <code>` to start with a design, `--dry-run`, `--overwrite`, `--no-check`. Kirana's packages, the registry among them, are installed at the release's version, written exactly. |
| `kirana-style ui add <item…>`          | Install items and every item they need: each file under your alias for its type, its imports pointed at your aliases, the npm packages added with your package manager, each item recorded in `kirana-style.lock.json`. `--dry-run` writes nothing; `--overwrite` replaces files you changed. It then checks what it wrote with `kirana-style check` (`--no-check` skips that).                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `kirana-style ui outdated [item…]`     | List your installed items whose registry has a new version or changed files, from `kirana-style.lock.json`. Exit 1 when one does.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `kirana-style ui diff [item…]`         | For each installed file the registry or you changed since it was installed, the lines between your file and what installing it now would write.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `kirana-style ui update [item…]`       | Write what the registry changed since an item was installed and keep what you changed; a file both changed stops it until you look (`ui diff`) or pass `--overwrite`. Items an update newly needs are installed with it. `--dry-run`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `kirana-style ui remove <item…>`       | Delete the files of an item you left as installed and drop it from the lockfile, unless another installed item needs it. `--dry-run`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `kirana-style ui preset <code>`        | Change your project's design: the code read with the design system's own layouts, `ui.design` and `<html>`'s attributes set, and every installed component placed again for it, its style modules the registry's flattening for the new design. A file you changed stops it until you pass `--overwrite`. `--dry-run`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `kirana-style ui view <item…>`         | Show what an item is: its version, type and description, the Kirana versions it was checked with, its dependencies, its style modules, each framework's bases with their files, and the files every framework installs. `--json` prints the items as read.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `kirana-style ui search [query]`       | List the items of your registries' indexes whose name, title or description holds every word of the query; without one, every item. `--registry <namespace>` searches only that registry (repeatable), `--json` prints the results.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `kirana-style ui validate <document…>` | Check registry items, indexes and lockfiles: each against its schema, and every file's hash against its content. A document is a file, a URL, or an item of your registries. Exit 1 on a problem, 2 without a document or with unusable settings.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

Building a registry and an MCP server come next. A command asked for before its
release says it is not in this one yet.

A registry is static JSON: one document per item at a URL template holding
`{name}`, and an index, the item named `index`. An item carries its style modules
as written, one source for every framework, and its markup per framework and
base, and every file carries a SHA-256 hash of its content. What a project
installed is recorded in `kirana-style.lock.json`.

The schemas are exported by `@kirana-style/registry/schema`, and served at their
ids for editors and other tools; a document names its schema with `$schema`:

- [an item](https://kirana.style/schema/registry-item.json)
- [an index](https://kirana.style/schema/registry-index.json)
- [the lockfile](https://kirana.style/schema/lockfile.json)
- [the `ui` settings](https://kirana.style/schema/settings.json)

```console
$ kirana-style ui validate public/r/card.json
public/r/card.json: /name must match ^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$
public/r/card.json: /frameworks/react/base/files/0/hash does not match the content, whose hash is sha256-…
```

Your registries are named in `kirana.config.*` under [`ui`](/docs/reference/config#ui),
which the compiler accepts and never reads. An item of one is named with its
namespace, and a name alone is Kirana UI's:

```console
$ kirana-style ui validate @acme/card @acme/index
@acme/card: a valid item
@acme/index: a valid index
$ kirana-style ui validate @acme/private
@acme/private: @acme: its header Authorization reads ${ACME_TOKEN}, which is not set
```

Each document is fetched afresh, over `https:` (or `http:` from your own
machine), or read from disk for a path; a request gives up after 30 seconds.

`init` starts a project. In a fresh Vite app:

```console
$ kirana-style ui init --base base
kirana: config: create kirana.config.ts
kirana: adapter: add @kirana-style/vite to vite.config.ts
kirana: stylesheet: import the stylesheet in src/main.tsx
kirana: types: create src/kirana.d.ts
@kirana/kirana 0.0.0
  + src/lib/kirana/axes.ts
  …
setup: tsconfig.app.json: paths "@/*": ["./src/*"]
setup: vite.config.ts: resolve: { tsconfigPaths: true }
setup: kirana.config.ts: ui {"framework":"react","base":"base"}
setup: kirana.config.ts: spreads installConfig (./src/lib/kirana/kirana.ts)
setup: src/main.tsx: imports @/components/ui/reset.css
setup: src/main.tsx: sets <html>'s classes from htmlStyles
packages: npm install @kirana-style/core@0.3.2 …
kirana-style.lock.json: 1 item(s) recorded
```

The design system says what a project needs from it, and `init` puts each part
where Kirana's own setup put Kirana:

- its configuration, spread into `kirana.config.ts`;
- its stylesheets, imported after Kirana's;
- its styles for `<html>`, as `sx` on the `<html>` element where a layout renders
  one (Next.js, TanStack Start), or set from the entry in an app whose
  `index.html` is static.

What it cannot change safely, it prints as a step to do by hand. A template's own
styles of `:root` and `body` (Vite's `src/index.css`) still apply over the design
system's: remove them, as you would for shadcn/ui.

`add` installs an item after the items it needs, and stops before writing
anything when a file you already have would change:

```console
$ kirana-style ui add button
@kirana/kirana 0.0.0
  + src/lib/kirana/axes.ts
  …
@kirana/sx 0.0.0 · react/base
  + src/lib/kirana/sx.ts
@kirana/button 0.0.0 · react/base
  + src/components/ui/button.styles.ts
  + src/components/ui/button.tsx
packages: npm install @base-ui/react@^1.9.0
kirana-style.lock.json: 3 item(s) recorded
```

Each line says what happens to a file: `+` it is new, `=` you have it as it is,
`!` yours differs. A component names each icon once for every library, and you get
your library's own component in its place, from its package (`ui.iconLibrary`,
Lucide by default). The lockfile keeps two hashes per file, the registry's and
what was written, which is how later commands tell a registry's change from
yours.

`view` shows an item without its files' content, before you install it:

```console
$ kirana-style ui view @acme/button
@acme/button 1.2.0 · component
Button: Displays a button.
from https://acme.dev/r/button.json

  kirana      ^0.3.2
  registry    @acme/spinner, separator
  packages    @kirana-style/core ^0.3.2
  axes        style, radius
  styles      ui/button.styles.ts
  react/base  ui/button.tsx · @base-ui/react ^1.0.0
  react/aria  ui/button.tsx
  vue/ark     ui/button/Button.vue, ui/button/index.ts
  files       lib/utils.ts, app/globals.css
```

`search` reads every registry's index, each entry with the bases of each framework
it supports:

```console
$ kirana-style ui search --registry @acme
@acme/button    1.2.0   component  Button  react base, aria · vue ark
@acme/note      0.1.0   lib
@acme/login-01  0.10.0  block      Login   react base
$ kirana-style ui search login form
@acme/login-01  0.10.0  block  Login  react base
```

A document that cannot be read is named with what failed, after what could be
shown, and the command exits 1. With `--json`, each prints one object:

| Command  | Prints                                                                                            |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `view`   | `{ items, failures }`: each item as read                                                          |
| `search` | `{ results, failures }`: each index entry with its `reference` (`@acme/login-01`) and `namespace` |

Each failure is `{ document, message }`.
---
# Editor support
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tooling/editor
# Editor support

<!-- ::editor-banner -->

Object styles move the CSS out of the markup: you read `sx={styles.card}`, not a
class list. The Kirana language server brings it back where you are reading, and
answers questions a class list never could: **which value wins, and why**.

It is `kirana-style lsp`, a command of the compiler you already installed. It runs on the
same compiler session as your build, so what the editor tells you is what the build
does, never an approximation of it.

## Light through every line of your styles

A Tailwind class list shows what an element gets; object styles hid it. The
language server puts it back on every line, coloured by kind, and answers the rest
on hover. Pick a feature to see what it shows: every picture is the server's real
output for one file.

<!-- ::editor-showcase -->

## Pick your editor

- [VS Code](/docs/tooling/editor#vs-code-and-its-forks): Extension
- [Cursor](/docs/tooling/editor#vs-code-and-its-forks): VS Code extension
- [Windsurf](/docs/tooling/editor#vs-code-and-its-forks): VS Code extension
- [Antigravity](/docs/tooling/editor#vs-code-and-its-forks): VS Code extension
- [Zed](/docs/tooling/editor#zed): Extension
- [Neovim](/docs/tooling/editor#neovim): vim.lsp.config
- [Helix](/docs/tooling/editor#helix): languages.toml
- [Any LSP editor](/docs/tooling/editor#any-other-editor): kirana-style lsp over stdio

Every editor runs your project's own `node_modules/.bin/kirana-style lsp`, from the
`kirana-style` package. Upgrading Kirana upgrades the editor with it; there is no
extension version to keep in step. A project still on 0.1.0 has `kirana` there
instead, and the extensions find that too.

### VS Code and its forks

VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf and Antigravity take the same extension. It finds the
server in your project, walking up to a monorepo's root, and starts it for
TypeScript, JavaScript, Vue, Svelte, Astro and HTML files (HTML for Angular
templates).

Install **Kirana** from the
[VS Code Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=kirana-style.kirana)
in VS Code, or from [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org/extension/kirana-style/kirana)
in Cursor, Windsurf, Antigravity and VSCodium: search "Kirana" in the
Extensions view. In a remote workspace (WSL, SSH, a container), install it on
the remote side, where your project and Node.js live.

If your project has no `node_modules/.bin/kirana-style` (a checkout of Kirana itself,
say), point the extension at a binary or script:

```json
{ "kirana.server.path": "packages/kirana/npm/cli/bin/kirana-style.ts" }
```

A relative path is resolved against the workspace folder; a `.js` or `.ts` path
runs with `node` (22.18 or later).

### Zed

The Kirana extension registers the server for TypeScript, TSX and JavaScript, for
Vue, Svelte and Astro components once Zed's extensions for them are installed, and
for HTML in Angular templates.
Until it is published, add it with **zed: install dev extension** from
`packages/kirana/editors/zed`.

It finds the server in this order:

- the binary named in Zed's settings, below;
- the project's own, when the `package.json` of the folder Zed opened lists
  `kirana-style`;
- a `kirana-style` on `PATH`.

Zed does not let an extension look inside `node_modules`, so in a monorepo whose
root does not list the package, name the binary in the settings:

```json
{
  "lsp": {
    "kirana": {
      "binary": { "path": "/path/to/kirana-style", "arguments": ["lsp"] }
    }
  }
}
```

### Neovim

Neovim 0.11 and later:

```lua
vim.lsp.config("kirana", {
  cmd = { "node_modules/.bin/kirana-style", "lsp" },
  filetypes = {
    "typescript", "typescriptreact", "javascript", "javascriptreact",
    "vue", "svelte", "astro", "html",
  },
  root_markers = { "kirana.config.ts", "kirana.config.js", "kirana.config.json" },
})
vim.lsp.enable("kirana")
```

### Helix

In `languages.toml`:

```toml
[language-server.kirana]
command = "node_modules/.bin/kirana-style"
args = ["lsp"]

[[language]]
name = "tsx"
language-servers = ["typescript-language-server", "kirana"]

[[language]]
name = "vue" # and "svelte", "astro", "html"
language-servers = ["vuels", "kirana"]
```

### Any other editor

Run `kirana-style lsp` from the project root and connect over stdio. It runs beside the
TypeScript server and answers styling questions only: property names and token
keys are TypeScript's, through `@kirana-style/core`'s types.

## What you get

### The style card

Hover an element's `sx`, a `css()` call or a recipe and you get its card, laid out
the way you read a style:

- **What it is**: the expression (`styles.card`) and the handles it merges, each a
  link to where it is defined, as in `Merges 2 handles: base + wide if on`.
- **The box model**, drawn as DevTools draws it: margin, border, padding and
  content nested, each side's value on its side, the content's size and layout in
  the middle, the corners rounded by the border radius.
- **Resolved**: every property that applies, in source order within layout, box,
  size, colour, type, border, effects and motion, with `rem` in pixels, the token
  a value reads, and a swatch for each colour, split light and dark for a pair.
- **When**: the values that depend on a breakpoint (`md`), a state (`:hover`), a
  pseudo-element, or a guard in the `sx`, shown as `if on`.
- **Compiled CSS**: the rules the stylesheet carries, with their size.

Hover a **property** instead and you get its entries in precedence order, with the
ladder step that put each one where it is: the answer
[`kirana-style trace`](/docs/tooling/cli) gives on the command line. Hover a **token** for
its value in both colour modes, and whether a theme can reassign it.

VS Code draws the box model as a picture in your theme's colours, with the
properties beside it, each property name in its group's colour: layout blue, box
green, size cyan, colour orange, type yellow, border purple. Other editors show the
same card with a text drawing and the properties below it.

### Inline summary

At the end of every element's line, a muted hint says what it ends up with, in the
vocabulary of a class list: `▦ grid · gap 1rem · p 1rem · m 0.5rem 1rem · +4`.
Hover the hint for the card.

- The mark is the layout: `▦` for grid, `⇶` for flex.
- Margin and padding read as their shorthand.
- A value under a guard leads with it: `on: p 2rem`.
- A `{...props(a, b)}` spread is summarised too, from the handles it names.

In VS Code each part is coloured by its group, as the card colours properties:
layout blue, box green, size cyan, colour orange, type yellow, border purple. There
is no red, which reads as an error, and the colours are your theme's own. Kirana's
icon leads the hint; `kirana.inlayHints.icon` and `kirana.inlayHints.opacity` tune
it. Other editors show it in the hint colour.

Above each `css()` and `recipe()`, a code lens counts declarations, conditional
entries and bridged values, and **used by N elements** lists the elements whose
`sx` names it, in every file. Clicking the counts opens the compiled CSS beside the
file, read-only, in one reused tab.

### Style Inspector (VS Code)

**Kirana: Open Style Inspector** opens a panel in the Explorer that follows the
cursor. It draws the box model, the layout, the colours with a light and dark
switch, and every declaration with its source. Its chips turn conditions and
guards on and off (`:hover`, `md`, `on`), and the values that apply then are the
compiler's answer, not a guess: the server simulates the cascade for exactly that
set.

### Style Fold (VS Code)

With `kirana.fold.enabled` (or **Kirana: Toggle Style Fold**), a long one-line
`css({ … })` reads as its summary, after Kirana's icon, until the cursor is on its
line: Tailwind Fold, for object styles. In `dim` mode the text stays and its opacity
drops instead, and a minimum length keeps short objects as written; the settings
are [below](#settings). **Kirana: Fold Styles** folds every multi-line style object
with the editor's own folding.

### Colours

Colour literals and colour tokens get a swatch. A `light-dark(…, …)` pair gets one
per mode, and the picker edits that mode alone. The picker writes the format the
colour is written in, so an `oklch()` stays `oklch()`; click the colour at the top
of the picker to switch to hex or `rgb()`. It edits literals only, never a token
reference, so a theme stays the source of a token's colour. A token's swatch shows
its light value, and hover shows both.

### Completion

Where TypeScript cannot help:

- **Condition keys** inside a property's value (pseudo-classes, attributes,
  `@media`, `@container`, `@supports` and `base`), listed weakest to strongest, the
  order the [precedence ladder](/docs/styling/precedence) applies them.
- **`select.`** offers `descendant` and `child`.
- **Keyword values** for the property you are writing (`alignItems: "cen` →
  `center`), from the CSS specification's own grammar.
- **Utility strings** in `sx="…"`: your grammar's variants, roots and scale keys,
  each with its value.

### Diagnostics, fixes and refactorings

Every [compiler diagnostic](/docs/tooling/diagnostics) appears as you type, at the
property it is about. Two have one exact fix, offered as a quick fix:

| Diagnostic            | You wrote  | The fix        |
| --------------------- | ---------- | -------------- |
| `unitless-length`     | `width: 5` | `width: "5px"` |
| A misspelled property | `colr`     | `color`        |

Code actions also offer:

- **Extract to `css()`** on an inline `css({…})` in an element's `sx`: a named
  handle above the component.
- **Inline** a handle used once.
- **Vary at md** and **Vary on :hover** on a plain value: it becomes
  `{ base: …, "@media (width >= 48rem)": … }`, ready to change.
- **Show compiled CSS**, **Explain precedence** for the property under the cursor,
  and **Convert Tailwind classes to `css()`** on a `className` string, with the
  engine of [`kirana-style migrate tailwind`](/docs/migration/from-tailwind).

### Structure and navigation

The outline lists a file's styles, recipes, tokens and relations. With the cursor
on a key, every element in the file that receives it is highlighted, and on an
element, the keys it receives. Go to definition on a token opens its entry in
`defineTokens`; on a relation read (`card.within(…)`) it goes to where the anchor
is applied. Find references lists a token's or relation's uses, and workspace
symbols search every token and relation in the project.

### Vue, Svelte and Astro

Components get all of it. Script blocks compile as the build compiles them, and
each template binding gets its hint, card and colours, inside a loop too:

| Framework | Binding   | Loop      |
| --------- | --------- | --------- |
| Vue       | `:sx="…"` | `v-for`   |
| Svelte    | `sx={…}`  | `{#each}` |
| Astro     | `sx={…}`  | `.map()`  |

A diagnostic in a script lands on its line in the component.

### Server templates

In Blade, Twig, ERB, HEEx and Edge files, each name passed to `kirana(…)` gets
the same hover, colours and summary as an `sx`, from the class map's modules (the
`classes` setting of your configuration). A name no module exports is underlined
as `unknown-class-name`, before the helper would fail on it at runtime. The editors
send these files to the server as:

| Editor  | Languages                                             |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| VS Code | `blade`, `php`, `erb`, `twig`, `phoenix-heex`, `edge` |
| Zed     | PHP, Blade, HTML/ERB, Twig, HEEX                      |

### Angular

`[sx]="…"` bindings get the same hint, card and colours, in a component's inline
`template` and in the `.html` file its `templateUrl` names. A template reaches the
handles through a member of the same name, which the server reads as the module's
own handles:

```ts
protected readonly styles = styles
```

An HTML file that no component names as its template is left alone.

## Settings

| Setting (VS Code)               | Default | What it does                                                                 |
| ------------------------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `kirana.server.path`            | empty   | The binary to run; empty is the project's own. `.js`/`.ts` runs with `node`. |
| `kirana.inlayHints.enabled`     | `true`  | The summary after `sx`.                                                      |
| `kirana.inlayHints.maxLength`   | `100`   | The longest summary, in characters; `0` for every declaration.               |
| `kirana.inlayHints.colors`      | `true`  | Colour the summary by group; off, VS Code's one-colour hint.                 |
| `kirana.inlayHints.icon`        | `true`  | Kirana's icon before each summary.                                           |
| `kirana.inlayHints.opacity`     | `0.85`  | How strongly the summary reads, from `0.1` to `1`.                           |
| `kirana.codeLens.enabled`       | `true`  | The counts above `css()` and `recipe()`.                                     |
| `kirana.hover.diagrams`         | `true`  | Draw the box model as a picture; off, a text drawing.                        |
| `kirana.rootFontSize`           | `16`    | Pixels per `rem`, for the pixel equivalents.                                 |
| `kirana.inspector.followCursor` | `true`  | The Style Inspector shows what the cursor is on.                             |
| `kirana.fold.enabled`           | `false` | Style Fold for long one-line style objects.                                  |
| `kirana.fold.mode`              | `fold`  | `fold` writes the summary in place; `dim` lowers the object's opacity.       |
| `kirana.fold.opacity`           | `0.4`   | The opacity of a dimmed object.                                              |
| `kirana.fold.minLength`         | `40`    | Shorter objects stay as written.                                             |
| `kirana.fold.icon`              | `true`  | Kirana's icon before a folded summary.                                       |
| `kirana.trace.server`           | `off`   | Log the protocol messages to the **Kirana** output channel.                  |

Other editors pass the same switches as `initializationOptions`:

| Option                 | What it does                                                                                                                                         |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"summary": false`     | Turns the inline summary off.                                                                                                                        |
| `"codeLens": false`    | Turns the counts above `css()` off.                                                                                                                  |
| `"rootFontSize": 16`   | Pixels per `rem`.                                                                                                                                    |
| `"images": true`       | For a client that renders `data:` images in hovers. It sends `"theme"` (`light` or `dark`) too, and updates it with the `kirana/theme` notification. |
| `"commandLinks": true` | For a client that runs trusted `command:` links.                                                                                                     |

## How fast

On our shadcn/ui port (`packages/ui` and three applications, indexed in 166 ms, with
61 component files open), a hover answers in **1.2 ms** at the 95th percentile,
diagnostics refresh **7.1 ms** after an edit, and the server holds **65 MB**. The
budgets are 50 ms, 200 ms and 300 MB.

## Limits

- **Components are read by a scanner.** The build parses Vue, Svelte and Astro with
  their own compilers (and Angular's templates are its own, merged at runtime); the server, which cannot load them, scans the same blocks and
  bindings, and a test over every example holds the scan to the frameworks' parsers. A
  template binding that reads only a Svelte `<script module>` handle gets no hint.
- **The summary shows what the compiler knows at build time.** A value returned
  by a function it cannot see into (`sx={mergeSx(a, b)}`, a hand-written variant
  helper) has nothing to summarise, where the same values as an array,
  `sx={[a, b]}`, do. A recipe called with a variant known only at run time
  (`button({ variant })`) is not summarised yet, and `sx` passed to one of your
  components is summarised inside it, on the element that receives it.
- **One project per server.** The root is your workspace folder or
  `kirana.config.*`'s directory; editing `kirana.config.*` restarts the server.
- **Uses are found by name.** Declarations, anchors and reads come from the
  compiler; uses in other files are matched by their written names, so a token
  imported under another alias is found under that alias.

## Troubleshooting

- **The status bar shows Kirana with a warning sign.** No binary was found:
  install `kirana-style` in the project, or set `kirana.server.path`.
- **Answers look stale after changing the configuration.** Run **Kirana: Restart
  Language Server**.
- **No hint after `sx={…}`.** Check that your editor shows inlay hints at all:
  `editor.inlayHints.enabled` must be `on` (some editors default to showing them
  only while you hold Ctrl+Alt). Set it in
  your workspace's `.vscode/settings.json`:

  ```json
  { "editor.inlayHints.enabled": "on", "editor.inlayHints.maximumLength": 0 }
  ```

- **The summary ends in `…`.** VS Code cuts every inlay hint at 43 characters. Set
  `editor.inlayHints.maximumLength` to `0` and Kirana's own limit applies
  (`kirana.inlayHints.maxLength`), counting what it leaves out at the end.
- **The card is taller than the hover.** VS Code fixes a hover's height at a quarter
  of the editor, at least 250 px; no extension can change that. Drag the hover's
  edge once and it keeps that size until the window reloads. Or open the Style
  Inspector, which has the whole height of the sidebar.
- **You want to see what is said.** Set `kirana.trace.server` to `verbose` and open
  the **Kirana** output channel.
---
# Lint
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tooling/lint
# Lint

`@kirana-style/eslint-plugin` reports what the compiler knows, where the code is
written, in the linter you already run.

Other styling lint plugins re-implement CSS validation in JavaScript, and drift from
the compiler they check. Kirana's rules read the compiler itself (the diagnostics,
the atoms each style compiles to, every token, how imports resolve), so lint and
build never disagree, and the plugin is mostly about the mistakes no compiler can
see: an override that silently loses, a forwarded `sx` in the wrong place, a class
that never reaches the DOM.

## Pick your linter

- [Oxlint](/docs/tooling/lint#oxlint): jsPlugins
- [ESLint](/docs/tooling/lint#eslint): Flat config
- [Biome](/docs/tooling/lint#biome): GritQL plugins


Under Oxlint and ESLint the rules are the same objects, and so are their results:
the same reports at the same places, and the same fixed text. A test runs every
rule through both linters on each change. Biome cannot run JavaScript rules, so
it gets the five that need no compiler, rewritten as GritQL plugins.

<!-- ::figure-lint -->

### Oxlint

Through Oxlint's JavaScript plugins, at Oxlint's speed:

```jsonc
// .oxlintrc.json
{
  "jsPlugins": [
    { "name": "kirana", "specifier": "@kirana-style/eslint-plugin" },
  ],
  "rules": {
    "kirana/diagnostics": "error",
    "kirana/sx-last": "error",
    "kirana/no-conflicting-props": "error",
    "kirana/override-keeps-conditions": "error",
    "kirana/no-classname-on-sx": "error",
    "kirana/no-dark-variant": "warn",
    "kirana/no-unused": "warn",
  },
}
```

### ESLint

Flat config:

```js
// eslint.config.js
import kirana from "@kirana-style/eslint-plugin"

export default [kirana.configs.recommended]
```

### Biome

`@kirana-style/biome-plugin` carries the rules that need no compiler, as
[GritQL plugins](https://biomejs.dev/linter/plugins/):

- `sx-last`
- `no-conflicting-props`
- `no-dark-variant`
- `no-class-helpers`
- `use-logical-properties`, in neither preset

Its presets turn them on:

```jsonc
// biome.json
{
  "extends": ["@kirana-style/biome-plugin/recommended"], // or /strict
}
```


A test runs each of them through Biome and through its ESLint original, and the
reports (line, column and message) must match. Each message starts with the
rule's name, since Biome files every plugin diagnostic under `plugin`. The
presets name the rules as `./node_modules/@kirana-style/biome-plugin/rules/*.grit`,
because Biome resolves a plugin path from the project; in a workspace member
whose `node_modules` sits higher up, list the files from there in `plugins`.

A Biome plugin matches syntax: it cannot ask the compiler or read another file.
What the other rules would report reaches a Biome project two other ways:
`kirana-style check` in CI, as pull-request annotations, and the
[language server](/docs/tooling/editor) in the editor:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
- run: npx kirana-style check src --format github --max-warnings 0
```


`no-unused` and `sort-properties` stay ESLint and Oxlint only: counting member
reads and ordering keys against the property table are beyond what GritQL can
express.

## The project root

The project root is the nearest `kirana.config.*` above the file being linted. In a
monorepo whose packages share a configuration, give the package its own
`kirana.config.ts` that exports it, or set `settings.kirana.root`. The project is
compiled once per lint run and each file once, however many rules ask; the native
engine must be installed, as for a build.

## Every rule at a glance

- [`kirana/diagnostics`](/docs/tooling/lint#diagnostics) (recommended): Every compiler diagnostic, at the property
- [`kirana/sx-last`](/docs/tooling/lint#sx-last) (recommended, autofix, also Biome): A forwarded sx that callers cannot override
- [`kirana/no-conflicting-props`](/docs/tooling/lint#no-conflicting-props) (recommended, also Biome): className or style beside a styleProps() spread
- [`kirana/override-keeps-conditions`](/docs/tooling/lint#override-keeps-conditions) (recommended, suggestions): A plain override that loses under [data-*]
- [`kirana/no-classname-on-sx`](/docs/tooling/lint#no-classname-on-sx) (recommended): A class that never reaches the DOM
- [`kirana/no-unused`](/docs/tooling/lint#no-unused) (recommended, suggestions): Styles and recipe options nothing applies
- [`kirana/no-dark-variant`](/docs/tooling/lint#no-dark-variant) (recommended, also Biome): Dark mode the page's chosen mode never reaches
- [`kirana/sort-properties`](/docs/tooling/lint#sort-properties) (strict, autofix): Property and condition order
- [`kirana/prefer-token`](/docs/tooling/lint#prefer-token) (strict, suggestions): A literal that repeats a token
- [`kirana/finite-bridge`](/docs/tooling/lint#finite-bridge) (strict): A runtime value that is really a variant
- [`kirana/no-class-helpers`](/docs/tooling/lint#no-class-helpers) (strict, also Biome): clsx, tailwind-merge or cva joining class strings
- [`kirana/restricted-properties`](/docs/tooling/lint#restricted-properties) (opt-in): Properties, or values of one, the project rules out
- [`kirana/use-logical-properties`](/docs/tooling/lint#use-logical-properties) (opt-in, suggestions, also Biome): A left or right side a right-to-left page should mirror

## Configs

| Config        | What it holds                                                                   | Rules                                                                                                                               |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `recommended` | The problems: what the build reports, and what loses a style without any error. | `diagnostics`, `sx-last`, `no-conflicting-props`, `override-keeps-conditions`, `no-classname-on-sx`, `no-dark-variant`, `no-unused` |
| `strict`      | Everything in `recommended`, and the stylistic and advisory rules.              | `sort-properties`, `prefer-token`, `finite-bridge`, `no-class-helpers`                                                              |
| neither       | A project's own policy, turned on by the project.                               | `restricted-properties`, `use-logical-properties`                                                                                   |

Biome's presets have the same names and hold the rules it can run. A rule in
neither preset is turned on by name, and under Biome by listing its file:

```jsonc
// biome.json
{
  "extends": ["@kirana-style/biome-plugin/recommended"],
  "plugins": [
    "./node_modules/@kirana-style/biome-plugin/rules/use-logical-properties.grit",
  ],
}
```

## Rules

### `diagnostics`

Every [compiler diagnostic](/docs/tooling/diagnostics), at the property it is
about, so a CI that only lints still fails on what the build would report.
Warnings and errors by default; `{ "minimum": "info" }` adds the informational ones
and `{ "ignore": ["unresolved-import"] }` drops names.

### `sx-last`

A component that forwards its caller's `sx` must put it last, or the styles after
it override the caller's, and the caller cannot tell why their style does not
apply. Autofix.

```tsx
<div sx={[styles.root, sx, active && styles.active]} /> // ✕
<div sx={[styles.root, active && styles.active, sx]} /> // ✓
```

A `className` handed down by a parent's `render` may follow it.

### `no-conflicting-props`

`className` or `style` written next to `{...styleProps(…)}` on one element: JSX
keeps the last one, so either the compiled styles or the attribute never reach
the DOM. Move those styles into a `css()` handle and pass it to the same call.

### `override-keeps-conditions`

The pitfall of coming from StyleX: StyleX replaced a whole property, Kirana
[merges per condition](/docs/styling/merging). A plain value passed to a component
that sets the same property under an attribute condition keeps losing there:

```tsx
// Separator: alignSelf: { base: "stretch", '[data-orientation="vertical"]': "center" }
<Separator sx={css({ alignSelf: "auto" })} /> // ✕ still "center" when vertical
```

Two suggestions: set the value under the component's conditions too, or
`{ "*": null, base: "auto" }` to drop the component's entries. Interaction states
(`:hover`) are not reported: keeping a component's hover over your plain value is
usually what you want.

### `no-classname-on-sx`

`className` given to one of your components that takes `sx` and not `className`:
the class never reaches the DOM. A component that spreads the rest of its props
may pass it on, so it is not reported.

### `no-unused`

A style nothing applies: a key of a module-local styles object that no
`styles.<key>` reads, or a recipe option no call selects and no default names.
Exported objects and ones used whole are left alone, and so are Vue, Svelte and
Astro files, whose templates the linter does not see. Suggestion: remove it.

### `no-dark-variant`

Dark mode written the way other systems write it, which compiles without complaint
and which the page then ignores:

- A `prefers-color-scheme` condition in a style (a key of a style object, or a
  `media()` query) follows the operating system, not the mode the page chose, so a
  theme toggle that sets `color-scheme` never reaches it.
- A Tailwind `dark:` class left in a `className`, `class` or `sx` string names a
  class no stylesheet defines.

Put both values in a `light-dark()` [token](/docs/tokens/themes-and-modes), which
follows `color-scheme`. A `matchMedia()` call outside a style is left alone. Also
under Biome.

```tsx
css({
  color: { base: "black", "@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)": "white" },
}) // ✕
css({ color: color.foreground }) // ✓ light-dark(black, white)
```

### `sort-properties`

In `strict`. One order in every style object: layout, box, typography, visual, the rest, custom
properties, then nested blocks. A conditional value goes `base`, then at-rules,
relations, pseudo-classes and attributes: weakest to strongest, the order the
ladder applies them, so the source reads in cascade order. Order never changes
what Kirana compiles, so the fix is always safe; an object with a spread is left
alone. Autofix.

### `prefer-token`

In `strict`. A literal equal to a token's value (`color: "#0af"` where `color.brand` is
`#0af`) suggests the token, with its import, so a theme or a design change reaches
it.

### `finite-bridge`

In `strict`. A style factory whose value is bridged at runtime, such as
`(size) => css({ width: size })`, but only ever called with a few literals is a
variant in disguise. A recipe
variant compiles to static classes; the bridge costs a custom property and a
`style` attribute on every element.

### `no-class-helpers`

In `strict`. An import of a class-string helper:

- `clsx` and `classnames`, which join strings;
- `tailwind-merge`, which settles conflicts between them;
- `class-variance-authority`, which picks variants at runtime.

Joined class strings do not merge: two atoms for one
property both apply, and which wins depends on the stylesheet, not on the order
written. `cx` and `sx={[a, b]}` [merge per property](/docs/styling/merging), and
[`recipe()`](/docs/styling/recipes) compiles the variants `cva` would pick at
runtime. Also under Biome.

### `restricted-properties`

In neither preset: the list is the project's own. A property the options rule
out, or a literal value outside the ones it allows:

```js
// eslint.config.js
export default [
  kirana.configs.recommended,
  {
    rules: {
      "kirana/restricted-properties": [
        "error",
        {
          float: { reason: "Use flex or grid." },
          display: { values: ["flex", "grid", "none"] },
        },
      ],
    },
  },
]
```

A `float` then reports `float is ruled out in this project. Use flex or grid.`,
and a `display: "table"` reports
`display takes flex, grid, none in this project, not "table".`

A property is matched as written, so ruling out `margin` leaves `marginTop`
alone; list both to rule out a family. Every literal of a
[conditional value](/docs/styling/conditions) is checked, in `css()` and in a
recipe's base and variants. A token or an expression passes: it is the design
system's own. ESLint and Oxlint only, since a Biome plugin takes no options.

### `use-logical-properties`

In neither preset. A side or a corner of the inline axis written physically:

```tsx
css({ marginLeft: "1rem" })
// marginLeft stays on the same side in right-to-left text;
// marginInlineStart follows the writing direction.
```

On a page that is also read right to left, `marginInlineStart` moves to the right
with the text, and `marginLeft` does not. The rule covers margins, paddings,
`left` and `right`, the side borders, the corner radii, and scroll margins and
paddings. Top, bottom and sizes are left alone: they change only in vertical
writing.

The rename is offered as a suggestion, never applied by `--fix`: the two
properties agree only in left-to-right text, so the change is yours to make. A
page that is only ever left to right loses nothing to physical sides, which is
why the rule is off until you turn it on. The compiler's own
[`mixed-logical-physical`](/docs/tooling/diagnostics) warning stays on either
way: it reports a style that writes both kinds for one side. Also under Biome.

## This repository

The docs and demo apps lint themselves with `recommended`. Its first run found 19
ties the UI configuration had already declared impossible but that a tool run
inside `packages/ui` could not see, three real precedence ties, a shorthand that
could not be split, and 21 unused styles.
---
# Diagnostics reference
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tooling/diagnostics
# Diagnostics reference

Every diagnostic has a stable code and a kebab-case name. Neither changes meaning
once released, so you can suppress or raise one by name and trust it to keep
meaning the same thing.

A diagnostic about one property points at that property (`width: 5` in
`css({ display: "grid", width: 5 })`), not at the whole `css()` call, even when
the style object is declared in one place and passed to `css()` somewhere else in
the same module. The [editor](/docs/tooling/editor) underlines exactly that
property, and the [lint plugin](/docs/tooling/lint) reports it there.

The table below is generated from the compiler's own catalogue at build time, so
it cannot drift from what the compiler actually emits.

<!-- ::diagnostics -->

## Severities

- **error**: the output would be wrong. The build fails, and the level cannot be
  changed.
- **warning**: the output is valid but probably not what you meant.
- **info**: something worth knowing: a runtime bridge, a lowered target.

Any non-error can be re-levelled, including to `"off"`, in
[`diagnostics`](/docs/reference/config).

## The ones you will actually meet

**`sx-on-external-component`**: you gave `sx` to a component that does not read
it. Spread compiled props instead:
[styling other people's components](/docs/styling/external-components).

**`unused-sx`**: a component takes `sx` and never applies it, so callers think
they can style it and cannot.

**`ambiguous-precedence`**: two values could both apply and the ladder cannot
order them. Nest one condition inside the other, or declare the pair exclusive:
[precedence](/docs/styling/precedence).

**`mixed-logical-physical`**: a box has both logical and physical longhands set,
in a way whose outcome could mislead. Pick one axis family. It also covers an
inline logical inset beside a translate that moves along x: translates have no
logical form, so the element is off centre in right-to-left text. Use a physical
inset with the translate.

**`unreachable-entry`**: an info. A condition key nested in another that it can
never meet, such as `'[data-side="top"]': { '[data-side="bottom"]': … }`. Nothing
under it can apply, so it is left out of the stylesheet. Two libraries' states the
configuration declares apart with `exclusiveAcross` are left out the same way, but
quietly: nesting them is how a style is written once for every library.

**`select-state-on-parent`**: an info. A pseudo-class nested under a `select`
target, `[select.child("a")]: { color: { ":hover": … } }`, is the state of the
element carrying the style. For the link's own hover, write it into the target:
`[select.child("a:hover")]`.

**`unsplittable-shorthand`**: a shorthand whose value cannot be split into
longhands exactly, usually `border: var(--something)`. It stays whole, which means
a later style cannot remove just one of its longhands.

**`dynamic-bridged`** (info): a value became a custom property because it is only
known at runtime: [values known at runtime](/docs/styling/dynamic).

**`relation-without-anchor`**: a style reads a relation whose anchor is never
applied, so it can never match: [relations](/docs/styling/relations). A build
checks the relations whose module it compiled; `kirana-style check` checks them all.

**`invalid-fallback`**, **`invalid-position-try`**, **`invalid-view-transition`**
and **`invalid-counter-style`** report a value the browser would drop or misread:

| Diagnostic                | What it catches                                                                                     |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `invalid-fallback`        | A [`firstThatWorks()`](/docs/styling/fallbacks) run whose values set different longhands            |
| `invalid-position-try`    | A property a [`positionTry()`](/docs/styling/anchor-positioning) block ignores                      |
| `invalid-view-transition` | A [`viewTransition()`](/docs/styling/view-transitions) part that is not one of the four             |
| `invalid-counter-style`   | A [`counterStyle()`](/docs/styling/at-rules#counter-styles) descriptor or system that draws nothing |

**`unresolved-import`**: an import a style depends on could not be resolved, so
its value compiles as a runtime value. Check the specifier and your tsconfig
paths. An import no style reads, such as a string from a Vite virtual module
passed as a prop, is a runtime value already and is not reported.

**`import-cycle`**: a value a style reads comes through an import cycle, and the
message names it (`core/states.ts → core/kirana.ts → core/states.ts`). The module
that closes the cycle reads the other one before it has been evaluated, so the
value compiles as a runtime value. Move what both modules need into a module of
its own that neither imports back. A type-only import (`import type`,
`import { type … }`) holds no value and never makes a cycle.

## Reading one

```console
$ kirana-style check src
error[KRN1301] unknown-condition: ":hover" is a condition, and conditions nest
inside property values (src/card.tsx:12:3)
  help: write `property: { [condition]: value }`
```

Code, name, message, location, and a help line that says what to do. `kirana-style check
--format json` gives the same fields as data.

<!-- ::diagnostics-figure -->
---
# Debugging styles
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tooling/debugging
# Debugging styles

A style is not doing what you expect. In rough order of likelihood:

## 1 · Is the module compiled?

If `css()` runs in a module the compiler never saw, it throws with a message that
says exactly that. If you see the error, the fix is the adapter: `kirana()` must
be in the bundler's plugin list, and before the framework plugin.

## 2 · Is the element yours?

`sx` on a component from a package does nothing. The compiler warns
(`sx-on-external-component`), so check the terminal, and see
[styling other people's components](/docs/styling/external-components).

## 3 · Did a merge keep an entry you meant to replace?

The most common surprise: a later `color: "grey"` replaces only the base entry, so
an earlier `:hover` colour still applies. Write `{ "*": null, base: "grey" }` when
you mean "and nothing else"; [Merging](/docs/styling/merging) has the rule.

## 4 · Ask the compiler

```bash
kirana-style trace src/components/card.tsx:24 padding-top
```

It lists every candidate declaration for that property, marks the winner, and
names the ladder step that decided. If your value is not in the list at all, the
problem is upstream: the style is not on that element.

<!-- ::figure-trace -->

## 5 · Check the conditions

- A condition as a **top-level key** is an error, and the message says so.
- A state beats a breakpoint: that is the ladder, not a bug.
- A relation read needs its anchor on the element whose state you are reading.

## 6 · Look at the CSS

The stylesheet is plain CSS with one declaration per rule, so devtools tell you
the truth quickly: inspect the element, read the class list, and look for the
declaration. A class that is present but crossed out is a precedence question
(step 4, ask `trace`). A declaration that is missing entirely is a compile
question (check the terminal).

## 7 · Animations that do nothing

Transition the property you actually set: `translate`, `scale` and `rotate` are
not `transform`. See [animation](/docs/styling/animation).
---
# Installing components
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tooling/components
# Installing components

`kirana-style ui` copies components from a registry into your project, as
shadcn/ui's CLI does: the files become yours. It installs one source for every
framework, rewrites its imports to your aliases, adds the packages it needs, and
records what it wrote so it can update it later without losing your edits.

The commands live in their own package:

```bash
npm install --save-dev @kirana-style/registry
```

In a folder with nothing installed yet, the package runs on its own, as
`npx @kirana-style/registry <command>`, the same commands under another name.

## Setting a project up

```bash
npx kirana-style ui init
```

`init` works on a new app or one you already have:

- it sets Kirana up where the project lacks it, as `kirana-style init` does;
- it maps the `@/*` alias in `tsconfig.json` when the project has none, and tells
  Vite to read it; a JavaScript Next.js app gets the `tsconfig.json` Next.js
  would write, and TypeScript, since the components are TypeScript;
- it installs the registry's design system and wires it in: its configuration in
  `kirana.config.ts`, its reset beside Kirana's stylesheet, its styles on
  `<html>`.

To start from nothing, take one of Kirana's examples, as the release you run has
it:

```bash
npx @kirana-style/registry init --template vite-react my-app
```

The project it makes runs `kirana-style ui` by itself: `init` adds
`@kirana-style/registry` beside Kirana's other packages, each at the release you
ran, written as that exact version.

Start with a design by its preset code, which a design system's site gives you:

```bash
npx kirana-style ui init --preset k2bS6
```

Name the framework or the base when the project depends on more than one, or a
component has several:

```bash
npx kirana-style ui init --framework react --base aria
```

## Adding components

```bash
npx kirana-style ui add button dialog
```

Each component comes with the components it needs, in order. Its files land under
your alias for their type, `@/components/ui` for components by default, and its
icons are drawn with your icon library. The packages it needs are installed with
your package manager, and Kirana checks what was written before your next build.

`add` never changes a file you already have unless you pass `--overwrite`.
`--dry-run` shows what it would do.

## The lockfile

`kirana-style.lock.json` records each installed component: the registry it came
from, its version, the framework and base, and for each file two hashes. One is
of the registry's content, the other of what was written. Commit it.

The two hashes are how the later commands tell the registry's change from yours:

```bash
npx kirana-style ui outdated
npx kirana-style ui diff button
```

## Changing the design

A design system says which axes it has (a style, a base colour, a radius …) and
how a preset code holds them. Give a code to `init`, or change it later:

```bash
npx kirana-style ui preset k2bS6
```

`preset` writes the design to `ui.design` and sets its attributes on `<html>`,
where your design system's styles are. Then it places every installed component
again: a registry that flattened its style modules for the new design gives you
that build, with only the new style's values in it. A file you changed stops it
until you look, or pass `--overwrite`.

## Updating and removing

```bash
npx kirana-style ui update
```

`update` writes what the registry changed and keeps what you changed. Where both
of you changed the same file, it stops before writing anything: `ui diff` shows
the two sides, and `--overwrite` takes the registry's. A registry that changes a
component's files without a new version is refused.

```bash
npx kirana-style ui remove dialog
```

`remove` deletes the files you left as they were installed and keeps the ones you
changed. It refuses a component another installed one still needs.

## Your registries

Kirana UI's registry is known as `@kirana`. Name others in `kirana.config.ts`,
under [`ui.registries`](/docs/reference/config#ui), and install from them by
namespace:

```bash
npx kirana-style ui add @acme/card
```

[Publishing a registry](/docs/tooling/registries) describes the format, for
your own.
---
# Publishing a registry
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/tooling/registries
# Publishing a registry

A registry is static JSON anyone can host: one document per item at a URL that
holds the item's name, and an index. A project names it in `ui.registries`, and
`kirana-style ui` reads it as it reads Kirana UI's.

## An item

An item is one document, valid against
[its schema](https://kirana.style/schema/registry-item.json). Its style modules
are written once, for every framework, and its markup is given per framework and
base:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://kirana.style/schema/registry-item.json",
  "name": "button",
  "type": "component",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "registryDependencies": ["kit"],
  "styles": [
    {
      "path": "button.styles.ts",
      "type": "ui",
      "content": "…",
      "hash": "sha256-…"
    }
  ],
  "frameworks": {
    "react": {
      "base": {
        "files": [
          {
            "path": "button.tsx",
            "type": "ui",
            "content": "…",
            "hash": "sha256-…"
          }
        ],
        "dependencies": { "@base-ui/react": "^1.9.0" }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

List every framework and base the item supports, and only those. A base names
the packages and items only it needs beside its files.

## Files and imports

A file's `type` says where it installs:

| Type                                     | Installs                                     |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `ui`, `component`, `lib`, `hook`, `page` | under the project's alias for that type      |
| `file`                                   | at its own `target`, from the project's root |

Every file carries `hash`, the base64 SHA-256 of its content after `sha256-`.

A file names another installed file by the type and path the item lists it with:

```ts
import { axes } from "@/registry/lib/kit/axes"
```

Installation rewrites that to the project's alias, such as `@/lib/kit/axes`. A
component that draws an icon names it once for every library, as shadcn/ui's do:

```tsx
<IconPlaceholder
  lucide="ChevronDownIcon"
  tabler="IconChevronDown"
  hugeicons="ArrowDown01Icon"
/>
```

## A design system

An item of type `design-system` carries its wiring in `setup`, which
`kirana-style ui init` follows:

```json
"setup": {
  "config": { "module": "@/registry/lib/kit/config", "export": "kitConfig" },
  "stylesheets": ["@/registry/ui/reset.css"],
  "document": { "module": "@/registry/lib/kit/document", "export": "htmlStyles" }
}
```

What each entry is for:

| Entry         | What `init` does with it                                                   |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `config`      | spreads it into the project's `kirana.config.ts`                           |
| `stylesheets` | imports each where the project imports Kirana's stylesheet                 |
| `document`    | puts it on `<html>` as `sx`, or sets the classes from a static app's entry |

## Its design, and flattened builds

A design system also says, in `design`, what `kirana-style ui preset` reads: each
axis as the attribute it sets on `<html>`, with its values (the first the
default); the axis your registry flattens for; and the layouts of its preset
codes.

```json
"design": {
  "axes": {
    "style": { "attribute": "data-style", "values": ["nova", "vega"] },
    "radius": { "attribute": "data-radius", "values": ["default", "none"] }
  },
  "flatten": "style",
  "presets": {
    "k": [
      { "axis": "style", "values": ["nova", "vega"], "bits": 5 },
      { "axis": "radius", "values": ["default", "none"], "bits": 3 }
    ]
  }
}
```

A code is the layout's letter and a base-62 number holding one index per field,
from bit 0. Fields may also set `framework`, `base` and `iconLibrary`.

An item can carry its style modules flattened for each value of that axis and
each base, beside the modules as written. Installation takes the build for the
project's design, and the modules as written for a design you did not build:

```json
"flattened": {
  "axis": "style",
  "builds": {
    "vega": { "base": [{ "path": "button.styles.ts", "type": "ui", "content": "…", "hash": "sha256-…" }] }
  }
}
```

Build them with the checks that prove a flattened module renders what the module
as written does for that design: the installer takes them as they are.

## The index

The index is the item named `index`, valid against
[its schema](https://kirana.style/schema/registry-index.json): your registry's
name and each item's name, type, version and bases. `kirana-style ui search`
reads it.

## Checking

```bash
npx kirana-style ui validate public/r/button.json public/r/index.json
```

`validate` checks each document against its schema and each file's hash. Run it
in your registry's CI before you publish.
---
# What works today
Source: https://kirana.style/docs/project/status
# What works today

Kirana is on npm, at a 0.x version: before 1.0, a minor version may change the
API. It compiles three real applications in our shadcn/ui port (a demo, 60+
shadcn blocks and one page per component), and its own test suite keeps 100 %
line coverage. The [changelog](/changelog) lists every release.

## Built

- `css`, `cx`, `props`, `recipe`, `relation`, `select`, `keyframes`, `defineTokens`, `defineTheme`, `mode`, `firstThatWorks`, `positionTry`, `counterStyle`, `viewTransition`, `media`, `container` and `supports`
- The `sx` prop in React, Preact, Solid, Qwik, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Angular and Ember (as `[sx]` in Angular templates and the
  `sx` helper in Ember's); see [supported frameworks](/docs/frameworks/overview)
- Conditions: pseudo-classes, attributes, compounds, at-rules, nesting
- The precedence ladder, layers, and the ambiguity diagnostic
- Tokens: inlined, variable, per-mode, registered (`@property`)
- Themes and colour modes
